Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is Viktor Toth self-taught in physics? How did he do it?
Answer: I just came across this question. Thank you kindly for your interest. Yes, I am mostly self-taught. I had a good beginning. My high school was, and remains to this date, the leading high school in Hungary for mathematics. I won, or finished near the top in several national math championships. I then studied engineering, but I also worked with both engineers and physicists in the early days of the microcomputer revolution in Hungary, which was tremendously educational. I am proud of the fact that I am reasonably skilled with the soldering iron, too, and that gives me an appreciation for physics as the science of tangible, measurable things. My advice to others who wear the same shoes as I: Don't deceive yourself. Ignorance is not an excuse. Not having enough time is not an excuse. Yes, learning modern physics is hard. I'm still struggling with many concepts, and I expect to struggle until my last day on this Earth. I've seen too many smart people fall into the trap of, "I am ever so smart, if I cannot comprehend it without effort, it cannot be right" and I do not wish to follow their example. Don't try to rewrite, improve, or replace a theory just because you haven't taken the time and haven't made the effort to understand it thoroughly. When you live outside an academic environment, it is especially easy to fall into traps such as viewing yourself as a misunderstood genius who is shunned and rejected by the "establishment". Don't do this. As my example shows, the academic "establishment" won't reject you just because you are an outsider... but what you do has to make sense and your argument must be based on solid knowledge, not ignorance.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why does Victor Toth say that QM respect causality when Heisenberg said that quantum mechanics establishes the final failure of causality?
Answer: I presume that “Victor Toth” would be me. Why do I often stress that the equations of quantum mechanics or quantum field theory are causal? Because they are. There is not a hint of probability in the Schrödinger equation. There is not a hint of probability in the path integral formalism, or in field equations including operator-valued fields that obey the canonical commutation relation. There is not a hint of probability even in Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics. Which is to say, you redo the calculation a thousand times, you get the exact same deterministic result a thousand times. Probabilities and the breakdown of causality happen when we interpret these equations. The standard interpretation is that these equations determine the state of the quantum system and that moreover, that state is represented by a probability amplitude that in turn determines the probabilities of various observed outcomes. There is no escaping this: it is impossible to predict, for instance, in the two-slit experiment the precise location where an electron hits the fluorescent screen, we can only predict the statistical distribution of electrons. But why? There is a simple reason for this. The quantum system is governed by equations that represent quantities, some of which are not local and not observable. In classical physics, we can predict the outcome of an experiment with arbitrary accuracy if we can observe the initial conditions with arbitrary accuracy. In quantum physics, the initial conditions cannot be observed with arbitrary accuracy. But suppose, just suppose, for a moment that we indeed live in the famed “simulation”. And that the simulation accurately reflects our quantum reality. So this alien species builds this gigantic conventional computer that, however inefficiently and slowly, simulates our universe at the quantum level. So all of us in this universe would live in a quantum reality, with everything that it implies, including Bell’s theorem, probability amplitudes and all. One day these decide to build a backup. After all, we cannot have a major project without a backup! When the hardware is up and running, they momentarily pause the original simulation (we would not notice it of course since we would all be “paused” therein) and create a bitwise backup. Then they push the button and the original and the backup computer would continue running from the same initial state: a state that we, living in the simulation, cannot measure or access, but which is trivially accessible to the aliens who run the simulation. Well, guess what: Barring any hardware failures, the two simulations will never deviate from one another. They will, quite deterministically, evolve exactly the same way. We, living in the simulation, cannot predict the future with certainty; but the aliens’ computers nonetheless run as very predictable, very deterministic machines, no random number generators involved. In closing, however, I should mention that there is a minority view that contradicts what I described above: this is sometimes called the concept of “objective collapse”, which is to say, treating the concept of “wavefunction collapse” not as a mathematical abstraction, a mental aid, a simplification, but an actual, physical process. I don’t think “objective collapse” has any basis in reality, and I don’t think that it can even be developed self-consistently without creating an even bigger mess than the issues it intends to solve — doing away with the essential nonlocal nature of quantum mechanics — but if we accept the concept of “objective collapse” then probabilities rule, and causality is gone: my hypothetical aliens would need a real random number generator and their two simulations would diverge.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does a mass know in which direction to move in order to bend space-time?
Answer: A mass doesn’t “know” anything, it doesn’t need to move, and it doesn’t bend space-time. Other than that… Okay, allow me to explain. To be a source of gravitation, a mass does not need to move. The simple presence of mass (energy-momentum, to be precise) acts as a source of gravitation. Masses in the gravitational field of another mass do move, but in their case, the direction of motion is determined by the gravitational field itself: they accelerate in the direction of steepest change (i.e., “downward”). And no, mass does not bend spacetime. It is the source of the gravitational field. The gravitational field is “universal”, which means it affects everything the same way, no exceptions. As a consequence, it can be interpreted as a change in the geometry of spacetime. This interpretation can be helpful, can be useful, but only if we never forget that, interpretations notwithstanding, the gravitational field is just as physical a field as the electromagnetic field, e.g., carrying energy and momentum from place to place in the form of gravitational waves, just as the electromagnetic field carries energy and momentum from place to place in the form of electromagnetic waves (e.g., light). (As a reminder, Einstein himself cautioned us against taking the geometric interpretation too literally.) Lastly, even if we do interpret the gravitational field as geometry, we must keep in mind that it truly is spacetime geometry. So much so that, e.g., in the case of the gravitational field of the Earth, spatial curvature contributes only about one part in a billion. Or to put it differently, what we know as Newtonian gravity is due entirely to the rate at which clocks tick in a gravitational field; the relativistic correction due to spatial curvature is only a tiny, one-part-in-a-billion adjustment of the Newtonian value.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do black holes form in space and why are they not visible on Earth? Would their massive gravitational pull affect us on Earth?
Answer: Black holes form when very massive stars, having run out of fuel that would sustain a fusion reaction in their interior, collapse under their own gravity. Black holes are not visible from anywhere. Their defining property is that they are so compact, their surface gravity yields an escape velocity in excess of the vacuum speed of light. Viewed from the outside, the collapse seems eternal because the same extreme gravity causes also extreme time dilation, so the process never appears to reach its conclusion. Nonetheless, the black hole is so compact, no detectable light can escape it. So it truly is “black” in the sense that it emits no observable radiation. Its gravitational pull, however, is not any more “massive” than that of its progenitor star. Its gravity gets strong when you are near it, but only because you are near it; and the only reason you can get so near is because as a result of the collapse, it is very compact. For instance, if the Sun were to collapse into a black hole (it cannot — it is too small) its radius would be less than 3 kilometers. Contrast that with its actual radius, just a tad less than 700,000 km. So today, you cannot get closer to the center of the Sun than 700,000 km without hitting its surface. But you could get within 3 km of the “center” (it doesn’t really have one but that’s a story for another day) of a black hole of the same mass, and that close, its gravity would be about 50 billion times stronger even according to Newtonian physics. But the Earth? If the Sun were to collapse into a black hole, the Earth’s orbit would be unaffected. The Sun would vanish from the sky, no light escaping it anymore (not to mention that it just got a lot smaller!) but the gravitational field would remain exactly the same. Now consider that the nearest known black hole is roughly 100 million times as far away as the Sun, and that should tell you that we are quite safe: no, its gravitational pull does not affect us.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does only regular matter collapse into a black hole, or are dark matter and dark energy also pulled into it? Your recent reply to another question about destroying a black hole made the interior of one seem very similar to the early universe.
Answer: Gravity does not care what stuff is made of. Regular matter, dark matter (if it exists), it’s all the same for gravity. However, it is true that regular matter might collapse into a black hole more easily, as the standard model dark matter is supposed to be weakly interacting or not interacting at all. What it means in practice: when particles of regular matter collide, they can stick together: Their excess kinetic energy may be radiated away, e.g., as thermal photons. But non-interacting particles just fly through one another, without colliding or sticking. So regular matter can form growing clumps. This is much harder for non-interacting dark matter. But again, gravity does not care. A dark matter particle or a regular matter particle would meet exactly the same fate if captured by a black hole.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage?
Answer: Let me describe to you an imaginary journey into a classical black hole. ("Classical" in the sense that I am ignoring quantum effects, notably Hawking radiation, which might even prevent the black hole from forming in the first place. So let's say that you are not only in a very good spaceship, but you are also almost imprevious to extreme acceleration and extreme tidal forces. You hope into your spaceship, travel to the nearest collapsing sphere of matter that will ultimately form a black hole, and choose a trajectory that will end up in the black hole as well. If the collapsing matter has negligible pressure, its collapse will not be slowed down by any means. Yet to those on the outside, the process of the collapse will appear to slow as the cloud gets close to becoming a black hole. That is because of extreme gravitational time dilation: anything that happens near this collapsing cloud of matter will appear in slow motion to anyone far away. Not to you though. You will find that you will approach the surface of this collapsing cloud, but you won't quite be able to catch up with it. Meanwhile, however, as the gravitational field gets stronger, you will notice that what was a spherical surface below now appears to "curl up" on the sides. That is because of the gravitational deflection of light: many light rays that start off going upward will be bent downward, so they will appear to hit your eyeball from above! What was one a surface below begins to form a wall around you, and soon enough, it will feel like you are in a vertical tunnel, or well, its opening rapidly closing above you. Suppose you chicken out at the very last split second, punch a button, and with your Extremely Powerful Rocket [tm] you escape. Much to your surprise, you'll find that what has taken only a few seconds by your reckoning took a year outside. Or a thousand years. Or a quintillion years. This is why those on the outside can never be sure that the black hole even forms; no matter how long they wait, there's a chance that you re-emerge. It's only a question of how close you cut it before punching out. But what if you don't? Well, there will be a moment when the matter above your head closes up. There is no opening anymore. No walls really, either, as this is also the moment when you caught up with all the collapsing matter after all, so now you are inside the cloud. Inside a homogeneous (same everywhere) isotropic (no preferred direction) cloud of matter that forms a collapsing mini-universe, in which you are trapped. The moment when this happened is the event horizon. NOT a place. Not a location to which you can return. A moment — now a moment in the past — of time. So without a time machine, you are doomed. This mini-universe is a collapsing universe, the exact opposite of the kind of universe we seem to live in, outside of the black hole. Second by second, minute by minute it becomes denser. (Or millisecond by millisecond, if the collapsing cloud weighed "only" as much as, say, three times the mass of our Sun, or a million times the mass of the Earth.) Did I say same everywhere? Yes, I did. I meant it. There is no center, no edge of this cloud. This entire self-enclosed mini-universe is filled with matter everywhere. And you have very little time left. And perhaps that's when you recall something that you may have heard before in the past: The so-called "singularity" is not some center either. Rather, it is the moment in time when density, pressure, temperature, etc., everything in this mini-universe diverges, becomes infinite. The mini-universe ceases to exist (it's called geodesic incompleteness). Along with you, of course. Think this scenario through and now contemplate if it is even meaningful to talk about "destroying" a black hole. What exactly would that "destruction" do? Remember, to those on the outside, the black hole does not even exist yet, no matter how long they wait. Whereas for those on the inside, the black hole is the ONLY thing that exists, and its fate is sealed: soon enough everything, including time itself (!) comes to an end in this doomed mini-universe.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views?
Answer: Well, yes… but no. Allow me to explain. Or rather, allow me to begin my answer with a question: What do we call a “quantum computer”? Because the definitions, unfortunately, shift depending on who is offering the announcement of the day about yet another breakthrough, yet another declaration of “quantum supremacy”, or let’s face it, yet another request for research grants. So if money is no object, what can you buy that others might call a “quantum computer”? Well, you can certainly buy an experimental device that has a couple of qubits (the basic unit characterizing the capabilities of a quantum computer). You may get one for a few thousand dollars. Not very useful or practical, mind you, just an educational toy. If you have a lot more money, you can also buy a system (or more likely, have one custom-built for you) with more qubits, but apart from the sticker shock, be prepared for the need to set up a special facility to host, and support, the hardware. And in the end it, too, would amount to little more than an expensive educational toy, with no practical utility whatsoever. Or you can buy a system like D-wave’s quantum annealer, which is basically an analog computer that is particularly suitable for certain classes of optimization problems. But it is not a general purpose quantum computer. Which leads me to the answer I’d like to offer to my own question: a true, general purpose quantum computer is a scalable quantum computing machine. One that has as many qubits as I need, one that can be expanded with more qubits if necessary. This is not something that you can buy no matter how much dough you have, because it is not something that exists today, and may never exist in the future. Some compare the current state of quantum computing to the dawn of digital computers. But that is a false comparison. Sure, the Intel 4004 CPU was very primitive compared to its present-day counterparts. But the architecture was scalable. I could, in principle, build a circuit with a thousand 4004 CPUs. I could use bank switching and attach gigabytes of memory to a single 4004 CPU. Sure it would be damn inconvenient, cumbersome and very costly, but the system would work. There is no underlying physics principle that prohibits the existence of a million-CPU supercomputer with a terabyte of RAM, based on the 4004. It would be a darn stupid thing to build, but it can exist. This is not the case with quantum computing. You cannot add qubits galore, no matter how much money you have. The culprit is fundamental physics: the famous threshold theorem, in particular. The promise of general-purpose quantum computing is based on this theorem. You see, quantum computers are based on the premise that even though qubits have only two states when they are read, during the operation of the quantum computer it’s not those two states but their superposition, characterized by a continuous quantity (e.g., the phase of the wavefunction), that interacts with similar qubits in the system. The problem is that the qubits are not only entangled with each other, they also tend to get entangled with everything else in the universe. We try to keep the qubits as isolated from the environment as possible, to prevent environmental decoherence. This isolation is necessarily imperfect. But here is where the threshold theorem kicks in: If we can keep this decoherence below a certain threshold, there exist error correction algorithms that allow a system of qubits to emulate a perfect quantum computer with fewer qubits. The trouble is, this threshold has so far proven elusive. All those machines that I mentioned above, including cheaper commercially available units or pricier research installations? None of them are scalable. None of them beat the threshold theorem. Can the theorem be beaten? An entire industry, billions of dollars are wagered on that possibility. I am in a skeptical minority: I think it will prove to be a no-go theorem. Of course it is very possible that I am wrong. But until I see a credible announcement of a quantum computer architecture that beats the threshold theorem, my skepticism remains. So then, the answer to your question is that, well, yes, you can buy systems that are called “quantum computers” and they are not deceptive, you just need to know exactly what it is that they are selling. But no, you cannot buy a true, scalable general-purpose quantum computer because no such thing exists today.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How is mass not conserved when it's literally E^2-p^2, and both quantities are conserved?
Answer: The equation, m 2 = ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 , or simpler yet, using units such that c = 1 , m 2 = E 2 − p 2 , indeed describes the invariant rest mass of an isolated particle. However, it does not imply that rest mass is conserved in interactions. As a simple example, consider the collision of an electron and a positron. In the center-of-mass reference frame, their three-dimensional momenta are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction: p e = − p p where I used p to represent the 3-dimensional momentum vector. And of course both the electron and the positron have the same invariant rest mass m e . So before the collision, we have m 2 e = E 2 e − p 2 e , m 2 e = E 2 p − p 2 p , for the respective particles, from which we can also conclude that E e = E p = E (i.e., I dropped the superfluous index), so the total energy of the system is 2 E . The total momentum of the system is, of course p e + p p = 0 according to the rules of vector addition, and the total rest mass 2 m e . The collision annihilates the electron-positron pair, producing (usually) two photons. Energy and momentum are conserved. That means that the momenta of the two photons must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their vector sum is zero. And the total energy of the two photons is 2 E . This implies that each photon has energy E with a corresponding momentum of p = E / c in magnitude, pointing in opposite directions for the two photons. The rest mass, however, is now zero. As an aside, I would like to mention two more thoughts, not directly pertinent to what I just demonstrated, but food for thought, nonetheless. First of all, this reasoning can also inform you right away why an electron-positron pair cannot annihilate into a single photon. In the center-of-mass reference frame, the net momentum must be zero, both before and after; but the energy is nonzero. If the result of the annihilation was a single photon, it would have zero momentum but nonzero energy, which is not possible. Second, now that I demonstrated that the sum of rest masses is not invariant, allow me to offer a twist of the story. Imagine this whole thing took place inside a closed box. Both before and after, the respective particles (the electron-positron pair before the annihilation, the photons after) interact with the walls of the box that keep them confined. Well, guess what: the rest mass of the total system (measured, e.g., by measuring the force that is required to accelerate the box at a certain rate) remains unchanged throughout the process. Which is just a demonstration of the rather important point: namely that the rest mass of a system is equivalent to its internal energy-content. It does not matter what form that energy is in: kinetic energy, potential energy, even the rest masses of constituent bits. The rest mass of the box is the total internal energy of the box material and everything it encloses.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: We know that there is an equality between the active (MgA) and passive (MgP) gravitational mass for the same object, then on the moon for the same object should a reduction in MgP correspond to a reduction in MgA?
Answer: There is no reduction in gravitational mass, active or passive, on the Moon, Mars, in empty space, or anywhere else. An object’s rest mass (which also serves as its active/passive gravitational mass) is an intrinsic property that does not change at different locations. An object of a given mass weighs less on the Moon, but not because its mass changed, rather, because lunar gravity is weaker. The object’s mass remains the same. The force acting on it is reduced.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter?
Answer: Absolutely. In the context of cosmological physics, matter and antimatter are both “ordinary”, visible matter, made up of particles that interact with each other and with the electromagnetic field. Dark matter does not interact with the electromagnetic field (or if it does, it does so very, very, very weakly) and does not interact with normal matter (which includes antimatter). We don’t know what dark matter is (we cannot even be sure that it exists) but if there is such a thing, this is its defining characteristic. In contrast, antimatter very much interacts with normal matter. So much so, that this is how we know that even distant regions of the visible universe are dominated by normal matter, not antimatter. How do we know? Matter is everywhere, there are hydrogen atoms even in intergalactic space. If there were, e.g., distant galaxy clusters made of antimatter, the boundary region between antimatter and normal matter regions would “glow” in the gamma ray part of the spectrum from the occasional matter-antimatter interactions. Granted, in the very low density intergalactic medium, such collisions would be infrequent, but on the other hand, the volumes are ginormous, and the resulting gamma ray background would be observable.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Dumb question of the day: If we compressed a single gram of matter to the point of creating a black hole, would it sink to the Earth's core and eventually absorb the entire planet? What would happen, how would it progress and how long would it take?
Answer: Well, for starters, even if there was a known method to compress matter in such small quantities to densities far exceeding the density even in the interior of the densest neutron star, it would likely require energy far in excess of the 1 gram rest mass-energy of the matter that we started with. OK, so maybe we can start with 0.1 grams or whatever, so in the end, we create a 1 gram black hole after investing an insane amount of energy by a yet-to-be-discovered process. Well, that black hole would not last very long. It would release all its energy in 0.0000000000000000000000000465 seconds, give or take, mostly in the form of gamma radiation that would be at least ten orders of magnitude more energetic than the particle energies in the Large Hadron Collider. These gamma photons would of course be absorbed by whatever is nearby, resulting in extreme heat and ultimately a thermal explosion with a power comparable to that of the Hiroshima bomb. Kaboom! But suppose we got this all wrong and there is no Hawking radiation; so once created, our 1 gram black hole is eternal. It would indeed fall through the floor and… well, not so much sink as fall freely towards the center of the Earth, interacting only infrequently with the atoms it runs across during its journey. Why? Because it would be insanely, insanely small. Something like 15 orders of magnitude smaller than a proton. And its supposedly enormous gravity? Not that enormous if you think about it unless you get very, very, very close. You’d have to be within less than one tenth of a micron from this black hole to experience 1 g acceleration. Would this 1 gram black hole accrete matter? Yes, it would. I calculated its so-called Bondi accretion rate assuming it’s sinking in a nonrelativistic medium with a density ten times that of water and a speed of sound of 1000 m/s, which is probably not a gross misrepresentation of the Earth’s interior. Long story short, assuming I used my calculator correctly, it would take roughly 10 billion times the present age of the universe… for the 1 g black hole to double in size and become a 2 g black hole.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If black holes' horizons form infinitely far in the future, then how can they evaporate in finite time?
Answer: You stumbled upon a key potential contradiction between two things: But first: it is not the horizon that evaporates. Indeed, contrary to popular explanations (including Hawking’s own, from his popular science book) the actual equations tell a different story: Hawking radiation exists because the black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse and therefore, the past and the future boundary conditions are not identical. It is this difference that manifests itself in what distant observers see as outgoing radiation. (As an important aside, it should be mentioned that the characteristic wavelength of Hawking radiation is around 20 times the Schwarzschild radius. That alone should inform us that the horizon is not the source of that radiation.) So what does this mean? Do horizons never form? Maybe. Does a collapsing, evaporating black hole leave behind a “naked singularity”? Maybe. Does something else happen? Who knows, as the final moments of a black hole’s existence take place at the Planck scale, and we know nothing about the Planck scale, especially nothing about how gravity behaves at the Planck scale. The one thing we do know is that Hawking radiation is not predicated on the present-day existence of a horizon. If it were, there would be no Hawking radiation in the first place, since the horizon, even in classical general relativity, remains forever in any outside observer’s future.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible that our entire existence is contained within a black hole or space-time singularity without our knowledge of what lies outside of it?
Answer: No, it is not possible. Spacetime inside a black hole is a collapsing spacetime. To an observer stuck inside the black hole, it would appear quite the opposite to what we actually see in the cosmos: Instead of cosmic expansion, they would see cosmic contraction, with distant objects appearing at ever increasing blueshifts. The universe would be characterized by a future singularity, “the end of time”, characterized by divergent density and gravitational fields, and literally the end of time, geodetic incompleteness. As to the singularity itself, it is (apart from even more pathological versions) a moment in time, not a place, certainly not something you can can be “within”. Can you enter 5 PM next Tuesday and look around? It’s not a place. There is, however, one (speculative) possibility; The cosmos we see could be the interior of a time-reverse black hole, i.e., a white hole. A white hole is characterized by as past singularity (check) and, assuming matter is distributed within it more or less evenly, by the so-called Friedmann equations (check). But this is where spacetime geometry gets really tricky. The sentence “what lies outside of it” kind of suggests that there is a contemporaneous “inside” and “outside”. But that is not the way it works. Just as the event horizon of a black hole (and by extensions, everything within it) lies in the future of any and all observers outside of the black hole, the event horizon of a white hole (and anything within) lies in their past. Conversely, anything “outside” the white hole, from the perspective of someone inside the white hole, is part of the future. It has not happened yet. There is no contemporaneous “outside” where things happen outside our knowledge. Whatever exists outside is yet to happen, and will only happen, by our own reckoning, once we ourselves are “outside”. But the weirdest part perhaps is that we would not even know when that moment happens. Locally, crossing the event horizon is not in any which way special. There is no flash of light, no final message from a divine being to its creation, or any other indication that hey, “NOW” is the moment when you are no longer trapped inside a white hole! That day would look exactly like any other day. Yes, relativity is weird.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: After reading your answer to a question about mass and the Higgs field, I was wondering - why don't consider the 'rubber sheet' demo of gravity to be helpful?
Answer: There are several reasons, among them: I should add that I also speak from personal experience. I saw the rubber sheet analogy as a teen before I became familiar with the field equations of general relativity. Far from being helpful, the rubber sheet nonsense represented a obstacle to my understanding. It was not until I finally understood just how badly misleading this analogy is that I was finally able to make sense of Einstein’s field equations.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How can a quantum entanglement get broken?
Answer: Well, yes, but… maybe no. No, not trying to mock the question. Rather, I must call attention to the inadequacies of language. We use the expression, “broken”, which kind of implies that a special type of connection exists between a pair of entangled particles, and when it “breaks”, the connection is no longer there. But that is not how entanglement really works. For starters, everything is entangled with everything else all the time. So when we speak of “entanglement”, what we really mean is that we take a small system, say, a pair of particles and arrange it such that, at least temporarily, that pair is isolated from the environment as much as possible. So the pair, at least briefly and imperfectly, are only entangled with each other. What gets “broken”, then, is not the connection between the two, but their isolation from the environment. This is called “decoherence”: The nice, clean correlation between the behaviors of the entangled pair is now rudely contaminated, so to speak, with all kinds of random influences from, well, everything else in the rest of the universe.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can particles moving backwards in time leave a black hole?
Answer: Perhaps, if the following two conditions were true: These tachyons could indeed come back from the infinite future (again in the reference frame of outside observers) when the horizon forms, leaving the black hole. As far as we know, however, a) actual black holes have a finite lifespan due to Hawking-radiation, and b) tachyons do not exist (which is a Good Thing, otherwise our universe would not be causal, the future could directly impact the past.)

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why can't an observer just inside a supermassive black hole's event horizon escape if the gravity isn't strong enough at that point to tear him/her apart?
Answer: First, allow me to challenge your premise. To “tear him apart”, you don’t just need gravity; you need tidal forces, which is to say, differences in gravity. Tides happen because for instance, different parts of the Earth are different distances away from the Moon, therefore lunar gravity acts on them with different strengths. Take this to the extreme, and in the vicinity of a small black hole or a neutron star, the differences become so large, your head and your big toe will want to follow wildly different orbits… thus you get torn apart. Never mind that, you are right, in the case of a very large supermassive black hole, this does not happen. In that case, tidal forces remain weak near the event horizon. But then, it’s not tidal forces that prevent you from escaping. It’s the sheer strength of gravity, not how it varies from point to point. We can measure the force of gravity, in principle, by calculating how powerful your rocket would need to be in order to simply hover. To escape, you obviously need a rocket even more powerful than that. And guess what… at the horizon, you’d need an infinitely powerful rocket simply to hover. Yet… inside the horizon it’s not even this that prevents you from escaping. What this has to do with is not so much the strength of gravity but the nature of that event horizon. You see, so long as you are outside the horizon, the horizon remains forever in the future. At the “present” of any outside observer, the horizon will not have formed yet, no matter how long they wait. The only way for any observer to make the horizon happen is by crossing it. Otherwise, it remains forever an unattainable future moment in time. But once you cross it, something else happens. Now the horizon is part of your past. I repeat, it’s not a place that you can return to. It does not have a shape. It’s a past moment in time. To return to it, to escape, you no longer need a rocket: you now need a time machine. Which, when you think about it, makes perfect sense even from the outside observers’ perspective. Recall I mentioned that for them, the horizon remains forever in the future. So if you were to escape from the black hole, to an outside observer it would imply that you are coming back from that future. There we go again… time machine. To sum up: at the horizon, you need an infinitely powerful rocket just to hover. Beyond the horizon (which is a future moment in time until/unless you cross it, when it becomes part of your past) you would need a time machine to escape.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless?
Answer: Brian Greene’s “explanation” is one of many popularizations of physics that are intended to make difficult topics accessible to the “unwashed masses” but in reality, achieve the exact opposite. I would put it in the same basket in which I put the “rubber sheet” analogy of gravity, the “expanding balloon” description of cosmic expansion, even the “miniature solar system” models of the atom. Then I would put that basket out onto the curbside for collection. No, particles do not “burrow through” anything. If they “burrowed” through anything, that would mean a loss of kinetic energy through dissipative processes. Soon enough, everything would come to a halt, floating in some sticky molasses I suppose… But no, I swear, that is not how the Higgs works. Remember that mass is energy? No, mass is not “converted” into energy or vice versa. What we call inertial mass, or rest mass, is the internal energy-content of a thing. That’s what E = m c 2 is about, not about nuclear energy or converting anything into anything: It literally tells you that mass and (internal) energy are the same thing. Equivalent. Unsurprisingly, the equation itself is called the mass-energy equivalence relationship. In the Standard Model of particle physics, most particles start off as massless particles, but they interact with the Higgs field. However, the Higgs field has a very peculiar property. In empty space (i.e., the lowest energy state achievable, the vacuum) the Higgs field itself is not “empty”, so to speak. So particles can interact with it even when there’s supposedly nothing there. In effect, particles interact with the vacuum. Interaction means potential energy. (E.g., when two objects interact by, say, repelling one another, you need to invest energy to push them together, and that energy will be “stored” as their interaction energy while they are close to each other.) When an initially massless electron, for instance, interacts with the vacuum, it means it carries that interaction energy with it, no matter what it does or where it goes. And because the vacuum is everywhere, so to speak, the electron cannot get rid of that interaction energy. It’s always there. That interaction energy shows up, for all practical intents and purposes, as part of the energy-content of that electron. And as I stated above, energy-content means inertial mass. So the electron behaves as a massive particle, because no matter where it goes, what it does, it carries along that interaction energy with the vacuum Higgs field (to be more precise, the so-called vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v., of the Higgs field). So I stress, no “burrowing” is involved. The Higgs field has no rest frame, and how fast or how slow the particle moves with respect to this non-existent rest frame is irrelevant. In its own reference frame, a particle is always at rest. But it still has inertial mass, because the potential energy of its interaction with the Higgs field is there, no matter what.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What happens to an object that falls into a singularity? Does it turn into Hawking radiation or get crushed by gravity?
Answer: Okay, first of all, Hawking radiation is not about the singularity. It is about the collapsing matter that, in the far future, is supposed to form an event horizon that will hide a singularity (i.e., a moment in time even farther in the future of infalling objects, when they will cease to exist). Now there is a bit of a contradiction here, no doubt a reflection of the fact that the theory is incomplete, that Hawking radiation itself is a prediction of the “bastard child” of classical relativity and quantum field theory, called semiclassical gravity. But if we take the predictions literally… The event horizon is in the infinite future of any and all outside observers. In other words, when you follow infalling matter, no matter how long you wait, the process is reversible in principle; e.g., if one of the infalling “particles” happens to be an astronaut with an amazingly powerful rocket, he may turn around a year, a trillion years, 10 100 years from now and re-emerge, only seconds older as measured by his own clock. You can never be sure if he entered the horizon because no matter how long you wait, that moment remains in the future. This is at least what classical gravity theory predicts. But add quantum field theory, and we end up with Hawking radiation that results in the evaporation of the entire mass of the collapsing object in the form of thermal radiation in finite time. In other words, as seen by outside observers, all the collapsing mass (including our astronaut!) turns into Hawking radiation before the horizon can form. In this picture, our infalling astronaut would also encounter that Hawking radiation but at an accelerated rate as he approaches the (yet-to-form) horizon. The closer he gets to that horizon (which has not yet formed!) the more matter is lost, so the radius of the future horizon continues to shrink, eluding him. Even though he doesn’t reach the horizon, our astronaut is exposed to ever stronger tidal forces, and if he’s foolish enough not to put his rocket to use in time, he is eventually ripped apart by the famed “spaghettification” so yes, my bet would be that he turns into Hawking radiation without ever encountering the horizon, because the horizon ultimately never forms. But I am speculating. Informed speculation perhaps, but as I mentioned, ultimately we’re down to the dilemma caused by combining two theories that are not fully compatible: quantum field theory and a theory of gravity that stubbornly resists quantization (at least the “canonical” way).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do you know there is no speed of gravity?
Answer: For the same reason I know there is no speed of water. I look at a glass of water, and it’s perfectly still. I look at a fast-flowing river, and the water is moving, well, very fast. I look the icy moon Europa of the planet Jupiter, and I see tremendous quantities of water ice moving very, very fast around Jupiter. Or maybe not moving at all if I happened to stand on Europa’s icy surface? So what exactly is the speed of water? On the other hand, I do know, for instance, the speed at which certain influences travel in water. Though it is affected by things such as temperature or salinity, sound travels roughly 1.5 kilometers a second in water. That is true in the glass of water I hold in my hands, it is true in the rivers and oceans, it is even true on Europa. So then, gravity. A static gravitational field has no speed. Why would it? Speed measures change. There is no change when the field is static. However, if you are wondering how fast changes in the gravitational field travel, far from any specific source of gravitation: Why, it’s the same speed at which changes in the electromagnetic field travel, far from any sources (electric charges). It’s called the vacuum speed of light, light being the word we associate with a particular range of frequencies of electromagnetic waves, which also include radio waves, infrared and ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays. Similarly, changes in the gravitational field travel in the form of waves, and far away from sources (masses), those waves are transverse waves traveling at the same vacuum speed of light. But that is not the “speed of gravity” any more than the speed of light is the “speed of electromagnetism”. Forgive the pedantry here, but it is important to convey the correct impression: namely that speed is associated with the rate at which changes travel, the static field itself has no speed associated with it.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Has there been a mistake or intentional deception in the announcement of the discovery of the Higgs particle?
Answer: No, there is neither a mistake nor any signs of a deception. We’re talking about a discovery that was made over 12 years ago, and has been subjected to plenty of scrutiny since. A plot like this from the CMS experiment tells the story: What it tells us is that there is a slight bump at a specific energy level (approximately 125 GeV) in what appear to be the detections of correlated pairs of photons, and that this bump is consistent with what we would predict if we had a Higgs boson with a rest mass-energy of 125 GeV, decaying into a pair of photons. This is how particle physics experiments are made. Most subatomic particles are not detected directly, because they decay rapidly. However, we know what their decay products are supposed to be, and we can compare that against experiment. Before its discovery, we did not know the mass of the Higgs boson, and while certain mass ranges were excluded, estimates ranged wildly. However, once this bump was detected, things changed. The bump is not particularly significant visually, but it is very significant statistically. Of course just because there’s a bump, we cannot be certain if it is a bump due to the Higgs boson or perhaps something else. So refined experiments look at more specific properties and correlations. For instance, was the detected particle a true scalar (like the Higgs) or perhaps a composite particle that behaves like a so-called pseudoscalar? There were additional experiments that could distinguish between the two. Other hypotheses were also discarded. So now, 12 years later, I don’t think there’s any reason to doubt the validity of this discovery, any more than we might doubt, say, the discovery of the Z boson or the top quark. One question that may not be fully settled yet is whether or not the simplest, minimalist Higgs model is the valid model, or perhaps something more complicated. It would be interesting to see if we could detect a “triple Higgs” interaction, which is a Higgs boson splitting into two Higgs bosons (or equivalently, a Higgs boson emitting or absorbing another Higgs boson).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why did you disable the comments?
Answer: From my profile page: Regarding comments: When I was new to Quora, and knew nothing about this platform, in an abundance of caution I turned off every feature remotely related to spam or privacy, including comments. Since then, I contemplated turning comments back on, but unfortunately, while many comments are complimentary or offer helpful, constructive criticism, there are also the crackpots and trolls. Having to deal with them, even if it just means deleting the comment and blocking the person, would suck all the fun out of Quora for me. Given that the only reason why I am here is, well, to have fun (I enjoy reading, and learning from, insightful answers in topics about which I know little, but I also enjoy answering challenging questions in topics where I have expertise) I beg my readers’ forgiveness but comments will remain turned off on my answers for the time being. Thank you for your understanding. Yes, I understand that having comments disabled can be off-putting for some folks, and I apologize. By and large, however, seeing the nature of some of the comments that appear especially in response to popular physics answers, I find this less controversial than moderating comments, blocking people, or alternatively, leave my answers open to serve as platforms for Quora’s numerous cranks and crackpots. More importantly, folks who actually seek to help (as opposed to folks who merely want to use my answers to have their voices heard) never found it troublesome or beneath their dignity to contact me personally, and I can be quite grateful when they point out a mistake and give me a chance to correct my answers.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can you explain the Planck temperature? And at any point after the commencement of the 'Big Bang', did the temperature of the universe approach or equal the Plank temperature?
Answer: Can I explain the Planck temperature? Sure. It's a natural unit of temperature that we can use if we measure everything, including temperature, in units such that c = ℏ = G = 1. Of these equalities, c = 1 amounts to measuring time and distance in compatible units (say, 1 second vs. 1 light-second); ℏ = 1 amounts to measuring energy and frequency (inverse time) or wavenumber (inverse length) in compatible units. As for G , however, G = 1 amounts to setting a "natural" unit of energy relative to which everything else can be measured. If we have a natural unit of energy, we also have a corresponding natural unit of temperature, which coincides with a system in which individual degrees of freedom are associated with this energy. How fundamental is this natural unit? No one really knows. Planck units were first proposed more than a century ago by, you guessed it, Planck, but other than offering a "natural" system of units, do they have any physical significance? Many folks believe that our best theory of nature to date, quantum field theory, is only an "effective" theory, and that at the Planck scale, the theory breaks down. Others insist that at the Planck scale, quantum effects of gravitation become important. But these are speculative conjectures, not knowledge. The Planck scale is so many orders of magnitude beyond anything we can test experimentally or through astrophysical observations, we really have no idea how things truly work on that scale. So I suppose I lied. Maybe I cannot really explain the Planck temperature after all. Or the physical significance, if any, of any of the other Planck units. Other than that they serve as a sensible "natural" set of units in which it is easier to write down our equations. Same goes for times “after the commencement of the ‘Big Bang’”. The earliest we can go back to with any reasonable certainty of knowledge is about a picosecond after the ‘Big Bang’. But this time, the universe was many orders of magnitude colder than the Planck temperature. As to what happened before, whether even that picosecond was just a picosecond or an eternity, anyone can speculate, but no one knows. The so-called Planck epoch is much too far beyond what I’d even call “informed speculation”.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can you compare the gravitational constant to the speed of light? We don't know why it has magnitude, but it is just a fundamental property of the universe.
Answer: Not directly, but the reasons are much more subtle than you might think. There are some fundamental constants in Nature that are just ratios. Perhaps the most well-known is the fine structure constant, α ≃ 1 / 137.036 , that characterizes the strength of the electromagnetic interaction. It is a dimensionless quantity, which is to say its value is what it is, independent of whatever system of units we use to measure length, time, mass, electric charge and whatnot. The so-called Standard Model of particle physics has 18 such dimensionless parameters. Its popular extensions, which account for, e.g., neutrino masses, may have as many as 26 in total. However, the gravitational constant G , the vacuum speed of light c , and the (reduced) Planck constant ℏ are not among them. Why, you may wonder? Because these are not dimensionless constants, that's why. For starters, the vacuum speed of light is, well, a speed: its dimensions are length divided by time. Its value depends on what we choose as our standard for length vs. time. Although the definitions were changed and refined over time, they are entirely cultural artifacts: In the case of our most commonly used system, the units for both length and time were originally derived from the properties (circumference and rate of rotation) of a random planet in this universe, the planet we happen to call our own. This also implies that we can always drop our conventional definitions and just use c = 1 , i.e., use compatible units for length and time (effectively eliminating one in favor of the other, e.g., measure time in seconds and distance in light-seconds). Why don't we? Again, the reasons are cultural: they have to do with convention and convenience. Fundamentally it's no different from, say, pilots' choice to use incompatible units, namely nautical miles for horizontal distance and feet for vertical distance (altitude). What ultimately matters is not how the units are defined but the geometry they measure. The vacuum speed of light is no different; on its own, it has no real meaning. What has meaning is when we compare other speeds against this fundamental speed. If we can do this with the vacuum speed of light, how about the other two constants? The reduced Planck constant has units of energy times time. Or energy divided by frequency (inverse time). Again, it's a ratio. We can set ℏ = 1 by using suitable units, again effectively eliminating unnecessary units: we can now measure everything using variations of the unit of energy. And once again, the actual magnitude of ℏ does not matter; what matters is the ratio of other things measured against this quantity. But now we move on to the gravitational constant G and things change. Having fixed c = 1 and ℏ = 1 (and eliminating the units of length and time in the process, measuring everything in units of energy), we run into something weird. Yes, we can still fix G = 1 by a suitable choice for the fundamental unit of energy. But we find that unlike c and ℏ , G will not be dimensionless. It's not a ratio of two things. It will have the dimensions of inverse energy squared. This, as a matter of fact, is one of the fundamental reasons why naive attempts to quantize the theory of gravitation are doomed to fail. A coupling constant with negative energy dimensions yields a theory with untameable infinities that cannot be "renormalized". Whether this makes G more or less fundamental than, say, c , I don't know. There is a secret here that is yet to be uncovered by physics.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation?
Answer: I suspect that this question was at least inspired by the popular, but fundamentally misleading “explanation” that Hawking radiation is about the creation of virtual particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon, one of which is swallowed by the horizon, while the other is released as a “real” particle. This explanation, though it first appeared I believe in Hawking’s own popular science book, is nonetheless nonsensical, in direct contradiction with Hawking’s own 1974 paper (Nature 248 (5443)), which explains how gravitational vacuum polarization, along with the past-future asymmetry of a system in a perpetual state of collapse, leads to a net outgoing radiation. But I suspect there is also a misunderstanding here concerning the nature of particles, be they real or virtual, in the context of quantum field theory. Take the electromagnetic field. The classical theory is Maxwell’s: it’s a field theory, which is to say, it describes something that is present everywhere, with a continuously varying value from point to point in space and time. This field may be sourced by electric charges. If charges are absent, the field equations can still have nonzero solutions, which are in the form of plane waves traveling at constant velocity (the velocity that we know as the vacuum speed of light). When it comes to the quantum theory, we start with decomposing the field into elementary frequencies, kind of like how a sound can be decomposed into elementary pure sounds of different pitch. Each of these pure waves can be treated as a “harmonic oscillator”, which, in the quantum theory, has discrete levels of energy. It is these discrete levels, or packets, of energy that will be the field quanta, and it is these quanta that we perceive, under the right circumstances, as particles. When we write down the equations of fields, especially interacting fields, the equations include nasty summations (integrals) of ever more complicated interactions. As a mental aid, however, we can think of these interactions in terms of one unit, one quantum at a time, and even use neat little diagrams (the Feynman diagrams) as a bookkeeping device, keeping track of these terms. The arrows in that Feynman diagram are suggestive of particle-like behavior. Even though no actual particles are involved, it can sometimes be helpful to intuit these interactions as exchanges of “virtual particles”. Unfortunately intuition in particle physics is a dangerous business. Helpful, yes, but do not forget for a moment that these are merely bookkeeping devices. There are no miniature cannonballs, virtual or otherwise. Only interacting fields. The “particle” aspect is entirely imaginary, existing only in our heads, as a clumsy mental aid to help our limited intuition. That’s what “virtual” really means.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What would happen if something went through a black hole?
Answer: What would happen if something went through a black hole? Well, I’d say it’d be proof that time travel exists, and perhaps the television series Dr. Who is not a science-fiction show but a documentary. You see, the event horizon of a black hole is not something that is here, now, which you can go “through”. The event horizon of a black hole is a moment in time. In fact, so long as you are outside of that event horizon, it forever remains a future moment in time. And if you reach the horizon to get “inside” the black hole, the horizon becomes a past moment in time for you. So to go “through” a black hole (which is to say, enter the black hole and then re-emerge, in the finite future of any outside observer), you’d have to travel backwards in time. Kind of hard to do without a time machine like the aforementioned Dr. Who’s fames TARDIS.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: I’m confuzed, I know that black holes are made in space, but why can’t they be made on earth?
Answer: The only known mechanism by which black holes are created is gravitational collapse. The smallest amount of matter that can collapse into a black hole, its self-gravity overcoming pressure, is roughly three times the mass of the Sun. In other words, about a million Earths. You might as well ask why you can’t have an ant carry an elephant on its back.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Which is closer to realization, quantum computing, or fusion power? (by "realization" I mean results and mass implementation.)
Answer: Since I was asked… It might be my ignorance speaking, but I remain immensely skeptical about both. First, let me tell you something about fusion power. Or rather, let me quote a few sentences from a book on my bookshelf. “At the beginning of the 1950s, it seemed that success is not far away. But later, difficulties arose one after another […] To date, more than a hundred different models have been devised […] … When will the first fusion power plants be realized, when will the investigation of controlled nuclear fusion exit the constraints of laboratory experiments? According to Professor Igor Golovin, the world-renowned expert on thermonuclear research, it will be possible to develop Tokamak devices into electricity-producing equipment by the last decade of our century. L. Hirsch, one of the leading physicists of the American Atomic Energy Commission is a little more cautious. According to him the path from the first experiments to the worldwide spread of fusion power plants is longer, and we’re lucky if they will enter the world’s energy production market in fifty years.” I am sure the language sounds familiar. But here is the thing: What I just quoted is text from a book published in 1972. It was titled “Boys’ Almanac, 1973”, published in the Hungarian language (translation mine), a Christmas gift I received from my parents in 1972. Here is the thing about fusion. The only reliable known method of confinement — keeping light atoms hot enough yet close enough to one another to ensure that the undergo fusion at a decent rate — is called gravitational confinement, and requires the weight of an entire star like the Sun. And even deep in the solar interior, fusion remains very inefficient: It produces no more than a few hundred watts of power per cubic meter, which is no ore than what comes out of a well-maintained compost pile. Why is the Sun so hot then? Because it’s big. There are a ginormous number of cubic meters in its interior. That is a luxury we are not afforded here on the surface of the Earth. We don’t have a hundred thousand Earths worth of hydrogen and the room to store it. Rather, for a practical fusion power plant, we’d need something like several hundred megawatts per cubic meter. And we do not have gravitational confinement, so we have to devise all sorts of strange means, lasers, magnetic fields, you name it, to keep the plasma stable. But we also want to remove thermal energy efficiently, in order to use it, e.g., to drive a steam turbine and turn it into electricity. Except that in the case of fusion, temperatures are so high, most of that thermal energy appears in the form of gamma rays. Long story short, despite claimed successes, I remain extremely skeptical that fusion power will ever become useful as a practical, industrial-scale source of electricity. Now on to quantum computing. Don’t let the magical properties of the word, “quantum”, dazzle you. The basic premise is far simpler. It’s about digital vs. analog computing. A digital computer operates, well, on digits: 1, -23, 3.14159265359. An analog computer does not use digits but continuous quantities, such as a length, a voltage, an electric current, to represent quantities. For instance, an analog computer can add two numbers by combining two currents together and then reading off the result from the scale of an ammeter. There are certain mathematical problems that are difficult to solve on a digital computer. A good example is finding the factors of a very large number. Factorizing a 1000-digit number is beyond the capabilities of any digital computer now, or in the foreseeable future. Yet we know that far more efficient factorization algorithms exist for analog computers. The problem is that analog computers are very inaccurate. Try reading the needle of that ammeter with a precision of one part on a thousand. How about one part in a million? Quantum computers are fundamentally like analog computers. A “qubit” may have two “eigenstates” but its actual state is determined by the phase of its wavefunction, which is a continuous, analog quantity. When qubits interact in a quantum computer, it’s these analog quantities that interact. Again, analog computers are imprecise, and quantum computers are no exception. In fact, they are plagued by interactions with the environment (decoherence) which “collapses” qubits to those binary eigenstates. However, there exists an intriguing theorem, the threshold theorem: if a quantum computer can keep its error rate below a certain threshold, there exist error correction methods that allow it to emulate a “perfect” quantum computer. There, you have it. A perfect quantum computer is scalable (more qubits can be added without destroying its perfect-ness) and it can solve certain families of problems in ways digital computers cannot. But is this threshold achievable? Billions of dollars are wagered on that promise. Yet I am skeptical. Moreover, simply achieving the threshold is not enough; the number of qubits for error correction might still be excessive an impractical. So we need to do significantly better. In any case, I suspect (I emphasize: I do not know, this is my personal speculation) that the threshold theorem will be shown to be a “no go” theorem, someone cleverer and I proving through rigorous mathematics that the threshold is not achievable in principle. In any case, the threshold has not been achieved yet. Everything you see about quantum computing, all those claims of successes, “quantum supremacy” and whatnot, are basically side quests: the main quest remains unresolved.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is the observer effect in quantum mechanics a legitimate phenomena? What about the fact that before observers even existed the universe existed. We come from the universe causally but obsevers are only relatively recent.
Answer: Well, yes, but let’s define what an “observer” is in our description of quantum physics. We recognize that a quantum mechanical system is characterized not by numbers representing its positions, momenta, or other properties, but by “states”. These “states” can map into numbers when the quantum mechanical system interacts with an “instrument”. What that “instrument” is, doesn’t really matter, except that it is “classical”: its properties, such as its positions, momenta, etc., are all described by numbers as in classical physics. When a quantum system comes into contact with such an instrument, some of its parameters are briefly confined to numerical values (so-called eigenvalues). This is the most counterintuitive aspect of quantum physics: It can be “interpreted” either as a discontinuous (and retroactive!) “collapse” of the system’s state to the observed value, or we may choose to accept that the present-day evolution of the state of a quantum system is influenced (albeit in a way that has no observable consequences) by the system’s future encounter with the “instrument” so that it acquires the observed value in quantum mechanical (so-called “unitary”) evolution. This encounter with instruments is what counts as an “observation” in quantum physics. The instrument is the “observer”. Note that it does not imply sentience, consciousness, or anything of the sort. For all we know, the “observer” is just a brick. Moreover, we must keep in mind that such instruments exist only as mathematical idealizations. Actual bricks (or cats, or people, or electronics) are made up of a large but finite number of quantum particles, so while their quantum behavior is averaged out (they are “almost” perfectly classical things “almost” all the time) it’s not completely absent. In short, when you read the word “observer” in the quantum mechanical context, always keep in mind that for all you know, that “observer” is a dumb piece of a brick. Do not read more into the word than that.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: We know that gravity can affect light. Does light ever have any effect on gravity?
Answer: Indeed, light having energy-momentum, it can be a source of gravitation. Let me offer three examples. In some very large, very heavy, very hot stars, there is a significant quantity of trapped radiation, a “photon gas” trapped in the star’s interior. This contributes to the overall mass-energy of the star, hence its gravitation. In the early universe, during the so-called “radiation-dominated era”, light contributed more energy-momentum than ordinary matter, and thus the evolution of the expanding cosmos was primarily governed by this photon gas. This was long before the universe became transparent to light, so this trapped light was heavily interacting with matter, but nonetheless, it was the dominant source of gravitation. Some folks speculated about objects made up purely of electromagnetic waves, yet dense enough to turn into black holes. These balls of light, or “Kugelblitz” (German for ball lightning) probably don’t exist (in fact I recall reading some papers recently that argued that such objects cannot possibly form) yet they still represent a theoretical construct in which light serves as a compact source of gravitation, and remains trapped by its own gravity.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Are frames of reference in relativity examples of charts on a manifold? Thus, are Lorentz transformations maps between charts?
Answer: A chart on a manifold is a set of coordinates that covers all, or part, of a manifold. (In fact, a manifold is defined as a point set that can be covered by a finite number of finite-dimensional charts, each consisting of n-tuplets of real numbers.) A frame of reference, in turn, is associated with a specific observer. In special relativity, we can represent an inertial observer’s frame of reference with, e.g., a Cartesian coordinate chart with the observer at its spatial origin. Such a chart would cover the entirety of Minkowski spacetime. However, once we allow for accelerating observers, or worse yet, for the presence of gravitational fields, there is no longer a unique chart that we can associate with the observer. We can, however, associate with the observer a rigid frame of reference (sometimes described by the German word “vierbein” or, more generally, not restricted to four dimensions, “vielbein”) but these rigid frames are “nonholonomic”, which is to say, they do not provide a unique coordinate representation of curved spacetime in the observer’s vicinity. The (global) Lorentz transformation is a transformation between inertial coordinate systems in Minkowski spacetime. This can be generalized to curved spacetime but only as a “local” transformation with the transformation’s parameters varying from point to point.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If neutrinos always pass through everything, then how can it have any mass without interacting with the Higgs field?
Answer: First of all, neutrinos do not always pass through everything; they almost always pass through almost everything, but that “almost” makes a lot of difference. This is why neutrinos are detectable. This is also why neutrinos, when they are present in insanely large numbers and encounter very dense stellar matter, contribute a great deal when, e.g., a supernova explosion unfolds. As to the origin of the neutrino mass, in our best models to date neutrinos are one of the exceptions: Their mass is not due to the Higgs mechanism. Neutrino mass is weird. For neutrinos, mass eigenstates (when the mass is a well-defined number) and flavor eigenstates (when the flavor, or type, of the neutrino is well-defined) do not coincide. Confining a neutrino’s flavor by measurement makes its mass indeterminate and vice versa. This is accounted for not by the Higgs mechanism, but by what is known as a “mass mixing matrix”, the so-called PMNS (Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata) matrix. The manner in which this matrix is introduced into the theory is independent of the Higgs field. In any case, this has nothing to do with the fact that neutrinos have no electric or color (strong force) charge, so they interact only through the “weak” interaction: an interaction that is just as strong at short range as electromagnetism, but mediated by very massive particles which means that the interaction is extremely short range, making it effectively weak (i.e., a neutrino very rarely gets close enough to another particle to be influenced by it).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What are the 'rays' (not animals), or 'beams of radiation' that are not ElectroMagnetic radiation?
Answer: In the context of radioactivity, historically there have been three types of radiation considered, only one of which is electromagnetic: Speaking of electromagnetic radiation, radio waves including microwaves (yes, in your microwave oven), infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic radiation. (I listed them in the order of increasing frequency, which means increasing energy, decreasing wavelength. It’s these categories that people think about when they mention the “electromagnetic spectrum”.) After the alpha-beta-gamma categories were established, it was recognized that some radioactive elements emitted electrically neutral neutrons, so that’s another form of non-electromagnetic radiation. Then there are neutrinos, emitted, e.g., by nuclear reactors; they interact very weakly, so they are almost undetectable, although in stellar catastrophes, supernova explosions, an incredible neutrino flux plays a major role in how these astronomical explosions unfold. And there are also gravitational waves, including those that we detected, emitted during the final moments of black hole and neutron star mergers. Again, not electromagnetic.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How is the speed of gravity determined?
Answer: First of all, while I recognize that this is a bit of semantics, there is no “speed of gravity” any more than there is a “speed of electromagnetism”. Gravity is an interaction, it does not have an inherent speed. However, influences in the gravitational field, far from sources, travel as transverse waves, and these indeed do have a speed. Theory tells us that this speed is the same as the speed of influences in the electromagnetic field, i.e., electromagnetic waves such as light. While few had real doubts that this prediction is valid, its first observational test came seven years ago with the LIGO event GW170817. This gravitational wave event turned out to be the collision and merger of a pair of neutron stars, an event that was also detectable in a multitude of electromagnetic frequencies. The electromagnetic and gravitational signals arrived at the same time, even though they event took place some 130 million light years from here. This tells us that indeed, gravitational and electromagnetic waves traveled at the same speed. As a matter of fact, this had a direct impact on theory. There are proposed alternative theories of gravitation in which there is not one but two (or more) metrical fields, one determining the speed of gravitational waves, the other, the speed of electromagnetic waves. These “bimetric” theories were essentially falsified by the GW170817 observation.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the current understanding of dark energy using general relativity? Can GR provide any insights into the nature of this mysterious phenomenon in our universe?
Answer: To answer this question, I must first point out a very important fact: General relativity is not a theory of matter. It is a theory of gravitation. Insofar as matter is concerned, general relativity simply states that matter “couples universally and minimally” to the gravitational field: in technical terms, this is written as T μ ν = − ( 2 / √ − g ) δ S m / δ g μ ν , which is a mathematical equation that essentially tells us that the stress-energy-momentum of matter serves as the source of the gravitational field. But as to what that matter is, on that subject general relativity remains silent. That is not to say that we cannot speculate about the nature of matter. In particular, we often postulate that matter, whatever it is made of, behaves on large scales as an “isotropic perfect fluid”: that is to say, a medium entirely characterized by its density and pressure. (There is no directionality, no stresses, no viscosity, just density and pressure). A perfect fluid is easily characterized then by the ratio of its pressure and its energy density. In any sensible system of units, these two quantities are measured using the same units. Energy is force time distance, volume is area times distance, therefore energy density: energy divided by volume, is the same as pressure: force divided by area. Which means that the ratio of these two quantities is a pure number, not dependent on the choice of units. This number is zero for stuff with no pressure (sometimes called “dust”). It’s very close to zero for most “normal” matter. For a relativistic gas (gas so hot, its particles move around at nearly the speed of light) the ratio is 1/3. But really, a perfect fluid makes sense with that ratio being anywhere between -1 (yes, negative pressure) and +1. (Less than -1 means an unstable cosmos, more than +1 means a medium in which sound travels faster than light.) The rest is easy, so to speak. When we look at astronomical observations on cosmological scales, we find that the data can be modeled using general relativity if the universe is made up of 30% “dust” and 70% stuff with the aforementioned ratio being -1. We call this perfect fluid “dark energy”. Of the 30% dust, about 4% is “normal” matter (not exactly dust, but close, as most normal matter is not relativistic). The rest is “dark matter”. We have no idea what “dark matter” and “dark energy” are, although there are many proposals. The only thing we know about them is that they are, well, “dark” although “transparent” might be closer to the truth: They do not interact with (emit, absorb, block or reflect) light, indeed they do not interact with matter at all (or if they do, they do so very, very weakly). That’s all we really know about this “dark” stuff. Everything else is conjecture, since none of this “dark” stuff has ever been observed. And it is of course still eminently possible that none of this “dark” stuff exists, but rather, our theories are on the wrong track. In any case, the answer, if it comes, won’t come from general relativity. It will either be in a form that modifies general relativity (and does away with the need for “dark” things) or in a form of a better theory of matter, hopefully one with directly testable predictions so that it can be validated by observation.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible that centrifugal force is caused by a curvature of spacetime?
Answer: In the context of general relativity, the gravitational force and the centrifugal force have many similarities. Basically, both forces can be viewed as “pseudoforces” that arise in non-inertial reference frames. And both can be accounted for using the same mathematical machinery of covariant derivatives, Christoffel-symbols and the whole kaboodle. However, there is a crucial difference. In the case of the centrifugal force, spacetime curvature is zero. The pseudoforce arises because we are measuring it in a noninertial (rotating) reference frame. In contrast, in the case of gravity, spacetime curvature is not zero. There is no global coordinate transformation that can remove the effects of gravitation. Locally it is always possible to define inertial (freely falling) reference frames, but there is no “global family of inertial observers” who are at rest, or moving at uniform velocity, relative to each other. Another way of looking at it is this: There is a crucial distinction between the use of a curvilinear coordinate system (such as the coordinate system of a rotating reference frame) in flat spacetime, vs. curved spacetime, even though the mathematical tools that we can use to investigate them are the same.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the reason that quantum physics cannot be applied to curved spacetime?
Answer: Who told you that quantum physics cannot be applied to curved spacetime? Here’s the cover of one of the books from my bookshelf: It’s just one of several. As the title of the book suggests, we know how to do quantum field theory in curved spacetime. There are intricate nuances, to be sure, but the basic principles are sound and the theory works. Of course I recognize that you were probably told many times that gravity and the quantum theory do not mix, and this is the reason why a “theory of everything” remains elusive. But that is not entirely true. As these books imply, we can do quantum theory in the presence of gravity. The tricky part is introducing quantum matter as a source of gravitation. Einstein’s field equations connect the gravitational field and matter.
