In the quantum theory, the quantity representing matter (the so-called stress-energy-momentum tensor) is expressed using things that are… well, not numbers. The gravitational field in Einstein’s theory is, however, represented by numbers. So suddenly the equation turns into a “how many apples does it take to make an orange?” kind of a question. How can we resolve this? Well, there are two fundamental directions: Either use a classical representation of matter in Einstein’s field equations or turn gravity into a quantum theory. The former is called semiclassical gravity. The latter? Well, that’s where the problems begin: a naive quantization of gravity produces infinities that ruin the theory. In some quantum field theories, these infinities can be avoided using consistent mathematics. Not so in the case of gravity. So simple quantization does not work. That is not to say that we don’t have other ideas. Ideas that can be made to work, as a matter of fact. But here is where the real problem hits us: We have no experimental or observational data. Gravity is so weak, its quantum effects will likely never be observable directly. Indirect observation might be possible, but so far, nobody knows how. So we are literally clueless: Nature offers no clues as to which direction to take. Shouldn’t we be clever enough to figure it out nonetheless? It’s important to remember that the number of times humans have been able to figure something out about Nature without using observation or experiment as clues is… well, as far as I know, precisely zero. We may be clever monkeys, but we are not that clever. Without observational evidence, we don’t know which direction we should pursue. The one thing I can tell you is that semiclassical gravity (treating gravity as classical and the “average”, so-called expectation value of quantum matter as its source) works in each and every case that is accessible to us by way of experiment or observation.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does the fact we cannot reconcile relativity or classical mechanics with quantum mechanics suggest we might never be capable of developing a theory of everything? If so, does that imply physics (and science) cannot fully explain the universe?
Answer: What makes you think that we cannot reconcile classical mechanics with the quantum theory? It is reconciled just fine. The quantum theory builds upon classical mechanics (the Hamiltonian formalism). It refines it by recognizing, as valid states, states of a system that make no sense classically. However, classical mechanics re-emerges just fine in the limit of systems with a very large number of degrees of freedom or, alternatively, in the mathematical exercise of taking the Planck constant to zero. Special relativity is also doing perfectly fine with the quantum theory; quantum field theory, the foundational theory behind the Standard Model of particle physics, is fully relativistic. In fact, we can do quantum field theory even on the curved background of classical general relativity. Where things go awry is when we consider quantum matter as the source of classical gravitation. But here, an important statement is in order. It’s not that we don’t have perfectly sensible schemes to reconcile quantum matter and classical gravitation, either by quantizing gravitation or by taking the “semiclassical” approach of a hybrid theory. The fact that canonical quantization leads to a nonrenormalizable quantum theory of gravity is an issue but again, proposals abound as to how we might be able to overcome this obstacle. No, the real problem is not the lack of ideas. It’s the lack of data. Gravity is extremely, extremely weak. Direct detection of gravitons (assuming they exist) will likely never happen. Indirect detection of quantized effects of gravitation just might be possible, but I would not hold my breath. So here we are, without any real clues from Nature as to which direction to take. So it’s not so much that we cannot develop a theory of everything; rather, it’s that absent tangible clues, we simply don’t know which possible theory of everything to pick!

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Are ANY particles "real"? Or is every particle a excitation of some QCD field? Are protons therefore, excitations in a quark-gluon field? What about neutrinos?
Answer: Yes, all elementary particles are excitations of the corresponding quantum fields. (Composite particles, like the proton, are bound states of such excitations.) But ultimately, what is “real” and what is not “real” is a metaphysical question. So let’s start with a practical definition: Something is “real” if two observers agree on it, regardless of their own motion. For instance, absolute motion is not “real”: to an observer moving along with the object, the object will appear motionless. But relative motion is “real”: If one observer sees two objects moving at different speeds and/or in different directions, all other observers will see the same. The actual values will be observer-dependent, but no observer will see these two objects as not moving relative to each other. So in this vein, are particles real? Perhaps not. The particle-content that an observer sees may depend on that observer’s motion. An observer who is accelerating in an otherwise empty universe will see Unruh radiation, photons arriving from the apparent (Rindler) horizon that characterizes his acceleration. An inertial observer will see no Unruh radiation. Actually, the picture gets more complicated, since in order to actually “see” that Unruh radiation, the observer must interact with the electromagnetic field, which ultimately involves charges, so the inertial observer now sees the accelerating observer carrying accelerating charges and thus producing electromagnetic radiation… The devil is in the details, but the end result is that the two observers’ observed particle content is not the same. On a tad more technical level, it boils down to decomposing fields using a Fourier transform. What is the basis for that transform? The decomposition is not unique when accelerating reference frames are permitted. Decompositions with respect to different reference frames correspond to different descriptions of the same field in terms of particle-content. Having said that… as I said, “real” is in the eye of the beholder. When an electron hits the fluorescent screen of an old school CRT causing a flash of light that we see… how can we possibly say that this electron is not “real”? We may know that it is “only” an excitation of the electron field, and that a rapidly accelerating observer nearby might see, e.g., additional electron-positron pairs that we don’t see, but so what? The screen flashed. That’s an event. And ultimately, events are “real”, however they are interpreted in different observer reference frames, with whatever particle content might be associated with the event in these frames.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why doesn’t the Higgs field impart mass to a stationary photon? Is it theHiggs field that gives the photon mass while it is moving?
Answer: The answer is… a tad complicated. The Higgs field imparts mass on certain particles indirectly through two distinct mechanisms, both of which are linked to a fundamental property of the Higgs field: Its self-interaction potential. Without going into details, for most fields, the lowest-energy state is when the field is free of excitations. For instance, the electromagnetic field is in its lowest-energy state when there are no photons (which are the excitation quanta of the electromagnetic field). Not the Higgs field. Its lowest energy state is when some excitations are present. This is what is expressed through the famous “Mexican hat” potential that are sometimes shown in popular science publications. What this means in practice is that the “vacuum” in which the Higgs field is free of excitations is not really the vacuum: It can decay into a lower-energy state, in which the Higgs field has some excitations. This lowest energy state is what we know as the vacuum. This has two consequences. First, the Higgs field interacts with certain particles (charged fermions) directly. This means that in this new, lowest-energy vacuum, the nonzero excitations (nonzero vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v.) of the Higgs field interacts with those fermions (electrons, quarks, etc.) An interaction means energy, energy means mass… so those fermions, which were initially massless in the theory, now behave as though they had mass all along, carrying this interaction mass-energy as their rest mass. There is another class of particles, vector bosons, which mediate what is known as the “electroweak” force: a unification of the electromagnetic and weak forces. There are four such vector bosons, and they form a particular symmetry group that combines three of the four, while the remaining one has its own, different symmetry group. When the Higgs field leads us to that new, lower-energy vacuum state that I described earlier, the symmetry group of the three vector bosons gets broken. In practice, this manifests itself in the form of interactions that, again, show up as rest mass-energy for these three vector bosons (these are the bosons of what we know as the weak interaction, namely the Z, W+ and W- bosons). However, the photon is unaffected by this symmetry breaking. Higgs or no Higgs, it remains massless, because its unique symmetry group is different in nature, and not sensitive to the Higgs-induced symmetry breaking (it’s a so-called Abelian group). As I said… the answer is a tad complicated. I hope it’s not completely incomprehensible, though.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Did Edward Teller know about anti-gravity propulsion?
Answer: Neither Edward Teller, nor anyone else in the actual physics community knew, or knows, anything about “anti-gravity propulsion” because according to the physics we know, no such thing exists. It is possible of course that there is physics we don’t (yet) know that might make such propulsion possible. Personally I consider it highly unlikely. Our understanding of gravity may not be complete but it is reasonably robust. We have not only not seen anything in Nature that would suggest that anti-gravity is a real thing, there are plenty of fairly fundamental reasons to believe that it is not. Repulsive gravity is possible (dark energy is one example) but it does not quite work the way one would naively imagine “anti-gravity” to work. Concerning Teller himself, he is of course best known for his work on the Manhattan project and, more broadly, on nuclear and molecular physics. Gravitational physics was not his area of specialization. And while he notably advocated many schemes, some more outlandish than others, e.g., under the Strategic Defense Initiative, these were still rooted in well-established, experimentally tested physics, not science-fiction schemes like anti-gravity. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: As a function of a qubit's realizable states and their complex states in and out of superposition, would it ever be possible to have quadrabits, pentabits, etc, which possess the unrealized phase states of a qubit beyond 2 degreees of freedom?
Answer: There are several possible misunderstandings that may have motivated the phrasing of this question. A qubit is a two-state quantum system. That is to say, when we interact with a qubit, we “read” it as either one state or the other state. It should be stressed that it is not “two degrees of freedom”. It’s a single degree of freedom, with two eigenstates. However, and this is essential to how quantum computing works, when qubits interact, its the actual quantum states of these qubits that are at play: These are characterized by a continuous quantity, such as the phase of the wavefunction that determines the qubit’s state. An example for a quantum system that has two readable states would be a fermion like the electron: its spin is either +1/2 or -1/2. Yes, there are elementary particles with properties that have more than two states. E.g., a massive vector boson can have three spin states, +1, -1 and 0. However, these things are not convenient to use for quantum computing, in no small part because such elementary particles are difficult to create and are very short-lived! It’s hard to build a quantum computer from W or Z-bosons. Of course we are not restricted to using spin (or polarization), which restrict us to two states for fermions or the massless photon. But things get messy at this point. We likely end up with something that is no longer an elementary particle, but a more complex system of particles. Nothing wrong with that, mind you, and this will indeed be a quantum system with more than two states, but chances are it would just be a complex network of two-state elementary quantum systems, i.e., a system of qubits. Nonetheless, you stumbled upon something that’s real and a subject of research: qutrits are the three-state equivalent of qubits, and more generally, a d-state quantum system used for quantum computation would be called a qudit. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it fair to say that there is the equivalent of infinite acceleration at the event horizon of a black hole?
Answer: Yes, it is fair to say that there is infinite acceleration at the event horizon, but it requires a qualifier: We first need to decide what we mean by acceleration in this context. If you were to watch an object fall into a black hole, you’d see the following: As the object approaches the horizon, anything and everything will appear to slow down from your perspective. The object would become invisible as a matter of fact because all signals coming from it would be subject to exponentially increasing redshift, making those signals effectively undetectable. But assuming that nonetheless, you can continue to track the object’s motion, you’d find that it never actually reaches the horizon: From your perspective, its motion will appear to freeze, the moment of it reaching the horizon (indeed, the moment the horizon itself forms in the first place!) forever remaining in your future. If you were to fall freely into a black hole, you would of course feel no acceleration. You might feel tidal forces because different parts of your body would try to follow different trajectories: If the black hole is small (and by “small”, I mean any size smaller than the largest supermassive black holes) these tidal forces would in fact rip your body to shreds. But if the black hole is large enough, you might survive reaching, and getting past, the horizon (ignoring quantum behavior here and the role played by Hawking radiation). And at no point would you feel acceleration: you would be in free fall all this time. However! Suppose you are testing your Almost Infinitely Powerful Rocket (tm), by trying to hover as close to the event horizon as possible. You will find that the closer you are to the event horizon, the more force you need to stay in position. In fact, soon enough you’d be quashed inside your rocket, so perhaps it might be wise to just send an unmanned probe instead. The bottom line: you will find that no matter how powerful your rocket it, there’s a point near the event horizon where it’s just not powerful enough to stay hovering. At the event horizon proper, the rocket would need to be infinitely powerful, i.e., subjected to infinite acceleration, in order to stay motionless, and that, of course, is impossible. So yes, as I said, it is fair to say that there is infinite acceleration at the event horizon: It would take an Infinitely Powerful Rocket (which cannot exist) to overcome gravity at the horizon proper and just hover.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Classical physics says objects move because they were pushed. Quantum physics says objects tunnel spontaneously (and not pushed by anything). how can this difference be resolved?
Answer: Actually, neither of the statements in the question are correct, but let me get down to details. Classical physics says that the motion of an object may change (i.e., it accelerates) if a force acts on that object. Motion requires no pushing. A change in motion requires pushing. This was historically not evident to humans until early modern times, since it seemed that, for all practical intents and purposes, motion ceased unless things were pushed continuously. It was not until Newton and others that we learned that this cessation of motion required a force as well: the force of friction, air resistance or other “dissipative” forces that turned the macroscopic motion of objects into the microscopic motion (rotation, vibration, etc.) of particles that we recognize as (waste) heat. What quantum physics says is not that “objects tunnel”. Nothing of the sort. Tunneling is about states, not objects. A system’s state may be characterized, among other things, by its energy-content. In classical physics, a system may lose energy to its environment if a lower energy state is available, but it does not happen if achieving that lower energy state first requires climbing to higher energy state, i.e., climbing over a (fictitious) “barrier”. This really should not be terribly mysterious. A piece of wood is in a higher energy state than the ashes and smoke that it turns into when it burns. Yet wood does not combust spontaneously. That is because its higher energy state is metastable. We need to invest energy (light it on fire with a match) in order to overcome the energy barrier before the wood can combust on its own and turn into ashes and smoke, with the excess energy released as heat. And this is what tunneling is about: a quantum system may overcome that barrier even in the absence of a push. We picture this as the system “borrowing” energy from the vacuum but I caution against reading this too literally. What it basically means is that something that is impossible in classical physics is simply improbable in the quantum world. However, and this must be stressed, the quantum world may be probabilistic in nature but conservation laws, including the law of energy conservation, are not. They hold exactly even in the world of quantum physics. That energy barrier? The system never exists as an observable system in a transitional state with more energy than it began with. The system can be observed before tunneling and after tunneling, with the released energy in some other form (again, for instance, waste heat).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does a perfect fluid have a rest frame in relativity even though its different particles aren't at rest with respect to each other?
Answer: First of all, in the context of relativity theory a medium such as a fluid is a continuous medium. No particles are involved. The fluid may be in motion, which is to say, to every point we can assign a velocity vector, telling us how the infinitesimally small volume of the fluid at that location moves. This means that we can also apply a “local” Lorentz transformation, which is to say, a Lorentz transformation that varies from point to point, to remove this velocity, and find the “local” rest frame of reference. A fluid is a perfect fluid if, in this frame of reference, its state is described entirely by its density and pressure: there are no stresses present. It is of course true that real fluids are not continuous mediums but consist of particles. So the perfect fluid model is only approximately valid. It is useful when it comes to describing the average, bulk properties of matter; not so useful when we look at matter at the microscopic level, where particle interactions become relevant.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet?
Answer: We don’t observe particles. We observe specific properties of particles when we measure them. In an idealized measurement, when we measure a particle position for instance, it means we ensure that the particle interacts with a classical instrument that confines the particle’s position to a specific number (an eigenvalue). Consequently its momentum is completely unconfined. In a real measurement, our measuring instrument itself is made up of particles, so it’s not a purely classical instrument. Therefore, it does not perfectly confine the particle position to a number. Interpreting the particle’s state as a probability amplitude, it indeed means that, as per our measurement, we have something like a Gaussian probability distribution characterizing the particle’s position (or whatever property it was that was being measured).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light?
Answer: No, it is not true. First of all, in the context of relativity theory, it is important to remember that the concept of speed is relative. Things do not travel at some velocity, nor do that stay put. Things travel relative to other things. To give you an example that dates back to Galileo: Suppose you are on a sailing ship, sitting in a windowless cabin as the ship sails on perfectly smooth seas. You are staring at a glass on the table in front of you. The glass is not moving. Or is it? How could you even tell? Relative to you, the glass is at rest. Relative to the shore, it moves at some velocity (how fast do medieval sailing ships move anyway?) along with you and the table and the rest of the ship. But relative to the Sun? It moves about 30 kilometers every second! Or how about relative to the central region of the Milky Way? We’re now up to roughly 200 km/s. And then relative to some really distant objects in deep space, you, your glass and the table it sits own, your ship, the Earth, the Sun, the Milky Way all move at a speed close to the vacuum speed of light. And it goes both ways. From your perspective, it’s not you or the Earth that is moving so fast, but the distant galaxy! However, if there are aliens on that galaxy, they’d say it’s you who is moving and they’re the ones standing still. So as I said, motion is relative. And constant it is not. If there were no forces (including gravity) acting on objects, motion (relative as it is) would always be in a straight line at constant velocity. But there are forces. Gravity in particular (a force that we often interpret geometrically) alters the trajectories of objects. So they no longer move in a straight line or at a constant speed relative to other things. The Earth moves around the Sun, and its Sun-relative velocity changes in magnitude, too, as its orbit is elliptical. The velocity of the Earth relative to, say, Mars, is even more twisted. These specific examples notwithstanding if there is one thing that is worth remembering, it’s that velocity is always relative. That applies even to light in a vacuum. The magnitude of its velocity is the same for all observers, but the direction in which a light ray travels is different in different observer reference frames. (In fact, if you look up the concept of aberration in astronomy, this has been known since before relativity theory, for over 300 years as a matter of fact).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible for an object to become heavier than anything else in existence, including black holes, if it reaches lightspeed through acceleration?
Answer: Objects do not become heavier by acceleration. Objects gain kinetic energy by acceleration, as measured in the reference frame of other objects that do not accelerate along with the object in question. Decades ago, relativity texts often introduced the concept of “relativistic mass”, which lumped together the (intrinsic) rest mass of the moving object with its (observer-dependent) kinetic energy. Fortunately, this concept is not much used anymore and, well, good riddance, because it led to a lot of misunderstandings. So no, an object will not become heavier no matter how close to the vacuum speed of light it moves in some observer’s reference frame. (Keep in mind that motion is always relative: objects move relative to other objects, in their own reference frames they are always at rest.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: In relativity won't the electromagnetic force also cause time dilation in a similar manner to gravity, considering that time dilation due to gravity arises because it causes objects to accelerate and that applies to the electromagnetic force as well?
Answer: Gravitational time dilation is not due to acceleration. Gravitational time dilation is a direct effect of the gravitational field. But allow me to take a step back. In many of my answers I cautioned against taking the “geometric interpretation” of gravitation too literally. This advice is not mine; none other than Einstein himself argued against reading too much into this interpretation, and in his own published works, never ceased to refer to gravitation as a force. Yes, gravitation can be interpreted as a change in geometry. Moreover, because gravitation is universal, it affects everything the same way, regardless of material composition or other properties, and that includes our instruments with which we measure space and time. Literally, the geometry imposed by gravitation is the only geometry in town, the one-and-only geometry that we see using our instruments. Can electromagnetism be interpreted using the language of geometry? You betcha. There have been numerous classical attempts (five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein theory, Weyl’s theory of linear vs. quadratic ground-forms, Einstein’s attempt to study nonsymmetric gravitation) but also in the modern quantum fiel theory formulation, the electromagnetic interaction is represented by a so-called covariant derivative, which has a direct geometric interpretation. However! That geometry is not universal. It depends on the material properties of whatever it is that the field is acting upon. Notably, it depends on the charge-to-mass ratio. So sure, if we were to build a clock using electrically charged components and placed that clock in an electromagnetic field, its operation would change. But another clock, made from electrically neutral components, would not be sensitive to that electromagnetic field. This is not how gravity works: The presence of gravitation has the same effect on both clocks. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Have physicists studied if time is a constant throughout the universe, or varies according to environment (black hole, nebula, star, et cetera)?
Answer: Time is not constant throughout the universe. Doing away with the concept of “absolute time” is a key principle behind the theory of relativity. We also know this to be true experimentally. And no, I don’t just mean clocks carried by airplanes and spacecraft, demonstrating both velocity-related and gravitational time dilation. Modern atomic clocks are sensitive enough to detect an altitude difference measured in centimeters: given two identical clocks, the one on the floor would tick ever so slightly slower than the one on your desk. On a grander scale, when we look at the cosmological redshift of very distant objects, it is dominated by changes in the large-scale average gravitational field of the cosmos billions of years ago vs. today: again, time dilation. We can also see time dilation in, e.g., the spectra of compact stars. In short, our best theory to date tells us that time is not universal or absolute, and this is confirmed by numerous experiments and astronomical observations. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Did LIGO confirm that gravitational waves travel at the same speed as electromagnetism? If so, what is the connection between space wobble speed and the speed limit of space?
Answer: To answer the first question, well, yes, LIGO helped confirm that gravitational waves indeed travel at the same speed as electromagnetic waves. When I say “helped” it’s because it took the simultaneous (“multimessenger”) observation of events, notably a neutron star merger (GW170817), using both gravitational waves and electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays, gamma rays). These signals arrived at approximately the same time, even though they traveled roughly 130 million light years. Concerning the second question, it might be helpful to forget for a moment that we interpret gravitation as the “warping of spacetime” and (following Einstein himself) simply consider the gravitational field a physical field, much like the electromagnetic field. Both fields are massless, and therefore, both fields have solutions in empty space in the form of transverse waves that travel at the invariant speed of relativity theory, which we know as the vacuum speed of light. Granted, it is true that since gravity is universal, its observed effects, when interpreted as geometry, affect everything the same way, so we are justified to interpret gravitational waves as, well, “space wobbles” or whatever. But even if we go by this interpretation, gravitational radiation is very weak except near sources, so any such “wobbles” can be seen as tiny perturbations of a background, unperturbed spacetime. So we come to the same conclusion: These small perturbations travel at the invariant speed of the theory, i.e, the same speed at which light travels in the vacuum. Lastly, I’d advise against thinking of the vacuum speed of light as a “speed limit”. That’s an effect, not a cause. What that speed is, fundamentally, is not a limit but an invariant: If something travels at the vacuum speed of light for some observer, it will be seen as traveling at the vacuum speed of light by all observers. The “speed limit” business is a consequence. For starters, an observer is always at rest in his own reference frame. If the observer were to travel at the vacuum speed of light (which is the same for all observers, remember?) he’d be both traveling at the vacuum speed of light and standing still at the same time in his own reference frame, which is a contradiction. Moreover, we find that when we compare observers, if something is slower than the vacuum speed of light for one observer, it will be slower for all observers. Given that an observer is always at rest (i.e., slower than light!) in his own reference frame, he will necessarily be slower than the vacuum speed of light in all other observers’ reference frames. But as I said, this is a consequence. The fundamental statement is that an invariant speed exists; the “speed limit” business follows. Question: Do supernovas create gravitational waves? Can they be strong enough to influence the fabric of space but on a much smaller scale than merging black holes? Do gravitational waves have any negative influence on Earth?
Answer: To create gravitational waves, two things are needed: a) accelerating mass, and b) deviation from axial symmetry. So a symmetric collapse of a star, spinning or not, would not produce gravitational waves. However, if the explosion is sufficiently asymmetric, gravitational waves at detectable rates are possible. to be sure, the gravitational waves produced by even a highly asymmetrical supernova explosion would likely be many orders of magnitude weaker than the gravitational waves produced by black hole mergers. Nonetheless, they may be detectable at least by future detectors, if the supernova is close enough and asymmetric enough. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible to know what will happen in the future? Doesn't this violate causality, relativity and the laws of thermodynamics?
Answer: Before we talk about the future, let me ask about the past. Do you have perfect knowledge of the past? I sure don’t. I don’t even remember what I had for dinner last Friday. Of course I can create records and make sure certain things are remembered, but there will be questions to which I would not know the answer. And how about things that I was not present to witness, could not record, things that happened before my time, your time, before anyone presently alive was born? We can infer a lot of things. Julius Caesar existed, so he must have been born even though none of us were there to witness his birth. The Arizona crater is there so something, likely a meteor, must have created it even though this knowledge is inferred from what we can learn at the present, not recorded at the time of the event, estimated to have taken place some 50,000 years ago. But going beyond what we do know, it is a very valid question: what can we know in principle about the past and the future if all we have available to observe is the present? If this was a classical universe (no quantum physics) the answer would be… everything. That is to say that, in principle, if we had perfect knowledge of the positions and velocities of all particles everywhere at present, we would be able to model with perfection their past and their future. Quantum physics changes this in a rather non-intuitive way. It’s not that we cannot have perfect knowledge of positions and velocities of all particles. It’s that those positions and velocities do not even exist in the classical sense. Rather, those particles are described in terms of states (represented by the famous wavefunction) that may or may not correspond to specific values, but if the state corresponds to a concrete value of position, it cannot simultaneously carry a concrete value of velocity and vice versa. I stress, it’s not that we cannot measure it. Those values do not even exist in the classical sense. Therefore, any measurement that we can make “in-universe” is necessarily limited. As a result, we cannot infer the future (or the past!) precisely, only in terms of probabilities. There is still a manifest difference between the future and the past, because of thermodynamics, which defines an arrow of time thanks to entropy. But neither past nor future can be known with certainty. I said “in-universe” because there is an interesting twist. If only we knew the state (i.e. the wavefunction) of the system with precision, we could then infer the future and the past as accurately as we wanted to. But this state is not observable within the universe, only positions and velocities are, with the limitation I mentioned above. Suppose though that the world is a simulation, running on some advanced alien computer. The alien operator of that computer, who is not part of the simulation but exists outside of it, can pause the computation, take an exact reading of the computer’s state, and restart it. Or perhaps even run the simulation backwards. Or make a copy of it, and find that the copy produces the exact same outcome as the original. So that alien computer operator could indeed know, in principle, everything about both the past and the future. But we do not exist outside of the universe (indeed, we have no reason to believe that such an “outside” even exists.) In-universe, the full state of the physical system remains hidden from us. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How can space be two dimensional so objects on it curl it and make gravity while universe is 3D, like how we explain height in this system ، and how it works for quantum particles, and dark matter?
Answer: Space is not two dimensional and objects do not curl it. Incredibly bad, misleading, but unfortunately highly popular visualizations, however, sometimes depict space as a two-dimensional “rubber sheet” of sorts, curled by a mass in the middle. I cannot tell you just how incredibly, blatantly, stupidly wrong that visualization really is. For starters… the thing that is being “curled” in general relativity is not space but spacetime. Emphasis on the “time” part. Newtonian gravity in the context of general relativity is all about the rate at which clocks tick. Clocks tick slightly slower in a gravitational field. This, combined with a core principle of fundamental physics, the principle of least action, leads to trajectories that are bent, to object being deflected by, or forced into orbit around, other objects. Again, all this has to do with clocks. True, gravity also “curls” space, but not at all like in those stupid graphics that you see on the pages of popular science magazines and in some books. What basically happens is that distances do not behave like they would in Euclidean geometry. Distances, angles, shapes are distorted. But this distortion is absolutely tiny! Here on the surface of the Earth, the contribution of this distortion modifies Newton’s law of gravitation by around one part in a billion, no more. So please do not let these bad visualizations mislead you. Unfortunately such visualizations are quite common in the popular literature (and often used by authors even here on Quora). I have no doubt that they are intended to be helpful, but in the end, they achieve the opposite: They create a mental picture in the mind of the reader that then becomes very hard to unlearn. Short version: The geometric interpretation of gravitation is about four-dimensional spacetime, but in practical experience, only gravitational time dilation — the rate at which clocks tick in different gravitational fields — matters, all other distortions represent just tiny, tiny corrections. This applies to ordinary matter, dark matter, and the quantum theory, too (yes, we can do quantum theory in the presence of gravitation — a “proper” quantum theory of gravity is another matter, but that’s a different problem set.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Suppose a stationary object has ten nearby objects moving in different speeds and directions. Taking ten moving objects as reference, does the stationary object also experience 10 length contractions? In 10 directions?
Answer: No object is “stationary” in the absolute sense, and no object “experiences” length contraction. There is no “stationary” object because it would imply some absolute reference frame. No such absolute reference frame exists. On the other hand, an object is always at rest in its own reference frame. So what? You are at rest in your own reference frame whether you are sitting in a comfy chair at your desk or in a not-so-comfy economy class seat on an airplane. You are not at rest in other folks’ reference frames, but who cares? This was already known to Galileo: he imagined a traveler in a windowless cabin on a smoothly sailing ship, not being able to tell if his ship is moving or standing still. When other folks not moving along with you look at you from their reference frames, they may observe that you appear shortened in the direction in which you move relative to their reference frame. They may also observe that your watch ticks at a rate that differs from theirs. But none of this has anything to do with what you “experience”. Your body proportions remain unchanged and your watch ticks at exactly the same rate as it always did (assuming it’s a reliable watch) in your own reference frame. There is a reason why the theory is called the theory of relativity. It describes how things appear relative to other frames of reference! Nothing, I stress, nothing happens to you just because other folks, near or far, tens or millions of them, are moving relative to you. The fact that each and every one of them sees you with slightly distorted proportions, or measure your watch ticking at a rate that differs from theirs does not mean a thing insofar as you are concerned. So yes, your object would appear with different proportions from each of those ten objects’ individual reference frames. But the object proper would not “experience” any of that. In its own reference frame, its proportions never change. How others see it is not relevant. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: At 0 Kelvin, the motion of particles is completely halted. But is there a phase, under some circumstances, where the subatomic particles (electrons) also stop moving?
Answer: Sigh. You received many answers to this years-old question, but several of them seem united in terms of a key misunderstanding: "particles" are not miniature cannonballs and the classic concept of "motion" does not apply. But first of all, it's important to note that 0 K is not an achievable state. It is a consequence (or if you wish, a particular restatement) of the third law of thermodynamics. Having said that, the meaning of 0 K for a system is that it is in its unique lowest energy or ground state. It is not about motion or the absence of motion, it is about the fact that no lower energy state exists: The system can only receive energy by interacting with other systems, it can no longer transfer energy to those other systems. To elaborate further, think what thermal equilibrium means. You bring two systems into contact, energy flows from the warmer to the colder system until the two have the same temperature. At that point, the transfer of energy ceases. Now a system that is at absolute zero does not have any energy left to transfer to other systems; it can only receive energy from other systems if brought into contact with them. This statement remains valid in both classical and in quantum physics, but the meaning is different. If the world consisted of classical particles, miniature cannonballs, absolute zero would indeed mean that all motion ceases, and the system has no residual potential energy either that could bring parts of it into motion. In the case of quantum systems, the concept of "motion" may lose its meaning completely (atoms are not miniature solar systems with electrons orbiting!) but the basic concept remains the same: Absolute zero means that the system can only receive energy from other systems as it comes into equilibrium with them, it cannot release energy. Lastly, this has nothing to do with the uncertainty principle. Some characterized it as a limitation of our knowledge of particle positions and velocities. That is nonsense. As I said, particles are not miniature cannonballs. Their positions and momenta have no classical analogies. They are described mathematically by “non-commuting” entities, which is to say, their values are not at all like the ordinary number-valued positions that we are used to in the classical world. Sorry, we cannot intuit this. Math is needed. Suffice to say, it means that if one of these quantities, say, the position is momentarily number-valued, the other cannot be number-valued at the same time. The “particle” simply does not HAVE a classically meaningful position and velocity at the same time. But again, while this explains why I stressed the point that quantum particles are not miniature cannonballs, the thermodynamic principles here are equally valid in the classical and the quantum world. Quantum physics is not required to elaborate on the generic concept of a lowest energy state. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters?
Answer: Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the “electron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon”. That “virtual electron-positron pair” is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist’s mind. It is called “ virtual” because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac’s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn’t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the “Dirac sea” business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states “filled in”, unless a particle is missing, and it’s this “hole” that Dirac’s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac’s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac’s equation described them. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Could a device be invented that synchronizes the flow of time between vastly different gravitational fields, standardizing time measurement across space?
Answer: The answer is a flat no, but behind this answer lies an understanding of what time really is. I mean, in practical terms, not hifalutin’ philosophy. That is to say, what we measure as time in this one-and-only physical universe in which we, for better or for worse, live. One observed property of this physical universe is that in it there are things that tick. Not only do they tick, they tick reliably. Which is to say, if you have two such things, they will tick at the same rate. And even if you take them on distant journeys, when you bring them back together, they’ll still be ticking at the same rate. We call these things reliable clocks. It does not matter if they are cesium atoms or grandfather clocks. The only thing that matters is that they tick reliably, and they are reliably identical. Now you take two of these things and start counting the ticks. Then you let them off on different journeys. When you bring them back together, they’ll still be ticking in synch, but you will find that one may have counted fewer ticks than the other! And it depends on the journey it took. The one that traveled faster. Made more changes in speed or direction. The one that spent more time near heavy objects. Note that I have not mentioned any “flow of time” nor do I plan to, apart from this one mention on double quotes. There is no such thing. What there is, it’s a property associated with the paths of the respective trajectories of these reliable clocks: their world lines, that is. A kind of a “length” (though a rather non-intuitive concept of “length”) associated with these world lines. A reliable clock measures this length, called “proper time” along its world line. Different world lines have different lengths between the same points. But why is it surprising? After all, different paths between two points have different lengths in a map, too. Walking straight takes fewer steps than following a zig-zag path. Now I mentioned the proper time is counterintuitive, and it is true: Unlike lengths, proper time is the longest between two events when the clock is moving inertially, not accelerated in any way. Take two events. Say, right here, at my desk, at 6 PM tonight and at 6 PM tomorrow. My reliable clock counts exactly 86,400 ticks between these two events. But if you were to be here at 6 PM then blast off in your relativistic spaceship at high acceleration, turn around at some point, and get back at 6 PM tomorrow, your world line would have fewer ticks. The same thing happens in gravitational fields: a world line taking through a gravitational field will be measured with fewer ticks than another that takes a different path. Of course many other things affect the overall “length” of a world line, but this is the role gravitational fields play. In fact, reliable clocks can even be used to measure gravitational fields! (Today’s atomic clocks are sensitive enough to measure a difference in altitude amounting to no more than a few centimeters.) But ultimately, it’s not about any “flow of time” (sorry, I just broke my promise and mentioned it a second time). It’s about the “length”, i.e., the proper time associated with, different world lines. That proper time is the only actual concept of time that we can measure. Every other concept of time — e.g., coordinate time, “flow of time” (yikes! That’s the third time!) — is a mathematical or philosophical construct, not physical reality. Proper time is physical reality. In fact, ultimately all other measurements — measuring lengths, for instance, or speed — boil down to calibrating the measurements using reliable clocks and proper time in general relativity. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: For a long-duration moon mission, would an Earth-corrected time standard be required, or would periodic corrections to Earth time be sufficient?
Answer: It depends on what you want to achieve. As others noted, gravitational time dilation amounts to a roughly 60 microsecond difference per day. If you are only interested in making sure that you don’t miss your favorite TV show, you have nothing to worry about for at least a good half century, which is when the cumulative difference reaches about a second. But as they say, the devil is in the details[1]. What are you using your clocks for? If you are doing navigation using precise radio signals, GPS-like, then keep in mind that every microsecond amounts to about 300 meters when it comes to straightforward length measurements; depending on the geometry of the problem, when you are looking at satellites at an angle, the navigational errors can quickly add up to several kilometers. Needless to say, when you’re landing a spacecraft, several kilometers might mean the difference between a nice, flat region vs. the boulder-filled interior of a nasty lunar crater. Not good! Moreover, while it is true that the time dilation averages to about 60 microseconds a day, it is highly variable. The rate at which clocks tick on the Moon relative to terrestrial clocks (or clocks in intermediate orbits around the Earth, like GPS clocks) depends on many factors other than lunar gravity, including the gravity of the Earth itself, the gravitational field of the Sun (the Moon may be closer to, or farther from the Sun than the Earth at various points during a lunar orbit, and this affects relative clock rates) not to mention the relative motion of the respective clocks. Ultimately it is still a simple problem (just account for all the sources of gravitational time dilation and add them all up — nonlinear effects can likely be safely ignored as they are many orders of magnitude smaller) but it still requires making sure that everything is properly accounted for at the requisite level of accuracy. Long story short, my expectation is that before long, there will be a lunar reference time standard, likely as a result of some international agreement. Future missions, including missions that might be used to assist navigation in cislunar space, will probably use that standard. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What are the challenges and potential designs for a SpaceX Interstellar probe using miniaturized black hole propulsion, theorized to harness Hawking radiation as thrust?
Answer: I have no idea what may have inspired this question, but I can assure you that neither SpaceX, nor anyone else can realistically entertain a proposal to use “miniaturized black hole propulsion”. First of all, the only (ONLY!) known mechanism to produce a black hole is stellar collapse. For that, you need at the very least three times the mass of the Sun, which is a million times the mass of the Earth. The lifetime of that black hole is about 3.13 × 10 68 years, and at present, its Hawking radiation output is 10 − 29 watts. But let us suppose that some magic (not physics) allows us to create a “miniaturized” black hole. How miniaturized? Say, 1 metric ton? But wait, it evaporates in… about 46 nanoseconds. “Evaporate” is perhaps the wrong word, then. More like “tremendous explosion”, maybe a million atom bombs or something like. So let’s make it a little bigger, perhaps its more manageable. Say, 10,000 metric tons? OK, we’re a little bit better off, that black hole would last a full half day, the only problem is that it is still radiating at a rate of over 800 one-megaton hydrogen bombs’ worth of power every second, and that rate will increase as the black hole get smaller. Okay, so let’s get it down to 1 megaton/second, maybe we can live with that in some tremendous propulsion mechanism. Now we are onto something, this black hole lasts over 36 years. The problem is, it now weighs almost 300,000 metric tons. And its output? Why, it’s mostly in the form of extreme high energy gamma rays, and by extreme I mean extreme, comparable to the energy levels in the largest particle accelerators. Don’t get too close! Oh, and did I mention that you cannot shut it down? Hawking radiation doesn’t go away. Well, let me stop right now, and not even ask practical questions like how you’re planning to affix a black hole to the propulsion system. As the above should make it clear, the whole scheme is science-fiction and bad, lazy science-fiction at that, the kind tired scriptwriters with a bad hangover sometimes come up with when trying to keep alive an old science-fiction series that is several seasons past its prime… If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do scientists detect dark matter if it does not interact with light or other forms of matter except through gravity? How is it possible to observe something that does not emit light?
Answer: To date, dark matter has not been detected. Its existence is inferred from the gravitational behavior of visible structures, but it has not been confirmed by direct detection, despite numerous attempts to do do. These failures do not mean that dark matter doesn’t exist, but they did exclude several plausible theoretical models. Meanwhile, precisely because dark matter’s existence has not yet been directly confirmed, the door remains open to viable alternatives, in the form of modified theories of gravitation that do away with the need for dark matter in the first place. However, this is not as easy as it sounds. The “dark matter paradigm” fits the data reasonably well. Modifying the theory of gravitation comes with unexpected consequences. Einstein’s theory works at very high precision here in the solar system; a modified theory of gravitation would have to reproduce these results. Dark matter does a decent job at producing data consistent with the large-scale structure formation (gravitational “clumping”) of matter; most theories of gravitation run into trouble. LIGO observations confirm that gravitational waves and light travel at the same speed; many modified gravity theories would predict something different and are therefore excluded. And the dark matter model accurately reproduces the statistical fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background, another difficult challenge for modified gravity. That is not to say that the standard dark matter model does not have its own share of difficulties, ranging from the famous Hubble tension (different values for the Hubble parameter when measured “locally” vs. inferred from cosmological observations) to the unexplained emergence of mature early galaxies and supermassive black holes in the early universe. So I daresay the jury is still out. We shall see what happens; dark matter is probably a safe horse to bet on, but its victory is by no means assured. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is Sagittarius A star, the supermassive black hole in the center of the Milky Way actually in the center?
Answer: Sgr A* is in the “central region” of the Milky Way. The role this supermassive black hole may or may not have played in the formation of the Milky Way remains ill understood. However, there really is no such thing as “the center”. The center of what? The Milky Way? Which things are part of the Milky Way? What about distant star clusters orbiting the Milky Way? Satellite galaxies? Eventually it becomes a matter of convention. However we define the Milky Way, there corresponds to it a center-of-mass. But a different definition places that center-of-mass at a different location. Something similar happens here in the solar system. Astronomers, folks navigating spacecraft often talk about the SSB, the solar system barycenter. Sounds great until you ask… exactly what is used to calculate its location? Suppose we discover an ice giant, a Jupiter-sized planet somewhere in the Kuiper belt. A mass that large, that far from the Sun, if it is considered part of the solar system, would dramatically shift the defined location of the SSB. One definition is no more valid than another; it’s a matter of convention, not physics. What is physics is that in the solar system, the mass of the Sun dominates. Everything else is just debris. Planets do not orbit the SSB (yes, I know, even some NASA Web pages say that they do; those pages are plain wrong.) They follow elliptical orbits with the planet+Sun two body system’s center-of-mass as its focal point, with gravitation from the other planets only contributing minor perturbations. So the Earth orbits the Sun-Earth two-body system barycenter, with slight perturbations from Jupiter and the other planets; this barycenter is distinct from the Sun-Jupiter barycenter that Jupiter orbits. Going back to Sgr A*, it does not play a similar, dominating role in the Milky Way. It is massive, but its mass is dwarfed by… Never mind the whole Milky Way, the central region itself has thousands of times the mass of Sgr A*. So other stars in the Milky Way, including our own Sun, do not orbit Sgr A*. In a crude approximation, they orbit the barycenter of the central bulge of the Milky Way. That includes Sgr A* of course, but it is not dominated by it, not even close. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the origin of the energy resulting in an explosion during the merger of two neutron stars that do not result in a black hole?
Answer: Black hole, no black hole, the energy is there, the end result doesn’t matter much. At first it is gravitational potential energy: the “ability to do work”, i.e., bring things into motion. When the two stars are far apart but attracted to each other, as they get closer, they speed up. So potential energy “does work”, gets converted into kinetic energy. A good chunk of that kinetic energy is radiated away in the form of gravitational radiation as the two stars orbit each other in an ever tighter inspiral, reaching a substantial fraction of the vacuum speed of light towards the end. But then, kaboom, they collide. That means that whatever kinetic energy they have left (which is to say, stupendous amounts of kinetic energy when an entire star moves at a sizable percentage of the speed of light) is now converted into heat. Think of a large meteorite impact… and now multiply that by, I don’t know, maybe a 30-digit number. So if the end product is not a black hole, what we have instead is an object that is heated to insane high temperatures as a result. (This also becomes a factory for heavy elements. Chances are your own body contains quite a few atoms that were produced in such a collision.) As a matter of fact, more energy is released by the impact if the end result is not a black hole, as all that heat can radiate away, instead of being gobbled up by the resulting black hole. But in the end, it’s just plain old gravitational potential energy, converted into motion (kinetic energy) and, upon impact, into more random motion (heat). Nothing fancy, really, apart from the sizes and scales involved. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: The second quantum revolution would involve entanglement of qubits. Isn’t that the “spooky action at a distance” thought to be impossible?
Answer: Well, “spooky action at a distance” is indeed impossible but it is not needed to understand entanglement. There are two things that ought to be remembered as to what entanglement really means. First, by and large everything is entangled with everything else all of the time. When we call a specific system of states (particles, qubits, whatever) “entangled”, what we really mean is that we (briefly and imperfectly) managed to isolate that system from the rest of the universe so that at least temporarily, the system’s constituent bits are only entangled with each other. Second, the “spooky” part is not about action-at-a-distance but about certain characteristics of the system — e.g., its conserved energy, its conserved angular momentum — that are not localized in the first place. It’s not that particle A (or qubit A) “sends” something over a distance to particle B. It’s that the something in question was never specifically tied to particle A or particle B. It’s only measurable in full when we measure both A and B, and find their “spooky” correlation. This is the essential nonlocality of quantum physics, as demonstrated, e.g., by Bell’s famous theorem. Qubits represent an application of quantum physics, based on the promise that if the quantum system used for computation can be sufficiently well-isolated from its environment, error correction can be used for it to operate as though it was a “perfect”, i.e., perfectly isolated, quantum system. This is the essence of the famous threshold theorem. This threshold has not been reached, so scalable quantum computing is not yet a reality. (It may never become reality — some, myself included, remain skeptical.) Whether or not that happens, however, it is still the “same old, same old” quantum physics as before. For certain computational problems, a breakthrough may be revolutionary, but insofar as quantum physics is concerned, I see no revolution: It’s still the same physics, characterized, as before, by Schrödinger’s equation or, more fundamentally, by the canonical commutation relationships. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: At moment 0 in the Lambda CDM model, is there any speculation (speculation, of course, but commonly held belief) as to whether there was anything (matter/energy) "adjacent" to the singularity that became the observable universe?
Answer: There is no “moment 0” in the standard cosmological (Lambda-CDM) model. It’s indeed a “singularity”. Which is a mathematical concept, best illustrated by a simple function that is singular, say, y = 1 / x 2 . That function exists for all values of x except for x = 0. You can get as close to x = 0 as you want. But at x = 0 , the function does not exist. The value x = 0 is not part of its domain. Similarly, t = 0 is not part of the domain of the standard cosmological model and its spacetime. You can get as close to it as you want. A second. A picosecond. The Planck time. The Planck time divided by a very big number. Whatever it is, it has to be finite and greater than zero: that is, in the standard cosmology, t > 0 , not t ≥ 0. We can speculate anything we want about the value t = 0 , therefore, but it’s science-fiction, with emphasis on the fiction part, not science. Also, I should stress that the actual science of physical cosmology begins with the present (which we observe) and extrapolates our knowledge into the past, but only as far as we can, not farther. The farthest to which we can legitimately extrapolate our knowledge is roughly t = 10 − 12 seconds, when conditions were similar to the high-energy particle collisions in the LHC. Anything prior to this time is pure speculation already; indeed, we don’t even necessarily know for sure if that picosecond was a picosecond or an eternity. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Assuming you had a long enough cable which connects two people, would they be able to communicate if one was inside a black hole and the other outside?
Answer: No, they would not, but perhaps its instructive to consider what happens from the perspective of the two participants. First, the person outside the black hole. Keep in mind that from this person’s perspective, the formation of the event horizon remains forever in the future. He would see his friend rapidly disappear from sight, but not because he’s eaten up by the black hole, not yet; rather, because as he gets really close to the black hole, any signal from him will suffer extreme time dilation and as a result, also extreme redshift. So soon enough, no matter how powerfully he transmits, and whether he does so by way of light, radio, or just yanking the cable, everything he does will appear in extreme slow motion, and the frequency (hence the energy) of any signal is redshifted down towards zero. Conversely, any signal sent by the person outside towards his friend falling into the black hole will also slow down and take longer and longer to catch up with the infalling explorer. Soon enough, we see that even signal traveling at the speed of light are too late: They will appear to slow down as viewed by the distant observer, and would simply not catch up with the infalling observer before they hit the horizon. In other words, from the perspective of the outside observer: never. As to the cable itself, what we see is that the tension on the cable increases rapidly. By the time the infalling observer reaches the horizon, the cable would be stretched infinitely, with infinite tension. That of course cannot happen, so at some point, the cable snaps. The stronger the cable, the later that happens but it is inevitable, and it will happen before the infalling observer reaches the horizon in his own reference frame. To sum up: Even though the infalling observer may reach the horizon, that moment in time remains forever in the future for the outside observer; and before that happens, the cable will snap, guaranteed, regardless how strong it is. (But if by some magic — not physics, magic — it didn’t, it’d become infinitely long and as such, unsuitable for signaling as a signal would never arrive at the other end.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do string theory and quantum theory explain light not being able to leave a black hole since light has no mass? Do we need relativity theory to explain this?
Answer: Neither string theory nor the quantum theory are required for an explanation, and the fact that light has no rest mass (although it has energy-momentum, and is therefore subject to gravitation) is also irrelevant. What matters is that “to leave a black hole” you need to go back in time. Once “inside” the event horizon, that horizon is not a place that you can return to, but a past moment in time. For an observer outside the black hole, the event horizon remains forever in the future. For an observer who crosses the horizon, that event horizon becomes part of their past. So in both cases, “return” involves a) coming back from the far future (from the perspective of the outside observer) or b) going back to a past moment in time (from the perspective of the observer who crossed the horizon). In other words: time travel. You don’t need string theory or the quantum theory to explain why you cannot use a flashlight today to light up a scene yesterday. Not without a time machine anyway. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why would Americans rather drive their car for days than take the train?
Answer: I live in Ottawa, Canada. I occasionally visit New York City. By car, a comfortable drive with the occasional rest stops takes about 8 hours and that includes crossing the border. It's 12:30 PM right now. If I were to hop into my car at 1 PM, chances are it'd still be daylight when I get out of my car somewhere in Manhattan. Now suppose I take the train. Google Maps tells me that I could depart tomorrow at 6:07 AM and arrive in Montreal at 8:11 AM. Three hours later, I would depart on Amtrak's Adirondack train, which could deliver me at Penn station a mere 11 hours later, at 10:15 PM. OK, how about return? Well, I could board the same Adirondack train the next day at 8:28 AM, heading back to Montreal. I'd arrive at Montreal's Gare Centrale at 8:16 PM. Too bad, that's after the last train that day left for Ottawa, so I'd have to get a hotel room and board the first train next morning at 6:20 AM. I'd arrive back at Ottawa's main railway station at 8:25 AM, just three minutes short of 24 hours since my departure at Penn Station. This does not include the time it takes to get to or from the railway station but it’s thankfully short, as I live not too far from Ottawa’s main railway station. OK, I could take a plane instead. The flight time from YOW to EWR (Newark) is only 90 minutes. Of course I need to be at the airport at least maybe 2 hours early, to go through customs preclearing. And then there is the ride to/from the airport. So I’d have to leave my home at least 3 hours prior to the scheduled departure, and it’d likely take at least an hour and a half to disembark, get my luggage, get a taxi and get from the airport to Manhattan. Overall? At least 6 hours travel time if everything goes according to plan. Granted, it's a little less than the road trip, but not that much less. And far less convenient. What about environmental costs? Google tells me that with Porter Airlines, one flight option only produces 55 kg of CO2 per passenger. But that's not much less* than the CO2 I'd produce burning up less than one full tank of fuel in my Honda Accord. This gets even more pronounced if I don’t travel alone: That 55 kg is per passenger, whereas my Honda’s fuel consumption would not change noticeably just because, say, my beautiful wife joins me for the trip. Would I like to take the train to NYC? Absolutely. And a century ago, I could have. The Ottawa & New York Railway ceased operations in 1957. I could not find a timetable but I doubt travel times were any worse than traveling with VIA Rail and Amtrak these days. Probably quicker and more comfortable, as a matter of fact. But those days are gone. The railroads may have built North America but today, passenger rail service... well, sucks. *Edited: at first I thought the Honda would produce less than 55 kg, but it’s more likely 90-odd kg. Which, incidentally, is just a tad more than the per-passenger CO2 listed by Google for most flights.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If you were sufficiently close to two colliding black holes, would distortions in space caused by the gravity waves be fatal (ignoring all of the other fatal phenomena like the accretion disk and tidal effects)?
Answer: Well, technically yes, but by that time you are too close already and you’d be killed by those tides even in the absence of a collision and the resulting gravitational waves. [Pedantic note, with apologies: A “gravity wave” is what you see on the surface of the sea when it waves. A “gravitational wave” is a propagating change in the gravitational field away from sources.] The point is, gravitational waves are propagating changes. A single object produces a gravitational field that changes from place to place but it does not change over time in the inertial reference frame in which the object is at rest. But when we have two objects inspiraling towards each other, no such inertial frame exists. The gravitational field changes not just from place to place but also over time. These changes then ripple away towards infinity with ever decreasing amplitude, much like changes in the electromagnetic field do in response to electric charges undergoing accelerating motion. When the gravitational force changes from place to place, it represents a tidal force. Different parts of a body want to head in different directions or different rates. This can rip a body apart. There are tides near any gravitating object, and tides near a black hole can be very strong because we can get very close to a black hole (they are very compact). When the black holes inspiral, these tidal forces change. Those changes propagate. But they do not get stronger with distance, quite the contrary. And in the end, what kills us is not how the tidal forces change over time, but how strong they are in the first place. Get close enough to the black hole and you’ll find out! A little farther away, though… I once calculated that if you were about the same distance from the merger of two ~30 solar mass black holes as the Earth is from the Sun, you could actually hear the result as a loud rising then decaying sound. Yes, there can be sounds in space! Well, not exactly sounds as we know them, not a traveling longitudinal pressure wave in a medium, rather, transversal gravitational waves in the vacuum but in the end how they travel is not relevant; what is relevant is that at that distance, they are powerful enough to interact with our ears.
