Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is quantum? Which things fit the definition of quantum?
Answer: There are things that are “quantized”, which is to say, exhibit behavior that comes in distinct chunks, and the branch of physics that deals with these things is called therefore “quantum physics”. But to the extent that it even touches on the concept of “quantum”, it’s a consequence, not a foundation. Not anymore. At first, quantum physics was mostly empirical. Yes, it was based on the idea that atoms emit or absorb energy in such discrete chunks, or quanta. This was observed. This led, for instance, to Planck’s famous radiation law, which marks the dawn of quantum physics. But over time, we became a tad more sophisticated. Less then thirty years after Planck initiated his revolution, the “new” quantum theory of Heisenberg and Schrödinger emerged. It was no longer about atoms emitting and absorbing quanta, but something far more fundamental: the mathematical representation of the state of a physical system. In classical physics, constituent parts of a physical system can be characterized by a) where they are, b) how they move. In other words, their positions and their speed (or momenta). These can be represented by numbers. A position is just a set of coordinates. A velocity is a vector that can be characterized by a set of coordinates. As I said, numbers. Then comes the “new” quantum mechanics, which represents positions and momenta by… well, something else. Matrices in Heisenberg’s case, function operators in Schrödinger’s, but the bottom line is the same: These things are not numbers. Specifically, they do not behave like numbers do under multiplication. Take the momenta p and positions q of a system. In classical physics, we can multiply these numbers together and get a result that does not depend on the order of multiplication: p q = q p , or p q − q p = 0. But this is not how positions and momenta behave in the new quantum physics. They obey instead the relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and, well, i = √ − 1 . This leads to all sorts of weird consequences, which have been confirmed experimentally. Among other things… well, quanta. Take one of the simplest physical systems, a simple oscillator (the so-called harmonic oscillator). Describe it in terms of these non-commuting variables and you get a weird result: The oscillator cannot have arbitrary energies. Its energy is discretized, going up or down by one unit, or quantum at a time. Electrons in an atom are well described by such oscillators as a mathematical model. So there we have it, the quantized behavior of how atoms emit or absorb energy. But quantum physics in general is not really about quanta. It’s not about chopping things up into small units. That might have been the original inspiration more than a century ago, but it has become something much more nuanced. Planck’s quanta are still there, but as a consequence, not as a building block, of the theory. There are plenty of “quantum” systems that have no quantized behavior. E.g., a free particle can have any energy; nothing “quantized” there. The fundamental statement of the theory is not about quanta; it is about the behavior of those key variables, the positions and momenta of a physical system, and how this behavior is described by the mathematics of noncommuting things, as opposed to the mathematics of simple numbers. Like it or not, that is how Nature behaves, as demonstrated by countless experiments. That said, when we go beyond simple quantum mechanics into the realm of quantum field theory, things change a bit. A field, like the electromagnetic field, can be described as a sum of, well, pure waves really, by way of what is called a Fourier-transform. Each of these pure waves behaves like a harmonic oscillator, which we know how to describe using quantum physics. Each of these harmonic oscillators is characterized by those distinct chunks of energy by which the oscillator’s energy can increase or decrease. In quantum field theory, these distinct chunks of energy (and possibly other conserved properties, like charge or angular momentum) turn out to be none other than the things we’ve know, we’ve observed, as particles! So there you have it: elementary particles come closest to the concept of “quantum”. (Indeed, sometimes we even say so explicitly: e.g., “photons are the quanta of the electromagnetic field.”) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Uranium atom has energy E=mc^2 (chain reaction). Does every atom have 'hidden' energy E=mc²?
Answer: Contrary to many popular accounts, E = m c 2 has nothing to do with uranium atoms. At least not directly. Here is what E = m c 2 actually means, using the exact words that appear in the title of Einstein’s paper in which this formula (albeit in a slightly different form) is introduced: The inertia of a body is determined by its energy-content. It’s not about uranium. It’s not about splitting the atom, causing explosions, or converting mass into energy or vice versa. It’s the mass-energy equivalence relationship. When we say that an object has a certain mass, it’s just another way of saying that the object has a certain amount of energy-content. The factor, c 2 , is a conversion factor because we humans stupidly use different units for mass and energy, even though the two are equivalent. (Ultimately has to do with the fact that we use different units to measure space and time in spacetime.) That energy-content does not mean useful energy. It does not necessarily represent any ability to do work, make things move, go kaboom, heat them up, whatever. It might… but then again, it might not. And the relationship applies to everything. Take a quantity of firewood and a quantity of air. Their mass together includes the latent energy that can be converted into heat by combining the firewood with the air, i.e., burning it. That heat can be used to run a machine, do some useful work. If you had a sufficiently precise instrument, and you made sure you captured every last bit of the combustion products including gases, smoke, ashes, all of it: You would find that as a result of the combustion, what remains is ever so lighter, and the difference in mass is precisely the amount of heat that was extracted from the system. In practice, this is not a measurement that we can carry out, but only because the chemical energy in firewood is so many orders of magnitude less than the rest of its energy-content, we just don’t have instruments and methods that are sensitive enough. But E = m c 2 applies everywhere, to everything. And yes, it applies to nuclear reactions as well, but it’s not why nuclear reactions can take place. Nuclear reactions can take place because the stuff that goes in — in this case, uranium — has more energy-content than the stuff that is left afterwards. Really, it’s the same thing as with the firewood+air scenario, except that the proportion of energy-content that can be extracted this way is much greater in the case of uranium fission. But, I stress again, uranium fission is not happening because of E = m c 2 . It is happening because the system (a lump of uranium) goes from a higher-energy state (intact uranium atoms) into a lower energy state (fission products, e.g., iodine, cesium, strontium atoms) and the difference in energy can be extracted. The fact that, if you were to place the fission products on a scale afterwards, they’d weigh slightly less than the original lump of uranium is really irrelevant. It is true because mass and energy-content are the same, but so what? Again, I stress, the important bit was the difference in energy-content between initial and final state, not the fact that this energy-content determines the inertia (resistance to acceleration) of the thing. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why is it so hard to believe WW2 happened for those who didn't live through it, why is WW2 so movie like in many ways?
Answer: I did not live through WW2, but it is certainly not hard to believe or movie-like for me. I was born in Budapest, nearly 20 years after the war ended. Yet I grew up in a city where, especially in the smaller side streets, the scars of war were still all too readily visible. Damaged facades, bullet holes were everywhere in those old, turn-of-the-century mostly brick-and-mortar apartment buildings. (Many still have the scars in poorer, less well-maintained parts of the city or in spots not readily visible from the outside, such as internal courtyards.) And some historical buildings were still very much in ruins, such as those on historic Castle Hill on the Buda side. Another thing that was not terribly uncommon as I was growing up was the discovery of unexploded ordnance. Radio newscasts telling us that a street, an intersection was temporarily evacuated while bomb disposal teams were on scene neutralizing the threat. Still happens, by the way, though it’s much more of a rarity nowadays. More than that, my Mom lived through the siege of the city as small girl. She has many memories that she shared with me: The air raids that sent the family to the bomb shelter at Christmas, the damaged, looted apartment to which they returned many weeks later, corpses of humans and also horses, the latter sometimes surrounded by people who were carving them up for the meat. My grandmother still lived in that same apartment when I was growing up. She had a container, a large, shiny, repurposed aluminum can that she used to store flour. The can bore English-language markings courtesy of the American Red Cross, part of a post-war aid package to help a starving population. While my Mom and her family were hiding in that shelter, my father, much older, struggled to help his Jewish first wife and child and Jewish business partner with forged documents, which kept them out of the ghetto and ultimately, quite possibly kept them off the trains heading for Auschwitz. He could have been caught, carrying forged, still blank passports for instance when he was once stopped by an Arrow Cross patrol in late 1944. He was lucky: they did not search him. And of course the country I grew up in was at the time still occupied by forces of the USSR, the country that liberated the eastern half of Europe from Nazism, only to install their own version of totalitarianism in its place. So no, although (thankfully) I did not live through WW2, it is definitely not movie-like for me. People I knew, people close to me, but also places, buildings, streets all carried, sometimes still carry, tangible memories of that war.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Isn’t it true that the general theory of relativity suggests the existence of black holes, white holes, negative value e=mc2 energy, wormholes, quantum entanglement, cosmological, constant gravitational waves, and a host of other amazing things?
Answer: No. General relativity does not “suggest” any of the above. General relativity provides one thing: a set of equations that govern the behavior of the gravitational field. That’s it. End of story. R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G T μ ν . That is all. This equation has many solutions, just like Maxwell’s equations for the electromagnetic field have many solutions. Just because something is a solution of the field equations of a theory does not mean that this solution represents physical reality. Solutions for equations like this one are constrained by conditions. These could be “boundary conditions” (e.g., the expectation that the field vanishes large distances from a source). These could be symmetry conditions (e.g., the expectation that a compact mass has a spherical gravitational field that does not depend on time.) These expectations narrow down the range of solutions. So let’s pick apart the specific points listed in the question. Well, I hope my answer puts those questions into a proper perspective. We can be impressed by the magnificence of Nature and be grateful for our ability in these modern times to actually make sense of some of it without turning explanations into science-fiction fairy tales. Nothing wrong with science-fiction, mind you; my favorite genre. We just need to be careful not to confuse it with reality. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Could TV interferences be caused by radiation from the Big Bang?
Answer: First of all, I apologize for being nitpicky, but I see this expression often and I try to offer an important clarification: there is no “radiation from the Big Bang”. There is radiation of cosmological origin, but it was produced roughly 385,000 years after the presumed Big Bang (i.e., the earliest times when matter in the universe was extremely hot and extremely dense). By this time, matter in the universe cooled down, ionized gas recombined into transparent, neutral atoms (mostly hydrogen and helium) and became transparent to its own incandescence. This radiation, redshifted by cosmic expansion, arrives today at a microwave frequency that corresponds to thermal radiation at a temperature of 2.7 K, which is to say, very near absolute zero. That is the “temperature of deep space” if you want to be poetic about it: that is to say, if you left an object floating in deep space far from anything that emits heat or light, the object will cool to this temperature and no further. At this temperature, the object would be in thermal equilibrium with “deep space”, i.e., the cosmic microwave background (CMB). It is an often heard urban legend that on an analog TV set, the “snow” or “static” you see when a channel is not broadcasting is noise from the CMB. This is not really true. A reasonable estimate is that no more than a few percent of the noise picked up by a receiver in the FM or television bands is due to the CMB; the rest is a combination of the thermal noise of the receiver and other (mostly artificial) noise sources that are present in the environment. (For some details, see this StackExchange answer.) And it would not be “interference” in the sense the word is typically used. The CMB contribution is pure thermal noise. At its worst, it would show up as additional “snow” in the screen when an analog receiver picks up a very weak signal, or a slightly worse data rate, slightly higher error rate in case of a digital receiver. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift?
Answer: Relativity theory predicts two things that can result in redshift: Clocks in a gravitational field tick slower than clocks in empty space. Consider a light source that produces green light at a frequency of 6 trillion cycles a second. Suppose this light source is in a strong gravitational field. You observe it and measure that indeed, the light source produces 6 trillion cycles a second according to a clock right next to it. But then you measure that light using an instrument in deep space. The light appears yellow. You measure it and it's comes in at only 5 trillion cycles per second according to a clock next to your receiver. Even though the two clocks (the one in the deep gravitational well and the one in deep space) are identical, flawless clocks they will tick at different rates. For ever 6 ticks of the clock in deep space, the clock in the gravitational field will tick only 5 times. As that clock counts to 5, the source emits 30 trillion cycles. The clock in deep space will count six times as those 30 trillion cycles arrive. Now the funny business is that the speed of that light will be measured both at the source and at the detector at 300,000 km/s. Fewer cycles means longer wavelength, then. So the same light that appears to leave the source with a wavelength of 500 nm (that is to say, 500 nanometers between emitted cycles) will be measured at 600 nm between cycles at the receiver in deep space. This is gravitational redshift. Now this example assumed that the locations are stationary. What if they aren't? If the distance between the light source and detector decreases, each subsequent cycle will arrive a little sooner as it had less distance to travel. Conversely, if the distance increases, each subsequent cycle takes a tad longer to arrive. So this, too, can change the number of cycles that are received over a unit of time. This is the Doppler frequency shift (redshift if the distance between source and detector is increasing). Perhaps you were thinking about cosmology. Relativity theory also predicts another important thing: In the cosmos, on the largest of scales, matter is not at rest. Things are either flying apart or coming together (that is to say, the matter density of the cosmos is either decreasing or increasing over time). In our cosmos, things appear to be flying apart. When things are flying apart, the distance between them increases over time. So there is a Doppler redshift. But as the density of matter decreases over time, so does its average gravity. So if light traveled for a long, long time it's coming from a distant past when the gravitational field was stronger so clocks were ticking more slowly compared to the present. So there is also a gravitational component to this cosmic redshift. The Doppler part dominates for relatively nearby galaxies; the gravitational part, for very distant stuff. To stress, I am not talking about the individual galaxy's own gravitational field that can cause a small amount of redshift; I am talking about the overall average gravitational field (i.e., the average magnitude, say, of the curvature scalar, to be a tad technical) that changes over time as the matter density of the cosmos decreases. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity?
Answer: A black hole does not have immense strength or infinite density. Mostly, no infinite gravity either. Take a black hole that has the same mass as the Sun. Put it in place of the Sun. Guess what happens to the Earth? Apart from the lack of sunlight (which would be bad news for us humans) absolutely nothing. The gravity of that black hole is exactly the same, finite gravity as that of the Sun. Density? Sure, a stellar sized black hole is dense. Actual black holes do not form at a mass much less than about three times the mass of the Sun. But even neutron stars are insanely dense, many trillions of times denser than water. But… this may come as a surprise but very, very large black holes are not so dense at all! When we talk about the largest supermassive black holes, they can form at densities less than the density of ordinary water. It’s only when the black hole is relatively small (by that, I mean, three times the mass of the Sun, which would be “only” a million times the mass of the Earth) that such insane densities are encountered as matter collapses into a black hole. And then, the gravity. As I said, at the same distance as the Sun, a one solar mass black hole has the same gravity as the Sun. Far from infinite. So let’s get a little closer. In the case of the Sun, the closest we can get to its center is about 700,000 kilometers, before we collide with the Sun’s surface. At that distance, solar gravity is powerful (about 30 times the gravity of the Earth at sea level) but far from infinite. And you cannot get any closer, because now you would be inside the Sun. But now take that black hole. A black hole with the same mass as the Sun has an effective radius of only about 3 kilometers. Going from 700,000 to 3… as you know, gravitational acceleration is proportional to the inverse square of distance. So now we are up to trillions of times Earth gravity! And that’s just the Newtonian result. Once we take relativity theory into account, there is, after all, one infinity to deal with. At exactly the event horizon, you would literally need an infinitely powerful rocket exerting an infinite force to hover. But that’s because the event horizon has this strange spacetime geometry: “hovering” means the same thing as moving at the vacuum speed of light. Which, as we know, is not possible without an infinitely powerful rocket. But anywhere outside the event horizon, gravity is finite. And it’s strong not because the black hole’s gravity is stronger than the gravity of another object of the same mass, but simply because you can get that much closer to it. As another example, take the Earth. Its radius is roughly 6,370 kilometers or just under 4,000 miles. The radius of a black hole of the same mass? Less than 9 millimeters. Just over one third of an inch. Imagine something with a diameter of two thirds of an inch, not larger than what one of my cats would produce when he is constipated, a pebble really, that weighs as much as the entire planet Earth. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum?
Answer: Yes, electromagnetic waves have both energy and momentum. When an object emits some light in a specific direction, it is pushed backwards ever so slightly. Similarly, when an object absorbs or reflects light, it is pushed by that light. (Experimental spacecraft with solar sails use the momentum of sunlight to accelerate.) As to sound waves, you can even visualize it. A sound wave is a pressure wave. Recall what happens when a very loud sound wave hits, say, a window pane. The glass shatters. It shatters because of the force (change in momentum) as momentum from the incoming sound wave is transferred to the glass. So yes, sound waves also carry momentum. As do waves in general. Here, I just stumbled upon this article by a Charles S. Peskin that tells you everything you need to know about the momentum of waves. For a second, I thought it was the Peskin of "Peskin and Schroeder" fame, i.e., one of the authors of perhaps the best current textbook on quantum field theory, but no, that's another Pesking, Michael E. Even so, this write-up on wave momenta is good. Yes there's math but I think also enough explanation for it to make sense even if you skip over most of the equations. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If not wearing your seatbelt was a choice instead of law, would you buckle up or go without?
Answer: As a driver? Absolutely, I’d use my seatbelt. I’ve been in accidents. (Fortunately none involving personal injury to anyone). Therefore, I know both from theory and from practice what it means when the seatbelt not only keeps you safer (which you may not care about) but keeps you behind the wheel. Which means that if, after the accident, the vehicle is still (somewhat) controllable, you might regain control. You may be able to stop the vehicle before it causes additional harm to others. You may still be able to steer, preventing injury to others. All this is kind of hard to do if you have already left the vehicle through the windshield as a wingless projectile, or ended up on the rear seat as the vehicle spun about. Questions like this remind me of questions I sometimes see concerning religion: “If you are an atheist, what stops you from committing certain sins?” Here are a few words or phrases to contemplate: “Empathy”. “Compassion”. “Social responsibility”. In other words, even if you don’t care about your own safety in an accident, you could still consider that a seat belt might help you keep others, including quite possibly your own loved ones in that vehicle, safer. I know, I know, outlandish commie propaganda and all but hey, even Ayn Rand advocated enlightened self-interest: that is to say, the recognition that even if your own well-being takes precedence over that of the others, acting at least occasionally in the interests of the group might actually be beneficial to the individual…

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them?
Answer: They are neither white nor lighter than the space around them. In classical general relativity, a black hole is truly black: it absorbs all light that hits it, and emits absolutely nothing. You really cannot get more black than that. Even with Hawking radiation, the situation is similar. Sure, black holes radiate. But astrophysical black holes have Hawking temperatures that are just a tiny, tiny fraction of the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. In other words, even in this case, the black hole is a lot more black than the cosmos: it absorbs many orders of magnitude more radiation than it emits. So that’s why they are called black. Again, you really cannot get more black than these things. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Since the Bekenstein Bound and BH event horizons are the most information dense places possible, how probable is it that they are conscious?
Answer: I think this question was inspired, in part, by a misconception of the meaning, “information”. Allow me to show two character sequences of approximately equal length. First, this: To be, or not to be: that is the question: Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles. And now this: 8RfUd8yHHftN5juY5MPME1SxwcE7lNOAjjo6Q1jlKyK0hdwk 8DU86TeOGcyJZ1Gk2cEMAtRlBK1G0Sy1WU2xFwJ4sBCeQv15 qBV4pJKGcY28npr4GBDXoJQ1aHw09P9xGrJMqjJ3Jj8pXRWO C5jUXwiEWn2cLNFH91Qxnws3 Which of these contain more “information”? It is understandable if you thought it was the first example. The second case is, after all, just some printable ASCII gibberish, no useful content whatsoever. But that does not mean no information! In fact, if you feed both examples to compression algorithms, you will find that the algorithm does a much better job compressing Shakespeare’s lines than the random sequence of letters. In the end, significantly fewer bytes, significantly less information is needed to fully reconstruct the first example compared to the second. But we don’t even need abstract algorithms. Let me show you what I mean: To b, or nt to b: tht s th qstn: Whethr 'ts noblr in th mnd to suffr Th slngs nd arrws of outrgs frtne, Or to tk arms gnst a sea of trbls. Look at this text. I am betting that if you are a native English speaker, you have no trouble reading it even though almost 20% of the letters are missing. You can still unambiguously reconstruct the original. In contrast, if I were to remove but a single letter from the second example containing gibberish, you’d have no way of knowing what that letter was. There is no redundancy. Everything there is important information. We tend to associate information with order. We think there is more information in, say, in a picture on the CRT of an old-fashioned analog television set as opposed to the “snow” we see when the channel is not broadcasting. But in reality, the opposite is true: random noise carries a lot more information than an orderly broadcast. Of course no one said that that information is of any use. Put enough monkeys behind typewriters and the result may even include the four lines of Shakespeare above. But it will also include all other possible combinations of 170-odd letters and symbols, and you’d have no way of knowing what is useful and what is not. So no, a black hole’s event horizon is not conscious. If anything, it’s the opposite. Imagine your brain scrambled in a food processor. The result represents a lot more “information”! But a lot less knowledge. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: Why do people who use the metric system assume that 9meters is 32 feet when gravity is really 9.81m per sec per sec?
Answer: Well, for starters, “gravity” is not really 9.81 m/s^2. What is 9.81 m/s^2 is the average gravitational acceleration at sea level on a minor planet called Earth in one of the popular languages spoken by its inhabitants. The units in this expression were historically derived from the actual properties of the same planet (notably, its size and its rate of rotation) but that’s beside the point. In a small number of places on this planet, however, inhabitants prefer to use a different unit for length, originally inspired by the typical size of one of their appendages they call “feet”. The conversion factor is a simple one: 1 foot equals 0.3048 meters or conversely, 1 m = (1/0.3048) ft. The rest is easily done by way of using a calculator: 9.81 m / s^2 = 9.81 (1/0.3048) ft / s^2 = 9.81/0.3048 ft / s^2 = 32.2 ft / s^2, rounded to three significant digits in the decimal number system these inhabitants prefer (undoubtedly because their forepaws happen to have ten appendages in total, called “digits”). This simple calculation should not challenge any of the adult or near-adult inhabitants of the aforementioned planet, whether or not they are regular users of what they call the metric system or other systems of measurement. Utilizing the same skills and a calculating device, they can also easily calculate that 9 m = (9 / 0.3048) ft = 29.527559 ft to a reasonable number of decimal digits. Indeed, most of the inhabitants master the necessary skill set in an institution called “grade school”. Yes, I know, strange planet. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do atheists view adultery? Is it morally wrong to cheat on the person you are with, or is individual sexual freedom more important?
Answer: Since Quora threw this question at me, allow me to respond with a question of my own. Is fear of God the only reason you do not cheat on your poor spouse? In other words, is it all about you, never the other person? Is this all transactional for you? You act nice not because you have empathy, conscience, a sense of social responsibility, but because this is how you make your down payment for a nice room with a good view and great room service in the afterlife? If that is the case, shame on you. If that is the case, I’d rather go to hell than spend an eternity with the likes of you in your so-called “heaven”. I have no desire the spend any time in a heaven of hypocrites, sycophants of some vain, vengeful, tyrannical deity. But no, I will not seek a path to hell by cheating on my beautiful wife, nor by stealing, killing or otherwise doing harm to others, be they strangers or people close to me. Not because I fear your imaginary sky daddy. But because I am, or at least aspire to be, a reasonably decent human being living in a reasonably decent human society.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Are atheists aware that they're about to go to hell for quadrillions of years? In hell, you get tormented everyday.
Answer: Suppose you are right. Suppose there is an afterlife, and a day comes when we are judged, with our souls perhaps condemned to eternity. Am I going to be judged by my deeds? Sure, I made mistakes. To quote the immortal Sinatra, regrets I’ve had a few, but then again, too few to mention. And yes, there were times when I bit off more than I could chew. But I ate it up, faced it all, and, well, did my best to stand tall. Will your favorite deity or deities then judge me by my deeds? By how I lived my life? In that case, I have little to fear. Or is your deity a shallow, vain hypocrite? Someone who cares not how you lived your life, only takes church attendance? Who offers an afterlife where those who proclaim their “love of god” win because no matter what sins they commit, so long as they dutifully arrive for Sunday service, all is forgiven? Well, if that’s your deity, I say bugger him. I’d rather spend an eternity in hell than be a sycophant in a tyrant’s court. But you know what? I think you have it wrong. At least if you are of the Christian persuasion. Read some Dante. Consider what happens in his vision of hell. Compare the fate of the virtuous pagans — folks who are in hell for the sin of not acknowledging Christ, either through no fault of their own (newborn, folks who lived before Christ or in far-off lands) or folks who rejected Christ for reasons of conscience — against the fate of hypocrites, including numerous popes. The sole punishment of the virtuous pagans is that they don’t enjoy God’s presence. Otherwise, they are untouched by Satan. The hypocrites, in turn, ended up in one of the deepest pits of hell. Or going back further, think of the Old Testament, the roots of all Abrahamic religions, the story of how humans were cast out of the Garden of Eden. Humans who were created in “God’s image”, which is to say, endowed with free will. A free will that was then tested when Satan tempted them to eat the forbidden fruit: Fruit from the tree of knowledge, knowledge to tell good and evil apart. In other words: a conscience. This Abrahamic god is not interested in blind obedience or church attendance. He is wiser than that. He is interested in how you listen to your conscience. And that’s why I do not fear your imaginary afterlife. Because even though I do not believe in deities or a supernatural afterlife, I know enough about the Abrahamic family of religions to know that God does not rule by fear. If you allow yourself to be guided by fear of hell, you are already on the wrong path, of that I am certain. And that is true whether or not God actually exists.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can a massless photon be depicted with kinetic energy since kinetic energy involves mass, yet a photon is massless which diametrically discredits Planck's and Einstein's disjointed theories?
Answer: Kinetic energy does not necessarily involve mass. For particles that have nonzero rest mass, the expression for kinetic includes their mass. But kinetic energy is a much more general concept, a constant of the motion if you wish, applicable to all systems that are governed by equations that are time translation invariant. And yes, that includes massless photons. In the “disjointed” theory of relativity, of course, time is an observer-dependent concept. Invariance under spacetime translations, however, implies the conservation of a four-dimensional quantity, the so-called four-momentum of the object. Once a specific coordinate system is picked, this four-momentum can be split into an energy term and a three-dimensional conventional momentum term. But this split is, again, observer-dependent. For objects with rest mass, there exists a reference frame in which the object is, well, at rest. In this reference frame, obviously there is no kinetic energy. There is still an energy term, however; it’s the rest mass-energy of the object. In all other reference frames, the energy term is the sum of the rest mass-energy and the kinetic energy of the object. If the object is massless, however, it has no rest mass and no rest frame; the energy term is entirely due to kinetic energy in all reference frames. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is a photon? Is it an object? I ask because photons are always moving at lightspeed, and no object can reach lightspeed.
Answer: Well, technically, an “object” can travel at the vacuum speed of light (in fact, only at the vacuum speed of light) if it has no rest mass. In that case, the dispersion relation E 2 = ( m c 2 ) 2 + ( p c ) 2 becomes just E = p c , that is, the momentum and energy of the object are proportional to one another. Of course an “object”, or test particle, is just an abstraction of classical physics. We know that such things do not exist in a quantum reality. Nor are electrons, photons, etc., “objects”. Even in ordinary quantum mechanics, they are not miniature cannonballs: they are characterized not by positions or momenta but by states, which may translate into specific position or momentum values under the right circumstances that we perhaps call a measurement, but most of the time, the states are more complicated than that. But ordinary quantum mechanics really doesn’t know about photons. For that, we need quantum field theory, in the form of quantum electrodynamics. We know from Maxwell’s theory that far away from charges, in otherwise empty space, influences in the electromagnetic field travel as plane waves at the invariant velocity c . (This invariance is what inspired special relativity after all). In the quantum field theory, the energy of these waves can only increase or decrease by predetermined units, or quanta. When something interacts with the electromagnetic field, this increase or decrease registers, or can be interpreted as, the emission or the absorption of a particle. We call these quanta or particles photons. So what travels at the vacuum speed of light is, well, light, electromagnetic waves far away from sources (charges). Particle-like behavior is observed when these waves are emitted or absorbed, leading us to the mental model of thinking of a ray of light as a bunch of photons (which is misleading since we know for a fact since the beginning of the 19th century, the famous Arago-spot and all, that light is a wave, not corpuscular in nature). Short story: Particles in quantum field theory are not miniature cannonballs, but unit excitations of fields. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can general relativity be considered a quantum theory? If yes, what are some examples of its application in that field?
Answer: No, general relativity is not a quantum theory. It is a classical field theory, like Maxwell’s electromagnetism. Maxwell’s theory can be “quantized”, which is to say it is possible to turn it into a mathematically self-consistent quantum field theory. The biggest problem with quantization is that the resulting quantum field theory may appear nonsensical at first, producing divergent (infinite) results. However, there in many cases, these divergences are superficial in nature, and a more thorough analysis reveals that quantities that correspond to things we can actually observe consistently remain finite. These theories are said to be renormalizable. Unfortunately, for general relativity this approach does not lead to a renormalizable quantum field theory. Which is why so much effort has been made in the past several decades, trying to come up with alternative ways to tame general relativity and arrive at a self-consistent quantum theory. The biggest problem is lack of data: quantum effects of gravitation, if they exist at all, are so weak, they may forever remain undetectable. So we have competing approaches but few or no hints from Nature as to which one is worth pursuing. But no, as I said at the beginning of my answer, general relativity is a classical theory of gravitation, not a quantum theory. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there any visible light from the Big Bang or just radiation? If there is visible light, what color would it be and why? If not, how do we know that the Big Bang occurred?
Answer: If by “Big Bang”, we mean the presumed initial moment of the universe, there is no light, radiation, or anything from this moment. And we do not know if such a moment occurred or not. But that is because the unfortunately named (let’s not forget, the expression was coined by one of the theory’s critics, the astronomer Sir Fred Hoyle, back in 1949, when he was an advocate for an alternative, “steady state” cosmological model) “Big Bang paradigm” is not about any big bangs, really. It’s about the recognition that we live in an expanding cosmos, and the science of extrapolating backwards, based on what we know about gravitation and particle physics, trying to reconstruct the universe’s past history. We can go back to when the universe was presumably 385,000 years old, give or take, and it first became transparent to its own incandescence. This white light, which was emitted everywhere in every direction, can be seen today as the microwave background radiation. Wherever you look in the cosmos, behind everything else you see a distant patch of gas, emitting light; except that this light, its wavelength increased by more than a thousandfold by cosmic expansion, is only detectable by antenna as radio waves. We can go back further, based on science that we know, science that we tested in the laboratory, in large particle accelerators. In fact, we can go back to when the universe was roughly 1 picosecond old, and the conditions resembled the highest-energy collisions in the Large Hadron Collider. But no further. Speculating beyond that is truly pointless. We have no data, no basis for comparison. Was that first picosecond really a picosecond? Or an eternity? Was there a “before” or was there truly a singular beginning and talking about “before” is like asking about Santa’s home a mile north of the North Pole? We simply don’t know. But we do know that we live in an expanding universe and that in the distant past, the universe was hot and dense. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why has the cosmic microwave background not been considered to predate time itself, and is therefore infinite?
Answer: The cosmic microwave background has nothing to do with predating time. It has to do with a specific epoch in an expanding and cooling cosmos, when the bulk matter in the cosmos (mostly hydrogen and helium) was becoming just cold enough to turn from an ionized gas into a gas of electrically neutral atoms. The radiation we see is thermal radiation (incandescence) from this hot gas, emitted everywhere, at that epoch, now capable of traveling freely in all directions. This radiation was emitted when the gas was roughly 3000 K in temperature. The cosmos has continued to expand since then. As a result the wavelength of this radiation has stretched by a factor greater than a thousand, resulting in today’s measurement of 2.7 K as the temperature associated with the radiation (now detected in the form of radio waves). But, I stress, all we are looking at here is opaque, hot, incandescent gas. Looking in the same direction tomorrow, the volume of gas we saw today is now transparent; the light we see tomorrow is light emitted slightly earlier by a slightly more distant volume of gas. That’s why the CMB never stops: Behind every volume of gas we see in a given day in a given direction, there’s more gas behind it, from which light takes a little longer to arrive. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do photons in a laser beam stick together so well because they are attracted to each other gravitationally and electromagnetically?
Answer: First of all, forget any mental image of photons that you might have as miniature cannonballs flying together. That’s not what photons are. In classical electromagnetism, light is just a plane wave. In case of an ordinary light source, there are plane waves with different phases and frequencies mixed together. In a coherent light source, all plane waves have the same frequency and phase. Photons are the “quanta” of the electromagnetic field. That is, in the quantum field theory of light, a plane wave of a given frequency cannot have arbitrary intensities. Its intensity will increase or decrease by discrete units. These units, or quanta, are what we call photons. Photons are examples of bosons, quanta that are subject to the Bose-Einstein statistic. You may have heard of the Pauli exclusion principle according to which fermions cannot be in the same quantum state. Bosons, on the other hand, love being in the same quantum state, so once they are in the same quantum state, they are less likely to become decoherent over time than classical (non-quantum) waves with similar properties. This also applies to the stimulated emission of laser light: Not only is it coherent light (all waves at the same frequency and phase) but that coherent light remains coherent with a higher probability than it would in classical electromagnetism. This changes the statistic when the photons from a laser beam arrive. So no, photons in a laser beam don't "stick together" due to gravity or electromagnetism. The apparent "sticking together" is a consequence of quantum physics, specifically the bosonic nature of photons and the process of stimulated emission in lasers. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there empirical evidence against John Moffat's modified gravity (MOG), also known as Scalar-Tensor-Vector-Gravity (STVG)?
Answer: Disclaimer: I have worked with John Moffat so my views may not be impartial. The essence of Moffat’s gravity is that metrical gravity is stronger than it would be in general relativity; however, this is canceled out by a repulsive force due to a vector field interaction of finite range. For a galaxy, this means that in its inner region (where cancelation due to the vector field is present) the behavior is Newtonian; farther from the center, galaxies rotate faster because the vector repulsion is now absent and thus, gravity is stronger. The coupling parameter that governs the strength of these interactions, and the mass parameter that governs the range of the vector force are both scalar fields (perhaps the same scalar field in disguise), so the values vary from system to system. As a result, the theory can do away with the need for dark matter. Dark energy may or may not have to stay. A key feature of the theory, which distinguishes it perhaps from families of modified gravity theories that offer behavior consistent with MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is that whereas MOND-like theories are governed by a fixed acceleration scale, MOG is governed by scales determined by the mass, and distance from, the source. MOG survives many observational tests. In the solar system, treating the Sun as a single source, the parameters of the theory have negligible values so we get general relativity at the post-Newtonian level. Multimessenger observations (neutron star mergers observed using both electromagnetic and gravitational waves) are consistent with MOG as, unlike many other theories, MOG only has one metric which implies that electromagnetic and gravitational radiation propagate at the same speed. MOG is also consistent with the apparent Newtonian behavior of massive but compact galaxies, as well as the Newtonian behavior of wide binaries. And MOG may actually work well, better even than the standard cosmological model, when it comes to colliding galaxy clusters, including the famed Bullet Cluster that was supposed to be a slam dunk case in favor of standard cosmology, but also clusters that challenge the standard model. And MOG is at least approximately consistent with large-scale cosmological observations, including the large-scale distribution of matter and the cosmic microwave background (though some problems remain). Personally, I find that the biggest challenge (which can make or break the theory) is to find a consistent analytic formulation for the scalar fields’ mass dependence in the weak field limit. This has not been done yet; we have semianalytic formulas that associate values for these parameters with compact sources, but that’s the best we’ve been able to derive. Resolving this question, along with addressing the assumption that MOG, despite the presence of the vector force, satisfies the weak equivalence principle (which kind of implies that perhaps there is a metrical formulation of the theory) are issues that I consider vey important but frustratingly difficult to tackle properly.

Question: Considering that the event horizon around Sagittarius A black hole reaches millions of degrees in temperature, how far away from the black hole itself would you have to be for the temperature to be a comfortable 70°F?
Answer: The Hawking-temperature associated with the Sgr A* event horizon region is not millions of degrees. It’s not even single-digit degrees. It’s a small fraction of a trillionth of a degree kelvin above absolute zero. The accretion disk (rapidly swirling, infalling material) around Sgr A* can reach millions of degrees due to internal friction and collisions. At no distance from it would you enjoy “a comfortable 70 F”, though. The bulk thermal radiation coming from this accretion disk is in the form of hard X-rays. We can calculate how far you’d have to be from it to receive a flux that would be consistent with being in a room with walls at 70 F, but I assure you, it would not be comfortable at all. Rather, though the energy deposited by those X-rays may keep you warm, your body would rapidly suffer irreversible damage as it absorbs such quantities of ionizing radiation, breaking up molecular bonds, destroying your cells’ DNA. Question: What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++?
Answer: The propagator for a massless scalar field, which obeys the Klein-Gordon equation ∂ μ ∂ μ ϕ = 0 , can be derived from the Green’s function of this equation, ∂ μ ∂ μ G ( x − y ) = δ 4 ( x − y ) that, in momentum space, becomes − k 2 ~ G ( k ) = − 1 , hence ~ G ( k ) = 1 k 2 + i ϵ , where we introduced a small imaginary term, as usual, to avoid the singularity at k = 0. By itself, this expression is not something you would compute numerically in a language such as C++. You may be able to derive expressions of this sort in computer algebra (either general purpose CAS with specialized packages or special purpose systems). The propagator is used in combination with the vertex rules of a theory to compute cross-sections corresponding to particle interactions. That computation itself may not be trivial as it involves divergent integrals that may need to be regularized in order to obtain meaningful results for observable quantities. In short, no, unless you first use C++ to build a CAS for quantum field theory, you would not be using C++ for this type of computation. You might use a CAS to derive an expression for an observable quantity that you then import into a C++ program for numerical evaluation (perhaps as part of a larger computation) but the propagator on its own is not something you’d likely use in C++. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can Hawking radiation (absorption of mass by a hypothetical particle and destruction of mass by a star) occur in a neutron star? Is it possible or not and why?
Answer: The answer is yes, and I can explain why both using simple reasoning and the math. On the simple reasoning side: If a black hole radiates Hawking radiation in the present, it cannot be because it’s a black hole as the black hole has not formed yet. The particles collapsing into a black hole take forever (as seen by outside observers) to reach the limit when they’d form an event horizon. This is the essence, e.g., of the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper that, in 1939, described for the first time this process of “continued contraction”. This also means that, at least in principle, the particles may interact with one another in the last minute, second, picosecond before forming a horizon (as measured in their own reference frame) and turn around; we can never be 100% certain that this won’t happen as the black hole has not formed yet! So perhaps it never will… yet there is Hawking radiation. But never mind the fairy tale. I hold in my hand a paper, well, a single sheet of paper really as Hawking’s paper really is short: It’s his 1974 publication in Nature, titled “Black hole explosions?” Let me quote two key sentences from this paper: “The β i j will not be zero because the time dependence of the metric during the collapse will cause a certain amount of mixing of positive and negative frequencies. […] The number of particles created and emitted to infinity in a gravitational collapse can therefore be determined by calculating the coefficients β i j . ” In short: What is needed for Hawking-radiation is not a horizon but a time asymmetry; specifically, the asymmetry due to collapse, as a result of which the past and the future are not identical. What this tells us is that any collapsing cloud of matter will emit Hawking radiation unless the collapse is halted by some interaction and the configuration becomes static. In the case of a black hole, the collapse never ends. In other cases, it may. But so long as the collapse is in-progress, Hawking radiation follows, according to Hawking’s own reasoning. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can quantum computers, optical computers, new semiconductors, improved energy efficiency, and various other methods make a 10^24flops computer (1 million times faster than today's speed) possible in 30 years?
Answer: Yes, except for the “quantum computer” bit. If nothing else, massively parallel architectures may produce extreme computing capacity. But quantum computers are not about speed or processing power. They are about doing things differently. Instead of operating on distinct digits, quantum computers internally operate on continuous quantities, namely the phase of the wavefunction in some shape or form. This effectively makes them analog computers, but with a twist: it is possible in principle to introduce error correction that makes a quantum computer capable of emulating an error-free quantum computer. The hard part, however, is that this error correction is possible only if the quantum computer is sufficiently well isolated from its environment, so that the wavefunction governing its behavior is determined entirely by the computer itself, not by the environment. The required level of isolation, or threshold, has not been achieved yet and some (myself included) wonder if it ever will be. If this threshold is not reached, truly scalable quantum computing will not become reality. But let’s suppose my skepticism is misplaced and the threshold theorem is beaten. So we have scalable quantum computers. Does this mean exaflops and such? Certainly not. The point of quantum computers is not speed. It’s their ability to run certain algorithms that have no counterparts on digital computers. That allows a (slow) quantum computer solve certain families of problems that would take an eternity to solve even with the fastest conceivable digital computer. These problems include, e.g., problems in number theory, which would allow a quantum computer, in principle, to break encryption algorithms. Meanwhile, offshoots of quantum computer research show promise in specific areas; e.g., quantum annealing to solve tough optimization problems. But, I stress, such solutions, though valuable in their own right, are not about the core promise of scalable quantum computing. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do white people ask for forgiveness for slavery?
Answer: I am white. I was born in Budapest, Hungary. My mother’s family on her father’s side has Romanian roots, even a very Romanian surname. As far as I know, a few generations ago his ancestors were peasants, serfs, at best a few of them perhaps tradesmen. On my maternal grandmother’s side, my great-grandparents, I am told, owned a stable in the late 19th century, which they lost in a bad business decision and thus ended up as live-in servants with a wealthier Jewish family. (May explain why, despite not being Jewish myself, I was brought up with more Yiddish words and expressions in my vocabulary than many of my Jewish friends.) My father was old when I was born. His father was a civil engineer in pre-WWI Temesvár, now Timisoara in present-day Romania. The family was well off, since being an engineer in those days meant something in the social hierarchy. I don’t know much about other ancestors except that they, too, were from all over the place, mostly I believe from Transylvania; as the family had no roots in nobility as far as I know, I am pretty certain that there, too, we’d find a mix of serfs, tradesmen and the like. In short, I’m pretty sure that going back, say, 200 years, if you found all of my ancestors, most of them would be working land they didn’t own, with limited freedom of movement. So tell me again, what the bleep am I supposed to apologize for? Oh wait, you judged me by the color of my skin as opposed to the content of my character? Sigh.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Was the German mathematician Hilbert's final derivation of the general relativity found to contain a key error by subsequent peer scholars? So Einstein is still regarded as the first person to publish the correct equations of general relativity?
Answer: I think it was a bit more nuanced than that. Einstein and Hilbert corresponded frequently in 1915, as they were both working on the problem of finding the field equations of gravitation. Einstein was trying to discover the field equations more or less heuristically. He was not concerned with the nature of matter. He left the stress-energy tensor essentially unconstrained other than its basic symmetry properties. His theory was a theory of gravitation, not matter. Hilbert, on the other hand, inspired in part by earlier work by Mie, was more specific. His stress-energy tensor was intended to be representative of what we today would call a classical "theory of everything", encompassing electromagnetic fields and matter. The two corrresponding frequently in November 1915. Based on what we know (see, e.g., Abraham Pais's scientific biography of Einstein), I think it is fair to say that the physical theory of general relativity is undeniably Einstein's (Hilbert himself referred to this as Einstein's theory.) It seems likely that they both discovered the field equations independently, though undoubtedly, they both benefited from their frequent correspondence. Hilbert deserves credit for showing us the way to derive the field equations of gravitation from an action principle, as opposed to just postulating them like Einstein did. It should be stressed perhaps that by late 1915, the goal was in sight and the nature of the theory that Einstein sought was clearly understood. The missing bit? It seemed clear that the gravitational field is represented by the contracted Riemann curvature tensor, i.e., the Ricci-tensor R μ ν . However, the Ricci tensor does not have the symmetry properties associated with the stress-energy tensor of matter, which is to say, the Ricci-tensor is not divergence-free. The key final step in formulating the field equations is the inclusion of the − 1 2 R g μ ν term in the field equations. This term would follow from Hilbert's action, but based on, e.g., surviving galley proofs, it appears that this final form was not yet present in Hilbert's initial draft, only in later (1916) revisions. (See also General relativity priority dispute - Wikipedia for some details.) Hilbert's "mistake" if it can be called that is that he was perhaps too ambitious: Using Mie's work, he was trying to construct "the foundations of physics" (the explicit title of his paper). In contrast, Einstein was focusing on "the field equations of gravitation" (that was the actual title he used). Hilbert's original approach, as explained by Pais, also contained mistakes not related to the specific form of the field equations. Further, Pais suggests (and he’s probably right) that although the two men corresponded frequently, they pursued very different approaches and different goals, and may have “talked past each other”, neither paying sufficient attention to absorb the approach of the other. Today, we call the tensor G μ ν = R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν the Einstein tensor; the field equations of gravitation are the Einstein equations; however, the action integral from which these field equations can be derived, S = ∫ d 4 x √ − g ( 1 2 κ R + L m a t t e r ) is called the Einstein-Hilbert action. Einstein and Hilbert had a bit of a dispute but their later correspondence remains friendly. The reason for the dispute probably had nothing to do with the actual discoveries in late November 1915, and may have had something to do with Einstein feeling that Hilbert plagiarized some ideas he presented in a talk (again, according to Pais). Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can Schrodinger's equation be proven to accurately describe quantum mechanics? Are there alternative methods for dealing with quantum mechanics?
Answer: Schrödinger’s equation defines nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. It can be deduced from the classical Hamiltonian, or from the canonical commutation relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , but either way: nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is Schrödinger’s equation. It’s not “proven” (never will be) beyond showing that the math is self-consistent; is is validated when experiments confirm the equation’s predictions. There are, of course, alternatives. There is relativistic quantum particle mechanics in the form of Dirac’s equation. There is relativistic quantum field theory, which kind of implies either the Dirac or the Schrödinger equation in the appropriate limit. And then there are tentative theoretical approaches that attempt to generalize the commutation relation, e.g., by introducing a length scale. The Dirac equation and quantum field theory (in the form of the Standard Model of particle physics) are mathematically self-consistent and are validated by experiment. Alternatives, not so much. Even when the math itself is robust, there is no validation in the form of observational evidence. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What does "non-local literally mean? Why is it important? How did Bell's theorem prove it?
Answer: Bell’s theorem offers insight into how quantum nonlocality works by looking at how distant events in quantum physics are correlated in ways that cannot happen in the classical world. But first, allow me to offer the “classic” classical example: socks. Suppose you travel. You pack your favorite pair of socks. Upon arrival in your hotel room in a distant land, you unpack and realize that only half the pair is present in your suitcase. You instantly gain knowledge that the other half is back at home, thousands of miles away, in your socks drawer. No magic here, of course. Although you only just observed it, the information was there all along. It was in the form of a “local” (carried with you all along) “hidden” (in your suitcase) variable. So now let’s take a look at a quantum physics experiment. We send two particles (say, two electrons) in different directions. The electrons are correlated: their total angular momentum is zero. We then measure both electrons at their respective arrival locations. If the spin of one of them is “up”, the other will be “down”, as expected. Conservation laws are, after all, strict and absolute. So far so good, this is just like the aforementioned socks. But now we introduce a twist. We now change the orientation of one of the measurement devices a little. The two receiving locations are no longer parallel, so we do not expect perfect correlation. But we do expect some correlation. Quantum physics predicts a correlation between the two locations that is just “too good” in a sense. It cannot be explained by classical physics, by local hidden variables. The electron at one of the locations somehow “knows” what the electron at the other location is doing, despite the distance between them, despite the fact that it’s not even clear which electron is measured first, as that depends on who is looking (i.e., the relativistic reference frame in which we describe the experiment). This is the essence of the mathematical statement that is known as Bell’s inequality. Conservation laws in quantum physics are generally like this. You cannot nail them down to any particular location or moment in time, but when you look at a quantum system that is isolated from its environment, it always obeys conservation laws exactly (no probabilities here, conservation laws are exact). Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does semiclassical gravity work and why does it not break down at the Planck length?
Answer: Semiclassical gravity amounts to the idea that we keep gravity classical, but describe matter using quantum field theory on the metrical background of gravity; we then use the expectation value of the stress-energy-momentum tensor in Einstein’s field equations, i.e., we write R μ ν + 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G ⟨ T ⟩ μ ν . Now this equation does not care about the Planck scale. The underlying quantum field theory may or may not work at or beyond the Planck scale, but if it does not, that’s not semiclassical gravity’s fault. It is generally assumed that gravity is a quantum field theory, and therefore, using the classical term on the left-hand side of the field equations is not going to work at or beyond the Planck scale, where quantum gravity becomes significant or dominant. But we don’t know this. Perhaps this ugly hybrid works across all scales! Another potential objection is that semiclassical gravity is at odds with the concept of wavefunction collapse. However, this objection is valid only if we treat wavefunction collapse as a physical process, as opposed to a mere mathematical convenience. This, really is the problem with gravity. Semiclassical gravity works a little too well. There are no observational clues that would a) invalidate it and b) point is in the right direction towards a better theory. The problem of quantum gravity is often described as some kind of fundamental incompatibility between general relativity and quantum field theory. That’s not exactly true; we can resolve this incompatibility in different ways. But which way? Without observational clues, we’re groping in the blind. Answer: Well, “derive” is a strong word since the equations of quantum physics are not so much derived but deduced. The Schrödinger equation is deduced from the classical Hamiltonian: H = p 2 2 m + V ( q ) , by observing that we can substitute − i ℏ ∇ in place of p (and perhaps i ℏ ∂ t in place of H , and the equation remains valid, both sides now being operator-valued, acting on the function ψ = e i ( p q − H t ) / ℏ , and then turning the tables around and opting to solve for ψ instead: H ψ = − ℏ 2 2 m ∇ 2 ψ + V ( q ) ψ . Unfortunately this approach works only in the case of the nonrelativistic Hamiltonian. The relativistic equivalent would be the dispersion relation, which we could write as H 2 = p 2 + m 2 , but “quantizing” this will not produce meaningful results. The presence of second powers ultimately leads to an equation that predicts, e.g., negative probabilities in the Copenhagen interpretation. Dirac’s “magnificent trick” amounted to taking the “square root” of this equation in the form (I’m now using ℏ = 1 to keep things simple): H ψ = ( − i α ∇ + β m ) ψ . This approach will not work if α and β are numbers. But what if they are not? What if they obey a set of commutation relations like α i β + β α i = 0 , α i α j + α j α i = 0 , α 2 i = 1 ,    β 2 = 1. (NB: α is vector-valued, hence the indices.) There. This works if α i and β are constructed using the Dirac-matrices γ μ , and the function ψ on which they act is itself a four-component entity. Written in the usual relativistic form, then, we end up with i γ μ ∂ μ ψ − m ψ = 0. As it turns out, the four components of ψ can describe the two spin states of a fermion (like the electron) and the corresponding two spin states of its antiparticle. As I said, it is not so much a derivation but a deduction. It is mathematically consistent but that does not mean anything. What matters is that it is validated against reality: the equation accurately describes what we see in actual experiments. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do objects bend or curve spacetime to produce gravity?
Answer: They don’t. Seriously, they don’t. Don’t believe me? See if you believe this quote: “It is wrong to think that 'geometrization' is something essential. It is only a kind of crutch [Eselsbrücke] for the finding of numerical laws. Whether one links 'geometrical' intuitions with a theory is a ... private matter.” You know who wrote this? A chap who went by the name A. Einstein*. Objects, indeed all material fields with a nonvanishing stress-energy-momentum tensor, serve as sources of the gravitational field. The gravitational field interacts with matter universally and minimally. Universal, in this context, means that the actual material constitution of matter makes no difference; the gravitational field does not care what matter is made of, only its stress-energy-momentum. Minimal, in this context, means that the interaction is confined to a mathematical form that determines inner products and volume elements and nothing else. A field that interacts with matter minimally can be reinterpreted using the language of covariant derivatives as geometry. Usually, this geometry depends on the material properties of matter; e.g., for electromagnetism, this geometric interpretation depends on the charge-to-mass ratio of the matter particle involved. Not so in gravity: Because it is universal, the “gravitational charge-to-mass ratio” is the same for everything, so the geometry is universal. But that means that everything is subject to this geometry, including our senses and our instruments. It is the only geometry that can be observed, so we can elevate this to a principle, or interpretation, and suggest that gravitation determines the geometry of spacetime. Whether or not we should think of gravitation this way is another matter. Gravitation is more than geometry. The gravitational field has a physical existence. It carries energy and momentum in the form of gravitational waves, just as the Maxwell field carries energy and momentum in the form of electromagnetic waves, such as light. Einstein understood this, hence his advice not to take the geometric interpretation as dogma. Matter does not “bend or curve spacetime”. Matter is the source of the gravitational field. This gravitational field affects everything universally, including any attempt to detect the geometry of spacetime. But spacetime is not a physical thing; matter and the gravitational field are physical things. *Einstein to Reichenbach, 8 April 1926, as translated by Lehmkuhl, in Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326, DOI: 10.1016/j.shpsb.2013.08.002 If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is a white hole short-lived if it continues to drain its energy and matter?
Answer: White holes are not short-lived. In our actual universe, in all likelihood they are not long-lived either, on account of the fact that they do not exist. They are mathematical constructs, not physics. White holes represent a family of solutions of Einstein’s field equations that are “time-reversed” versions of black holes. Literally. That’s it. Replace t with − t . These are valid solutions of Einstein’s field equations. That does not mean they exist as physical reality. We (think we) know how black holes form. The seminal paper on this subject, Oppenheimer-Snyder (Phys. Rev., 1939) shows that a collapsing cloud of matter, as viewed from the outside, will appear to continue the process of collapse indefinitely, seen increasingly in slow motion by outside observers. Since then, we have figured out that the “asymptotic end state” of this collapse at future infinity is the Kerr solution (unless the cloud has electric charge) of an axisymmetric black hole. Things that fall into a black hole do not come out. Things can fall into a black hole because they were outside the black hole in the past. Time-reverse all of the above and you end up with an “asymptotic start state” that is like the Kerr solution. Its gravity is still attractive. (Imagine playing the Solar System backwards; planets are still orbiting the Sun, just going backwards. Gravity did not turn repulsive.) Yet things do not fall into it. Why? Because they are not in it in the future. Yes, that’s what time-reversal means! We flipped the law of causality: Instead of the past determining the future, it’s now the future that’s determining the past and the present. The lifetime of white holes is infinite starting from the “asymptotic starting state” but if there were such things as astrophysical white holes, their days would be numbered. Just as a black hole may be, say, 1 billion years old, a corresponding white hole would “decollapse” completely in a billion years. As it does so, it would of course continue to violate not just the principle of causality but also the second law of thermodynamics. Anyhow, if there is one thing you want to remember about white holes: they are time-reversed black holes. They are not actual astrophysical objects, they are not black holes at the end of their lives evaporating by way of Hawking radiation. They are black holes with the clock running backwards. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: **Question for a physicist: ** How are stars born according to the general theory of relativity?
Answer: The general theory of relativity has very little to do with it, since stellar birth does not involve gravitational fields that come even close to being relativistic. So insofar as stellar births are concerned, Newtonian gravity will do just fine. The basic idea is this: When you have a cloud of stuff with minor density fluctuations, under the influence of gravity those fluctuations tend to grow over time. Where matter was denser to begin with, there’s more gravity, attracting more matter. Where matter was less dense to begin with, there’s less gravity and slower attraction. When the stuff is normal matter, say, mostly hydrogen, however, atoms and molecules eventually begin to collide. The infall becomes more randomized, kinetic energy turning into heat as atoms and molecules bounce off each other. It also means rising pressure, which will slow down the density growth. And that loss of kinetic energy to heat, which is radiated away? It means that stuff, once together, sticks together, having lost some or all of its kinetic energy that’d be needed for it to fly apart again. Continue the process for a while, and deep in the interior of the hydrogen cloud eventually the pressure and temperature become high enough for fusion. That is to say, hydrogen atoms will collide often enough, and powerfully enough, to occasionally fuse together. When that happens, a lot of energy is released in the form of high-speed particles like gamma ray photons, which then bounce into other things, transferring their kinetic energy, heating things up. Ultimately that heat escapes the cloud; viewed from the outside, the cloud begins to warm up, begins the glow, even as it continues to contract. Eventually, it settles down to an equilibrium between gravity and pressure. Meanwhile, its glow, its radiation, helps sweep away some of the leftover gas that did coalesce with the rest. What you’re left with is a fairly dense ball of gas, in the interior of which now nuclear fusion takes place at a steady rate. Not very fast, mind you; if the mass of the cloud is that of our Sun, chances are it’s producing no more heat per unit volume than a well-maintained compost pile. Except that it can continue doing that for billions of years. And that’s how a star is born. General relativity? The role it plays is minuscule, a tiny, tiny modification of Newtonian gravity. A few parts in a million, tops. Mind you, if that star is heavier, eventually it might collapse into an object with gravity so strong, general relativity can no longer be ignored, rather, it plays a major role. That would be a neutron star. However, that state comes at the end, not the beginning, of a star’s life cycle. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: The key idea of general relativity is the equivalence principle. What is the key idea of superstring theory? (The key idea only needs to be expressed in a short sentence. If it is more than one sentence, it will not be considered a true explanation)
Answer: Well, it may have to come in the form of two sentences, because “superstring” is really shorthand for “supersymmetric string”, and these two are distinct concepts. String theory is about generalizing the Lagrangian theory of a zero-dimensional point particle and its path in phase space to that of a one-dimensional object and the corresponding sheet in phase space, still subject to the action principle and amenable to quantization. Supersymmetric theories are theories that are invariant under a transformation group that establishes a relationship between bosons and fermions, such as the super-Poincaré group. So there you have it, a single sentence after all: Supersymmetric string theory is a Lagrangian theory and the corresponding quantum theory of world sheets that is invariant under a transformation that exchanges or otherwise relates bosons and fermions. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: To what extent is classical thermodynamics being undermined by quantum mechanics?
Answer: Classical thermodynamics (that is to say, axiomatic thermodynamics) doesn't care about quantum physics at all. It is an axiomatic formulation of the theory that defines, and establishes relationships between, quantities such as heat, entropy, or temperature. On the other hand, the development of quantum physics was very much influenced by the desire to be compatible with the core concepts of thermodynamics. Einstein's 1905 paper on the photoelectric effect, which is one of the foundational papers of the quantum theory, is a perfect example, as it was in part thermodynamic arguments that led Einstein to the conclusion that the electromagnetic field itself must be quantized. Beyond classical thermodynamics we have statistical physics, which relates the macroscopic quantities of classical thermodynamics to the microscopic details of a many-particle system. Thermodynamics in quantum physics follows a similar path, but extends the concepts to cover uniquely quantum phenomena, such as entanglement. However, at no point does any of this undermine classical thermodynamics; if anything, quantum physics a) relies on it and b) complements it. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why does Viktor Toth's claim that "Anything with energy-momentum interacts with the gravitational field" not imply that energy-momentum contributions from the gravitational field should add to the right hand side of Einstein's field equations?
Answer: The claim is not mine; it is standard general relativity. The assumption, e.g., in the Einstein-Hilbert formalism, is that the variation of all matter fields, combined, with respect to the metrical field of gravitation, yields the energy-momentum tensor, which then appears on the right-hand side of Einstein’s field equations. The energy-content of the gravitational field itself is another matter. It, too, is present in Einstein’s field equations but not in the form of an energy-momentum tensor but rather, in the form of the self-interactions of the gravitational field itself. I.e., it is encoded in the left-hand side of the field equations. Furthermore, whereas the energy-content of matter fields is well localized (the energy-momentum tensor of matter fields has a well-defined value that varies from point to point and from time to time) the energy-content of the gravitational field is non-local, which is why we do not have a tensorial representation of this quantity. In certain cases, it is possible to represent the gravitational field’s energy-content using pseudotensors, but that’s another story altogether, and has been a subject of research, and questions, for well over a century.
