Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do white holes emit Hawking radiation? If no, then would it be the absolute opposite? If so, how would it affect the white hole and space time around it?
Answer: White holes are theoretical constructs, time-reversed versions of the Schwarzschild (or Kerr) solutions of general relativity. Take the words, “time-reversed”, very seriously. The Schwarzschild solution is not about the object that is the source of gravitation. It is about the gravitational field everywhere surrounding that object, all the way to infinity. In other words, the entire cosmos. So when we say “time reversed”, we are talking about a time-reversed cosmos. Hawking radiation is predicted based on an analysis that places quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of a gravitating object. Contrary to popularizations, the radiation arises not because of the presence of an event horizon (which, in the case of black holes, remains forever in any outside observer’s future) but because of a past-future asymmetry in an object in a state of perpetual collapse. Now reverse time and see what you get! Incoming radiation. That’s what a white hole does. It absorbs Hawking radiation due to its gravitational vacuum polarization. How can that be? Again, take time-reversed very seriously. Think about this for a moment. You can’t fall into a white hole, right? But wait… a white hole still has attractive gravity! Time-reversed means that something orbiting a white hole would be going backwards compared to what you might see under identical circumstances near a black hole, but when you go backwards around a circle, it’s still a circle. So why can you not fall into a white hole? Because you are not in the white hole in the future. Again, time-reversed. It means causality is thrown out the window, and the future determines the past or the present. Compared to that, the idea that the white hole’s gravitational vacuum polarization somehow causes the rest of the universe to contribute to its “negative” Hawking radiation almost sounds quaint. Oh, did I say that white hole are theoretical constructs? Let me stress that again. Mathematical games, not observed physics. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly?
Answer: Oh my, this is a hard question to answer... at least in a form suitable for a Quora answer. Let me try to keep it as simple as possible, which means necessarily skipping over some details, but still. You know what vectors are, right? Basically, quantities that have a magnitude and a direction. You may have learned to form inner products of vectors, but that's a misleading notion on its own right. The inner product is formed between a vector and a "covector". One way to think about it, perhaps, is that whereas a vector may be measuring a length and a direction, a covector is measuring the change of something along that length. So whereas vectors are measured using, say, meters or feet, covectors are measured using "inverse" units of length, i.e., meters or feet are now in the denominator. So say, a vector measures a length in a certain direction as 1 meter. Or 100 centimeters. Someone says that they have distributed marbles with a density of 10 marbles per meter. Or 0.1 marbles per centimeter. So now you form an inner product... between a 1-meter vector and the marble density of 10 marbles per meter. Multiply the two, and you get 10 marbles. Change the coordinate system from meters to centimeters: Now you have a 100-cm vector and 0.1 marbles per cm. Multiply the two and... again you get 10 marbles! The inner product between a vector and a covector yields a "scalar", a pure number that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system. This is important. So then, we can actually "define" a covector as the thing that maps a vector into a scalar by applying the inner product. What do you call a thing that maps not one but two vectors into a scalar? Wait, two vectors? Why would we want to do that? Well, how about characterizing how a force works on a surface. The force is a vector. The surface, a small surface element that is, can be characterized by a vector: its "normal" vector indicating its orientation and size. In continuum mechanics, we look at surface elements and the force acting on them. That force can be present due to pressure and stresses in the material. The point is, we need to relate these two vectors together... and the relationship is accomplished by introducing a thing called the "stress tensor", which can basically form an inner product with this pair of vectors. This also happens to be one of the earliest (early 19th century!) applications of tensors in physics. And this then allows us to generalize. If a covector maps a vector into a scalar, a covariant rank-N tensor can map N vectors into a scalar. Conversely, a vector can map a covector into a scalar; so a contravariant rank-N tensor can map N covectors into a scalar. And it is then easy to form "mixed index" tensors that map a collection of, say, N vectors and K covectors into a scalar. That's what tensors do: establish a relationship between vectors and covectors, mapping them into scalar quantities that do not depend on the choice of coordinate system in which the vectors are measured or expressed. Rank-2 tensors can be easily represented using matrices (though technically, it's only the rank-2 mixed index tensors, which map one vector and one covector into a scalar, that should be written as such, rows corresponding to the covariant, columns to the contravariant features of the tensor.) Higher-rank tensors are not that easy to represent as they require either multiple matrices or higher-domensional (cubic, etc.) structures which are not easy to put on paper. One of the wonderful things about tensors, however, is that they allow us to talk about physics without picking a specific coordinate system! If a vector V and a covector U form a scalar, say, V ⋅ U = 1 , that equation remains valid regardless of the coordinate system chosen. This allows us to distinguish physics (the actual things) from mathematics (the representation of those things) very cleanly. Going back to the inner product, we can of course calculate the inner product between two vectors if we have a corresponding rank-2 covariant tensor that we use to map the pair of vectors into a number. The "metric tensor" does this. The number, in this case, may be the length of the small difference between two near-identical vectors. This turns out to be an effective measure of the intrinsic geometry of the plane, of space, of spacetime. Normally, this "metric tensor" is just a generalization of the Pythagorean rule to calculate distances. But things get more complicated in general relativity, where the geometry of spacetime varies from place to place. So say, take a vector. Displace it so that it moves a tiny distance away, following a closed path, arriving back at its point of origin. So now you have a second vector (the direction of the displacement); a third vector (the direction the displaced vector follows when it arrives back at the point of origin); and a fourth vector (the final vector after arrival). The first and the fourth vector would be identical in Euclidean space. They are not in general relativity. The rank-4 tensor that relates these four vectors is the "Riemann curvature tensor", its value changing from point to point reflecting changing curvature. The relationship between this curvature tensor and the presence of matter amounts to the fundamental statement of general relativity, in the form of Einstein's field equations. Well, that's the gist of it. As I said, I glossed over many details. But hopefully at least it's a meaningful glimpse of the role of tensors in physics, relativity theory in particular. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: When and why does semi-classical gravity break down?
Answer: Does it? Does semiclassical gravity break down? This is not a facetious question on my part. Semiclassical gravity works. It covers all regimes that are accessible to us, and all regimes that will likely ever be accessible to us, through observation and experiment. Semiclassical gravity amounts to the ad hoc replacement of the classical stress-energy-momentum tensor T μ ν in Einstein’s field equations with the expectation value ⟨ T ⟩ μ ν of its quantum field theory counterpart: R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G ⟨ T ⟩ μ ν . There. This equation works here, works in the laboratory, works in the bulge of the Milky Way, works near black holes, including phenomena predicted, like Hawking radiation, and phenomena observed, like gravitational radiation from inspiraling black holes or neutron stars. We are not happy with it. It’s inelegant. It is incompatible with at least some interpretations of quantum physics, notably those that, on some level, treat wavefunction collapse as an actual physical phenomenon. But mostly, it’s unsatisfying. Why can’t we quantize gravity? If it’s not a quantum theory, what’s behind this expectation value business? What justifies its use in the field equations? It is presumed that this equation ceases to be valid at or near the Planck scale. In fact, many assume that quantum field theory itself is just an effective theory that becomes invalid at the Planck scale. But for now, I’d say, the case remains open. Semiclassical gravity works. The possibility is there that it represents (at least insofar as we can discover it, given the observations that we can make in a 14 billion year old universe) the final word that we can ever say on the subject outside the realm of mathematically inspired, but observationally unconfirmed speculation. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space?
Answer: To move forward in space, you don’t need to do anything. Once a body is in motion, it remains in motion unless a force acts upon it… and in space, no such forces are usually present. However, if you want to accelerate a body, things change. Acceleration means a change in the body’s momentum. But momentum is one of those quantities that are always strictly conserved. So if you change the momentum of a body, the momentum of something else, somewhere, must change by an equal but opposite amount. Reaction mass could be that something else. This is how rockets work. However, if you find something outside of your space vehicle, perhaps you can change its momentum without throwing anything away. For instance, here in the vicinity of the Earth, you might be able to interact with the Earth’s magnetic field and accelerate; in exchange, the Earth itself would accelerate in the opposite direction, but given how much more massive the Earth is compared to a spaceship, this change in the Earth’s momentum is imperceptible. It might be possible to repeat the feat on larger scales, using, e.g., the magnetic field of the Sun or even galactic magnetic fields, albeit these fields are very weak so the sheer size of whatever equipment might accomplish this miracle likely makes the concept impractical. It is also possible to make use of the momentum of something already there, e.g., sunlight. Or the momentum of something we put there ourselves, e.g., light from a powerful ground-based laser. In both cases, the spacecraft would have a lightsail that, as it interacts with (and changes the momentum of) the light it receives, imparts a momentum on the spaceship that carries it. There is also gravitational assist: When there are at least two bodies in a system (and there are certainly more than two bodies here in the solar system) it is possible to follow a trajectory that changes direction with respect to one of the bodies, but changes direction and magnitude of velocity with respect to the other. Again, momentum is conserved: the motion of the bodies involved also changes. But again, bodies such as planets in the solar system are so much heavier than a spaceship, any change in their momenta will remain imperceptible. Throughout it all, however, the common theme is that books must always remain balanced when it comes to momentum. If your spaceship accelerates in some direction, something else — propulsion mass, a planet, rays of light, whatever — must accelerate in the opposite direction. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: While Hawking radiation one particle of a pair disappears in a black hole and the other one drives away from it. But why can't both of them vanish in the black hole?
Answer: As pointed out in another answer, that popular explanation of Hawking radiation, despite the fact that it comes from Hawking’s own popular book, is utter rubbish. When we look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper that describes what we now call Hawking radiation, a very different picture emerges. The black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This is important because it presents an asymmetry between past and future. The gravitational field of the black hole is responsible for what is known as gravitational vacuum polarization (rather crudely, conditions change as we approach the black hole, so the vacuum is “not the same” at different distances from it). When we apply quantum field theory, the differences between the past and the future, when applied as boundary conditions to describe the effects of vacuum polarization, result in a net outflow of radiation. The wavelength of this radiation is a bit of a giveaway already. The peak wavelength is roughly 20 times the black hole’s Schwarzschild radius. That alone ought to tell us that we’re not producing teeny-weeny particles near the event horizon; rather, the entire vicinity of the object is a source of radiation, due to the extreme effects of gravity. Or maybe not so extreme. The same equations can be applied to any system, really. Gravitational vacuum polarization is present wherever gravity is present. The difference is that a black hole is very, very compact so we can get very close to it and still stay in space. Just take the Earth: You cannot get any closer to its center than about 6,370 kilometers before hitting its surface. Replace the Earth with a black hole of the same mass and it’s less than a centimeter in size! When we get that close, there are of course more pronounced gravitational effects than at a distance of thousands of kilometers from the center. Of course “more pronounced” is in the eye of the beholder: an Earth-mass black hole would still only produce about 10 − 17 watts of radiative power, mostly in the microwave band. (This value, curiously, is about the same as the received signal strength from some of our most distant spacecraft, as picked up by the very large antennas of NASA’s deep space network.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass?
Answer: Such an old question, yet without a decent answer! The mass in F = m a refers to inertial mass. Inertia characterizes a body’s resistance to a force. You can see how when you divide this equation throughout by the mass m : a = F / m . Which is to say that given a force, a body’s resulting acceleration is proportional to that force, but inversely proportional to the body’s mass. The greater the mass, the smaller the acceleration: a body with more mass has more inertia, more resistance to motion. The term “rest mass” is synonymous with inertial mass. Consider, in fact, the title of Einstein’s famous 1905 E = m c 2 paper, which reads in English: Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content? This paper establishes the equivalence of energy-content and inertia(l mass). The term “rest mass” means the same as inertial mass. It came into usage along with another term, “relativistic mass”, which combines the inertial mass of a body (which is an intrinsic property) and its kinetic energy (which is observer-dependent). Fortunately this concept is not much used anymore as it is grossly misleading and has been the source of much confusion. I am guessing that “variable mass” in the question may have referred to this relativistic mass. Gravitational mass measures how a body interacts with the gravitational field. According to the weak equivalence principle, gravitational mass and inertial mass are identical. This is what allowed Einstein to generalize his original relativity theory (now called special relativity) and extend it to become a field theory of gravitation. A theory that treats inertial and accelerating reference frames the same way (Einstein’s original objective) naturally becomes a theory of gravitation when the reference frame associated with falling in a gravitational field does not depend on the material properties of the falling object. So to sum up, the mass m in F = m a is inertial mass; it is the same as rest mass; thanks to the weak equivalence principle, it’s the same as gravitational mass; as to the concept of variable (relativistic) mass, the best advice I can offer is to forget you ever heard about such a thing. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Mass and energy are equivalent. Heavy masses dilate time. Could enough energy in a closed container dilate time? If not, why not?
Answer: I have a feeling reading this question that it was inspired by some kind of (unfortunately fairly common) magical misunderstanding of “energy”. What do you think “energy” is? Is it something that we can scoop out of a container with a ladle? Use it to fill another container to the brim? Not really. By and large, energy can be two things: Potential energy or kinetic energy. Potential energy is associated with how things interact with each other, attracting or repulsing one another. This is the ability to do work: The ability to bring things into motion. Kinetic energy, in turn, is the energy associated with the motion itself. So then, going back to the question: To put “energy” in the box, we need to put things into the box: things that interact (with each other or even with themselves), things that move. And all these things will add to the energy-content of the box. As per the mass-energy equivalence relationship, it means that the box will have more inertia. More mass, in other words. and yes, that also means more gravity. But then, let me get to the second part of the question. Heavy masses dilate time? Not exactly. I know, we say that, I probably said that a few times, lazy language and all, but let’s keep in mind that the theory is called the theory of relativity for a reason: it’s not about what happens to time, it’s about what, for instance, two clocks measure that follow different worldlines between the same two events. I.e., how the two clocks behave relative to one another. And yes, by and large, clocks that spend more time in a gravitational field tend to count fewer ticks, but that’s because their worldlines are, in an abstract sense, “shorter”, not because of anything that might have happened either to the clocks or to time itself. So yes, a heavy box with plenty of energy-content will have more gravity, and as a result, clocks following worldlines that pass near the box may count fewer ticks. As to why that box is heavy, it doesn’t matter. Heavy always means more energy-content. Whether that energy content exists because we put lead in the box, or because we lined the inside of the box with perfect mirrors and then let in a tremendous quantity of light, never to escape… no difference. What matters, as I said, is the energy-content. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there a measurable amount of energy in a gram of mass?
Answer: Well, yes… but no. Yes, in the sense that mass and energy are equivalent. That is the true meaning of the famous equation everyone knows, E = m c 2 . It’s not about converting anything into anything. Certainly not about converting mass into energy. It simply is the mathematical form of Einstein’s statement that the inertia(l mass) of a body is equal to its energy-content. (The c 2 part is just a conversion factor between incompatible units.) But no, not in the sense of energy as “the ability to do work”, that is, putting things into motion. We extract useful energy from things when we can convert those things into other things with less energy-content. Take a quantity of combustible fuel and the corresponding quantity of oxygen. By allowing combustion to take place, we produce something that is ever so slightly less in mass (i.e., energy-content). The difference is extracted in the form of heat or pressure, which we can use to put things into motion. Or take something at a higher elevation, say, a large quantity of water. We allow it to flow downward, while spinning a turbine. The end result is that the water is now at a lower elevation, This means less gravitational potential energy. The energy extracted was used to bring the turbine into motion. But now take an inert lump of iron? What do you do with it? What’s the lower energy state you can bring it to? Without adding oxygen, you can’t burn it. If it’s not in a gravitational field, it cannot fall. It will not release energy either through nuclear fusion or nuclear fission. So… it’s a dead lump of iron. No “reasonable amount of energy” that can be extracted by any sensible means. (And no, annihilation with antimatter does not count. Someone would have to produce that antimatter in the first place.) So yes, technically, every gram of mass is equivalent to 89875517873681764 ergs of energy. That’s a lot. Comparable to an atom bomb. But in many (most? almost all?) cases, only a tiny fraction of this energy, exists as “energy” in the sense of the ability to do work, i.e., bring things into motion. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: From an outside observers point of view, a black hole never forms. The rest of the universe is an outside observer. So how can Hawking radiation ever escape to the outside universe?
Answer: As others pointed out, the popular account of Hawking radiation — a pair of particles popping into existence near the event horizon, one with positive one with negative energy, the negative energy particle being “eaten” by the horizon while the other escapes — is dead wrong. In fact, we can suspect this much simply by looking at the basic features of Hawking radiation. Its characteristic wavelength is about 20 times (!) the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. That alone should make it fairly obvious that Hawking radiation doesn’t really come from the horizon proper. Indeed, when we actually look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper (rather than his popular book) a very different picture emerges. Hawking radiation is deduced from a so-called semiclassical description of quantum fields: that is to say, quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of general relativity. This curved spacetime background is not static. An astrophysical black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This creates an asymmetry between past and future. When we extend the quantum fields using the appropriate “past infinity” and “future infinity” boundary conditions, the resulting configuration is not symmetric. This yields an outgoing flow of radiation, which is what Hawking radiation really is. This radiation originates from the neighborhood of the gravitating object, and it is a result of the “gravitational vacuum polarization” that is produced by the object’s gravitational field. The presence of a horizon is not essential to this process, nor does the radiation originate from, or from within, the horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why do electrons have mass, but photons don't? Aren't they both just packets of energy?
Answer: First of all, particles are not just “packets of energy”. They are “excitations” of the underlying field, but those “excitations” carry more than just energy: they are quantized packets of energy, momentum, angular momentum, and perhaps a variety of charges as well. Depending on the nature of the field it may or may not be a field with “rest mass”. A field is said to have rest mass when it interacts with itself (so even when it’s not interacting with anything else, it has potential energy) or if it interacts with what is called the nonzero vacuum expectation value (v.e.v.) of some other fields (in the actual universe, one such field exists, the Higgs field). In the quantum theory of electromagnetism there are two fields: the electromagnetic field and the field of electrons (or electronic field). These two fields are distinct, but interact with each other. Specifically, the electronic field can serve as a “source” for the electromagnetic field, on account of the fact that its excitations carry electric charge. The electronic field also interacts with the Higgs field v.e.v., so it has potential energy (i.e., its excitations have rest mass-energy) even when it’s not interacting with anything else. Interactions between the electromagnetic field and the electronic field can lead to the creation or annihilation of excitations: photons, or electrons. Conservation laws must always be satisfied, however. So for instance, a lone electron cannot emit a photon; in the electron’s center-of-mass reference frame, the electron has no kinetic energy, so emitting a photon would leave the electron with negative kinetic energy. Conversely, lone electrons cannot be created as that would violate charge conservation; rather, they come in the form of electron-positron pairs. Throughout it all, as I said, each excitation carries these conserved properties. The excitations of the electromagnetic field (photons) and the electronic field (electrons) are manifestly different. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does matter lose mass or energy by creating gravity? Gravity creates energy in the movement of all other matter. Doesn’t this have to be conserved? The law of conservation of energy. Or do we just not understand gravity?
Answer: Matter does not “create” gravity. Matter interacts with the gravitational field. Anything with energy-momentum interacts with the gravitational field. The potential energy associated with the gravitational field is usually negative. You need to invest energy when you lift something away from a gravitating body. You get that energy back when you let the thing fall. So if we take the energy between two bodies zero when they are far apart with negligible gravitational influence on one another, as they approach each other, they accelerate and energy is extracted from the gravitational field. So the field energy is negative. When astronomical bodies coalesce and form a self-gravitating structure, the negative gravitational energy is balanced by the positive kinetic energy that the bodies gain as they approach each other. Depending on how things unfold, they may remain in motion for a long time; or they may, for instance, collide, with all that kinetic energy turning into a more random form of kinetic energy, heat, which through repeat collisions of particles and the resulting acceleration, becomes electromagnetic radiation (light, heat, etc.) and is emitted into deep space. Or, if the bodies are very heavy and very compact, some of that kinetic energy might even turn into substantial quantities of gravitational radiation! That, too, can carry energy away from the system. Overall, the books remain balanced, as always. Conservation laws prevail. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space?
Answer: OK, it doesn't exactly work that way. Gravity doesn't slow time, speed time, or change lengths. However, according to the theory of RELATIVITY (never forget the name!) observers in different gravitational fields will measure things differently. So what takes 1 second according to the clock of an observer in a strong gravitational field may take 2 seconds according to the clock of an observer in a weak gravitational field. This of course implies that we have a spatially varying gravitational field, which changes from point to point. Cosmological models are usually homogeneous models: that is, they assume that on average, the gravitational field is the same everywhere, it only changes with time. Over time it becomes weaker in an expanding cosmos, because matter flies apart and becomes less dense. When dark energy is present, stuff flies apart faster. And the rate at which it flies apart decreases more slowly. The Hubble parameter, rather than going down to zero as matter becomes less and less dense, settles down on a nonzero value instead. Expansion continues. As a result of that expansion, there is redshift. Some of it is just plain old velocity-related Doppler, due to things flying apart. But some of it (over cosmological scales, especially) is due to the time-varying gravitational field. On average, matter is less dense today than yesterday, so its overall gravity is weaker today than yesterday, so clocks today appear to tick faster than clocks yesterday. A signal emitted billions of years ago at a certain number of oscillations per second will show fewer oscillations per second as measured by a clock today. Dark energy does not fundamentally change this, but it alters the rate at which cosmological parameters, including the redshift, evolve over time. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does dark matter convert into energy like baryonic matter (E=MC^2)? If so, what type of energy (not electromagnetic or dark energy)?
Answer: Contrary to millions of popular accounts that suggest otherwise (usually to dazzle their readership), the equation, E = m c 2 , is absolutely not about converting anything into anything. Here is the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduced this equation in its modern interpretation (the correct one, not the misunderstood reinterpretations): Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? (Does the Inertia of a Body Depend upon its Energy-Content, Annalen der Physik, 18:639, 1905). Let’s look at the title more closely. Inertia of course means inertial mass, the resistance of a body to acceleration. This is the mass m that appears in Newton’s second law, F = m a . Einstein’s question, which he answers affirmatively in the body of the paper, is whether the inertia of a body is determined by whatever energies are “stored” inside that body. Any by “energy”, we don’t mean anything mysterious. There really are only two types of energy worth considering. One is the energy of motion: kinetic energy. The other is the energy associated with positions (where a body is): potential energy. This is about how bodies relate to one another, attraction and repulsion and the associated energy. A special case is rest mass, which can be seen as a body interacting with itself. In quantum field theory, “particles” are in a sense illusions: what are real are the quantum fields. The quantum fields can gain energy from interacting with other quantum fields, and when they gain energy, it comes in the form of discrete lumps, “excitations”. These excitations may be detected in the right experiments as discrete particles. This is how particles are “created”. So when two quantum fields interact, their kinetic energies can transform, create new excitations, and new “particles” are born, so long as all other conservation laws are satisfied. It is not possible to create a single electron this way; that would violate charge conservation. But it is possible to create an electron-positron pair, in the right experimental setup, by allowing other fields carrying lots and lots of kinetic energy interact with the electron field (not to be confused with the electromagnetic field, the quanta of which are the photons). But it requires interaction. So moving on to dark matter: the standard “cold/collisionless dark matter”, or CDM model involves dark matter that does not interact (or if it does, only very weakly) with itself or with baryonic matter. So it does not matter how much kinetic energy is present in the form of dark matter, if it cannot transfer that energy to the Standard Model fields that constitute normal (baryonic) matter. Finally, one more comment on the terminology. The expression “dark energy” suggests some other type of energy! It is not. Words mislead us, especially when the jargon of a field or profession alters meaning. Theoretical physics has quite a few examples: the “vacuum speed of light” may not be the speed at which light travels (e.g., if we allow photons to be massive), gauge theories have nothing to do with gauges, modern particle physics is really the physics of interacting fields with “particles” only an afterthought and, well, dark energy is not energy, really, but a “perfect fluid” (which is not really fluid, lol) a medium that has uniform density and pressure with no shear or viscosity. In particular, dark energy is a perfect fluid with very large negative pressure. Not some mysterious form of “energy”, although of course, like all forms of matter, it has energy-content. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is gravity a force or a space? If it's not a force, then why is it measured in Newton? If it's a curved spacetime, then why isn't it measured in Einstein, or in curved metersecond?
Answer: First of all, let us settle the basic question. Is gravity a force? It is, of course, fashionable to dazzle laypersons with the pronouncement that “Einstein proved that gravity is not a force, it’s the warping of spacetime!” But some folks disagree. Here’s my favorite (though by no means only) quote on the subject: “It is wrong to think that 'geometrization' is something essential. It is only a kind of crutch (Eselsbrücke) for the finding of numerical laws. Whether one links 'geometrical' intuitions with a theory is a ... private matter.” (“Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.”) The gent who wrote these words back in 1926? Why, his name was A. Einstein. (Einstein to Reichenbach, 8 April 1926, as quoted by Lehmkuhl, Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326.) Now let me elaborate a little bit on the “gravity is not a force” business. It is not completely silly, after all. The geometric interpretation of gravity looks at freely falling reference frames as the gravitational generalization of inertial frames. What happens when you are in a noninertial frame? You feel fictitious forces, like the centrifugal force. When you stand on the ground, you are in a noninertial frame: The ground prevents you from falling. So from this perspective, gravity may be viewed as a fictitious force, or pseudoforce. However, there is a crucial difference. Pseudoforces are not associated with real, physical fields. However, the gravitational field is a real, physical field. Like the electromagnetic field, it has its own independent existence. Gravitational waves can carry influences, energy and momentum, from place to place the same way electromagnetic waves can. The gravitational force, whether or not we interpret it using geometry, corresponds to how the gravitational field, this real, tangible, physical field changes from place to place. Not to mention that if we insist on doing geometry, it is eminently possible to reinterpret electromagnetism using geometry! And no, I don’t even mean the “old school” attempts at geometrizing electromagnetism, like Weyl’s “linear groundform”, Kaluza-Klein theory in 5 dimensions, or Einstein’s attempt to unify gravity and electromagnetism using a nonsymmetric tensor field. No, I mean quantum electrodynamics: how the contribution of electromagnetism is captured in an eminently geometric object, the covariant derivative. Except… except that in this case, the geometry depends on the “charge-to-mass ratio” of the object at hand. An object that is heavy with little or no charge behaves differently from an object that is light and has a lot of charge. Gravity is not like this: the “charge” (gravitational mass) is the same as the (inertial) mass, so the ratio is always exactly 1. Therefore, the geometry is unique, not dependent on the object’s material properties. This may explain why the geometric interpretation of gravity is so very popular! Popular but all too often deeply misunderstood. Recall those wonderful rubber-sheet illustrations of how gravity curves space? Garbage. Seriously. That is because the part that corresponds to Newtonian gravity in general relativity has nothing to do with space. It has to do with time. Between any two events (not locations! Events: specific locations at specific moments in time) along the worldline of a freely falling object, the object follows a trajectory that maximizes time. In special relativity, this would be a straight line (inertial motion); in general relativity, the results are the well-known Keplerian orbits, at least up to a very good approximation. Curvature of space comes in as a second-order effect; here on the surface of the Earth, it’s a tiny, roughly one-part-in-a-billion correction. So yes, gravity is very much a force, its geometric interpretation notwithstanding. Like any force, it is measured in the SI system of units using newtons (when used as a unit, the word is not capitalized). Then again, pseudoforces are also measured in newtons, so even if we “buy into” the geometric interpretation, the unit of measurement would remain the same: it measures a force, which is acceleration times mass. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What happens to fermions that are forced to violate the Pauli exclusion principle?
Answer: I am guessing that what you have in mind are the Chandrasekhar-limit and the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit, governing the collapse of white dwarfs and neutron stars, respectively. Indeed, these are sometimes characterized in the literature (both professional and popular) as limits where the gravitational attraction overwhelms the degeneracy pressure due to the Pauli exclusion principle. But it is very important to recognize that the degeneracy pressure is not quite equivalent to the Pauli exclusion principle proper. It is a macroscopic manifestation of that Pauli exclusion principle. When the gravitational force becomes powerful enough to overcome the degeneracy pressure, something happens, but that something is not an actual violation of the Pauli exclusion principle at the particle level. As to what that “something” is: in the case of white dwarfs we have a pretty good idea. Crudely put, we can smash electrons and protons together, borrow some neutrinos and presto: we have neutrons. So we turned the degenerate matter inside a white dwarf into the “neutronium” that the neutron star is made of. The TOV limit is far more mysterious. What actually happens, as far as I know, is not well understood. There is speculation that the neutrons may break down into constituent quarks, forming some kind of quark matter, quark-gluon plasma I guess, but this may not really work, as we now have even more fermionic degrees of freedom than before, not to mention that at high energies, we end up creating even more quarks… My understanding is that we have neither the robust theory (it may require a working quantum theory of gravity) nor the experimental data to allow us any firm conclusions about how such things unfold. We basically know that there is an upper limit to the mass of neutron stars, and that they do collapse into likely black holes, but how it unfolds, I think, remains largely unknown, poorly understood. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Would you rather touch antimatter or a black hole?
Answer: You’d have to explain to me first how one could accomplish either, even if the consequences are ignored. A black hole’s event horizon is forever in the future. That means that to touch it, you either a) live forever, or b) actually fall into the black hole. Except that falling into the black hole, with the exception of some of the very largest supermassive black holes, means certain death even before you reach the horizon, because tidal forces will rip your body apart. In short, you cannot touch a black hole. And how do you touch antimatter? OK, technically if you’re eating a banana right now, chances are you’re “touching” some antimatter, the occasional positron that comes as a rare decay product of the K-40 isotope that can be found in living things, including bananas. But presumably, you meant “bulk” antimatter, such as a visible quantity of some antimatter liquid or solid. So the first question that pops into mind is… how is it stored? How is it isolated from the environment so that it doesn’t already go kaboom? OK, so maybe it’s a piece of antimatter iron, floating in deep space. Except that even in deep interplanetary space, there is matter: the occasional molecule of gas, even microscopic dust particles here and there. Still if you insist… I suppose you could float over to where that anti-iron piece is, and grab it with your hands, while wearing a spacesuit with gloves. Oops, that would be your kaboom moment. I suppose this is nonetheless a less unpleasant way to go though than being ripped apart by relativistic tides. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance.
Answer: It is credible, so long as you clearly understand what you are looking at. First of all, it is not a “NASA picture”. It is a picture produced by an international collaboration of radio astronomy observatories. The collaboration is called the “Event Horizon Telescope”, and they spent several years observing M87* to obtain a sufficient amount of data. The picture was synthesized from these observations. These radio telescopes, far apart, formed effectively a single instrument using a technique called very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Basically, the radio telescopes received signals from the same source, and these signals were then phase coherently recombined. The recombined signal was than fitted against various source models, including models of the M87 black hole as well as alternatives. The best-fit model wins! With the help of this model, the radio astronomy data was then processed to form an image. The image depicts “light” (radio waves) generated in the vicinity of and behind the black hole, partially obscured by the black hole’s so-called photon sphere. The result is the famous synthesized image, its color chosen for purely artistic reasons. So it is an image that is a result of credible science. But no, it is not a NASA image. Nor is it an actual photograph: the image was synthesized using a very complex set of methods, processing several years’ worth of observations made by a worldwide collaboration of radio telescopes. And there is certainly plenty of room there for knowledgeable criticism of the observations, their interpretations, the models and the methods. Such criticisms and questions did, in fact, appear since in the scientific literature. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible to use telescopes to observe the event horizon and beyond of a black hole, or does the gravity of the black hole absorb all light before it reaches us?
Answer: Here is the thing about black holes: No photon ever leaves the event horizon. This would be true even if we had pre-formed, “primordial” black holes in this universe, with fully formed event horizons. This is the very nature of an event horizon, nothing, not even light, can ever come from one. Add to this the fact that an actual, astrophysical black hole that forms as a result of gravitational collapse never really completes the process. Its event horizon remains forever in the future of any observer outside. So to “see” its event horizon, you’d need not a telescope but first and foremost, a time machine, to bring a signal from the future to the present! In short, no. Not even with an all-powerful telescope can you see what’s not actually there, namely light leaving a black hole’s event horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If there is a very, very tall tower, and a light source that spins around the top of it at a very high speed, would the shadow it casts ever be able to move faster than the speed of light?
Answer: Indeed, shadows, spots of light, even the start of the gap in a ginormous pair of scissors can move faster than the vacuum speed of light. So in theory, with a large enough laser pointer moving fast enough, you could create a spot of light on the surface of the Moon that moves around at a speed many times greater than the vacuum speed of light. Shadows can do this, too; in fact, when we infer, for instance, the existence of a planet orbiting another star when it briefly transits in front of that star, the shadow of that planet traverses our solar system typically much faster than the vacuum speed of light, as it crosses the Earth’s orbit. There is one common theme in these examples. None of them can carry energy-momentum or information from point A to point B. You can make a laser spot traverse the Moon very fast, but two astronauts standing on the lunar surface will not be able to manipulate that spot and use it to send messages to one another. There is another thing that can travel faster than the vacuum speed of light: light! That is to say, the so-called phase velocity of light. In some ionized mediums with an index of refraction less than one, the phase velocity is greater than c . But again, the phase velocity is not something that can be used to carry a useful signal. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does Einstein's equation demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy? Can this process be reversed to create more matter than needed?
Answer: It does not. The famous equation, E = m c 2 (which is not really called Einstein’s equation, but let me put pedantry aside for a moment) is absolutely NOT about any conversion of “matter” into energy. To explain what this equation IS about, first allow me to recall the title of the paper in which this equation (in a slightly modified form) is introduced: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” (Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? Annalen der Physik. 18:639, 1905.) The question is answered by the paper in the affirmative, establishing something important: that what we know as the inertia, i.e., the mass (its resistance to acceleration) of a body is, in fact, its energy-content. You add energy to a body (e.g., making it warmer), its inertia increases. You remove energy from a body, its inertia decreases. Notably, the equation is not about converting anything into anything. It is, in fact, called the mass-energy equivalence relation. Which is to say, it expresses recognition of the fact that a body’s mass (its inertia, resistance to acceleration) and its intrinsic energy-content (not to be confused with energy that exists relative to other reference frames, such as the body’s kinetic energy in a moving observer’s reference frame) are really equivalent: they are the same thing. Now about that pedantry bit: The expression, “Einstein’s equation”, is usually used to refer to the equation R μ ν − 1 2 g μ ν R = 8 π G T μ ν , which is Einstein’s (field) equation for gravitation, i.e., the fundamental equation of general relativity. Note that all along, I’ve been silent about the word “matter”. This concept is not even defined in relativity theory. The contribution of matter to the field equations is characterized by the stress-energy-momentum tensor T μ ν , but the theory remains silent about what “matter” really is. This is also true when it comes to E = m c 2 . Presumably a “body” would be made of “matter”, but again, the theory remains silent as to its nature. It only talks about its specific, measurable properties, namely its resistance to acceleration (mass) and changes in its energy-content. The closest thing to “creating” matter happens in particle accelerator experiments, when lighter particles collide with plenty of excess kinetic energy as measured in the reference frame of their common center-of-mass. The collision converts them into new particles, which may be heavier than the progenitors, which is to say that some of that kinetic energy of the collision now becomes the internal energy-content of the collision products. These products are usually short-lived, unstable particles however, so very quickly they decay back into lighter particles, with some (most?) of their energy-content now turning back into the kinetic energy of these decay products. But other than the fact that all along the process, mass-energy is conserved, the equation E = m c 2 has nothing to do with such processes of particle creation and annihilation. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why didn’t any computer scientists realize that Y2K was all nonsense?
Answer: Oh, it wasn’t “all” nonsense, but many of us were indeed concerned that it was overhyped. To boldly give myself credit, here’s what I wrote about it back in 1998 (!): The Y2K phenomenon. So you see, even as I complain about the hype, I also acknowledge that at least some of the concerns are valid. More importantly perhaps, I mention what is likely to become a far bigger headache than Y2K ever was: the Y2038 problem. You see, as I explain in this post I wrote 26 years ago, Y2K was mostly “cosmetic”: it was about, e.g., how dates were shown, not necessarily how dates were stored, managed internally. In contrast, Y2038 is a problem associated with what remains one of the most popular internal representations of dates in use, the standard UNIX signed 32-bit date format. To be sure, newer formats exist and their use is encouraged, but the “old” 32-bit format is still ubiquitous. And unlike Y2K, this format can be found, e.g., in embedded systems galore, including embedded systems with age-old, unmaintained software/firmware distributions. Systems that depend critically on being set to the correct date/time. And 2038 is “just around the corner”. OK, well, not quite but… Y2K was 24 years ago, 2038 is just 14 years from now. If the world is still in one piece in 2038, chances are we will survive this crisis as well, but if I am still around then (I’ll be in my mid-70s) I might feel tempted to stock up on some canned food, drinking water and firewood for our fireplace, just in case. Oh, and cat food. Must not forget cat food, otherwise we run the risk of becoming cat food ourselves…

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do black holes ever actually "finish" forming? Or does time dilation slow everything down to an 'asymptotic' process?
Answer: Again, remember the word “relativity”. Or to put it another way: who’s watching? For outside observers, the black hole never finishes forming. The moment of the event horizon coming into existence remains forever in the future of any and all outside observers. For infalling observers, the black hole forms. (Talking about a classical black hole here; quantum physics may change the picture). The infalling observers would find themselves in a collapsing mini-universe that contains everything that fell, will fall, into the black hole. Soon (by that I mean milliseconds to hours, maybe days, depending on the black hole’s size) the collapse runs to completion: In a reversal if the Big Bang scenario, the collapsing mini-universe reaches temperature and densities beyond which our physica is no longer reliable. If classical relativity is to be believed, however, the end result is a singularity, a final moment in time beyond which even time no longer exists: this mini-universe ends. But none of this can ever be observed from the outside. From the outside, the collapsing black hole is in a “frozen” state: no more information can be obtained from it since as exponential time dilation shifts every signal into obscurity, but the process never completes. Oppenheimer and Snyder called it “continued gravitational contraction”; some of the literature, including older English literature as well as the literature in some foreign languages call the resulting object a “frozen” star. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is the observational data that suggests that rotation curves of galaxies remains flat indefinitely a slam-dunk for MOND style theories of gravity or will traditional models ultimately prevail?
Answer: In my considered opinion, not even close. Though I'd avoid using the expression "MOND style gravity". MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is just an ad hoc modification of Newton's second law designed by hand to fit rotation curves and not much else. It is not a theory of gravitation. There are proper relativistic modified theories of gravitation, which are typically not characterized by an acceleration scale (like MOND is) and which can do more than just predict-by-design the rotation curves of galaxies. Anyhow, concerning indefinitely flat rotation curves: Here is the beginning of the abstract of the paper that, I presume, triggered this question: "We use a new deprojection formula to infer the gravitational potential around isolated galaxies from weak gravitational lensing. The results imply circular velocity curves that remain flat for hundreds of kpc [...]" Note the two key phrases: "New deprojection formula" and "to infer". So the presumed rotation curves are not a result of direct observation. They are deduced from a formula that was published by the same group last year, a formula that attempts to establish a relationship between the observed surface density of a galaxy and its gravitational potential. Even if this formula is justified, using it beyond (at most) a couple of hundred kpc becomes highly questionable. For most galaxies, at that distance there is already considerable gravitational perturbation from neighboring galaxies, so it is naive to expect neat, circular orbits, determined solely by the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. In contrast, here's a plot from a paper we published with John Moffat 10 years ago, in which we use actual data from astronomers (with references cited therein), extending all the way up to (almost) 200 kpc and demonstrating that the Milky Way's rotation curve is not flat, to show how certain modified gravity theories might work, but those that predict indefinitely flat rotation curves, notably "MOND-like" theories, actually fail. In the end, of course, more direct observations will help. But I've seen plenty of rotation curves of distant galaxies that already show a noticeable decline beginning at several 10 kpc or less, to be sincerely doubtful that indefinitely flat rotation curves are a thing. Question: If gravity is a bend in spacetime, why do objects fall straight rather than in a curved or parabolic direction?
Answer: Did you say spacetime? Very well, let’s look at a falling rock in spacetime. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why do people say a change in the speed of a light ray causes refraction? Isn't it the angle at which the light ray hits the boundary that causes refraction?
Answer: To understand how the speed of light in a medium is related to the angle at which the ray of light enters or departs that medium, it is necessary to remember Fermat’s principle of optics. Simply put, Fermat’s principle tells us that light follows, between two points, the quickest path. How does this work? Let me explain through a simple example. You have to get from point A to point B fast. You can run and you can swim. But you swim much more slowly than you run. And there is a river in the way. Look at my crude little diagram: Which path is faster? The red path is obviously shorter, being a straight line, but you spend a lot of unnecessary time swimming slowly in the water at an angle. The blue path is longer, but you actually gain time by reducing the amount of time spent swimming at the cost of increasing the time spent running. However, since you run faster than you swim, the overall effect is that you get to your destination faster. The exact angles can be calculated if we know how fast you run, how fast you swim, and the geometry of the two locations. And this is how light works when it passes through a medium in which it moves more slowly than in the vacuum. Rather than following a straight line, a light ray follows the path that is the quickest from any specific origin to any specific destination. (Well, actually, it’s not so much light rays as it really is a wavefront in the wave theory of light. That wavefront is subject to the usual constructive and destructive interference, but when we work it out and use, e.g., a useful mathematical approximation called the method of stationary phase, what we get in the end is precisely this result: a path that obeys Fermat’s principle.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If gravitons actually exist - is the gravitational constant the quantum of the force carrier action, which relates the energy carried by a bundle of gravitational force to its frequency?
Answer: No, a coupling constant is not a quantum of anything. A coupling constant determines how strongly two independent fields (in this case, the gravitational field and matter fields) couple to each other, i.e., how strongly they influence one another. The fact that the gravitational constant is not a mere number but it has units attached to it makes it particularly interesting. It means that we can always choose a set of measurement units in which G=1 and it simply disappears from the equations. At the same time, this plays a major rule in the difficulties associated with creating a viable theory of quantum gravity: “naive” quantization leads to a theory that misbehaves at high energies, with infinities that cannot be removed or tamed by reasonable mathematics. Other than that, though, it’s just a coupling constant. It measures how strongly (or weakly, as in this case) matter fields and the gravitational field couple to one another. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does your following statement make sense," a transparent material with a refractive index will of course change wavelength, by altering the speed at which the wave travels."? How does slowing light affect it's wavelength?
Answer: Think of electromagnetic radiation as a consequence of something wiggling. Wiggling back-and-forth. That wiggling creates waves. If the thing wiggles 1000 times a second, that means 1000 wave created per second. The distance between those waves? Why, it’s dependent on the speed at which the waves travel. Now suppose the waves enter a different environment in which they travel at a different speed. No waves are suddenly created or destroyed. It’s still the same 1000 waves as before. But if they travel faster, the gap between them will increase. If they travel slower, they’ll become more densely packed. The distance between the waves is the wavelength. As to why a transparent material alters the speed of the waves (and incidentally, it can actually increase that speed; the so-called phase velocity of light can be greater than the vacuum speed of light c), folks occasionally try to explain this (wrongly) by suggesting that in a material, photons bounce around. Well, they do sometimes, but that’s scattering, not refraction. Refraction is a wave theoretical thing. In a transparent material, the electromagnetic field’s boundary conditions are no longer the boundary conditions imposed by the vacuum. Rather, it is now the bulk electromagnetic properties of the material itself. And that changes Maxwell’s equations and also, their quantum field theory equivalents. In particular, it changes the speed at which the waves travel. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If geodesics always maximize proper time between two points along the path, then why does gravity pull things towards regions where time runs slower?
Answer: This is one of those concepts that requires some careful rethinking, and it’s not even the relativity part, really. It’s the action principle. The principle of least action is not about points along a path in space. It is about events. We know that our cannonball is at a certain position at a given moment in time. We know that our cannonball is at some other position at another given moment in time. So the endpoints of the trajectory and associated times are fixed. The question is, what trajectory does our cannonball follow? So suppose that you know that a satellite is at a certain point in its orbit at 12:00:00 noon exactly. You know that the same satellite it at some other point in its orbit at 13:00:00 exactly. What is its orbit? In the context of general relativity the principle of least action actually translates into maximum proper time. What trajectory did the satellite follow to get from point A to point B in exactly one hour? If it sinks too deep into the gravitational field of the Earth, its clock ticks slower. So less proper time. If it flies too high, it moves faster, and special relativity kicks in. That means less proper time again. Between the two there is a sweet spot. And when you work out that sweet spot, it corresponds to its Keplerian orbit with (very) minor relativistic corrections. Now suppose it’s not a satellite but a brick that you drop. At 12:00:00 exactly, you release it from an upper floor. At 12:00:05 it hits the ground. There, two events again. What trajectory did the brick follow? It could accelerate instantaneously to a constant speed. It could wait until the very last moment and then travel at the vacuum speed of light. But as it turns out, both these extremes would mean less proper time than gradual acceleration. Again, the endpoints and times (!) of the trajectory are fixed; the question is, how can the brick fall so that the proper time measured by a clock attached to it is maximal? The answer is (approximately) uniform acceleration. So I stress again that the tricky bit is to keep in mind that we are not maximizing proper time between two points along some path, with the time of departure and arrival up in the air. We are maximizing proper time between two events, both of which include a location and a time. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What distinguishes quantum mechanics from classical mechanics? Why is quantum mechanics necessary when classical physics can solve many problems using Newton's laws?
Answer: OK, let us start with classical physics. Specifically, with the simplest concept in classical physics: a small particle. Say you have a gun firing small bullets. In front of that gun, there’s a metal plate with two holes. Behind the metal plate, there is a wall. You are spraying the metal plate with your gun. Some of the bullets are blocked. Some make it through the holes. After a while, you will see something like this: That is to say, on the wall, there will be two compact regions with bullet holes. Now let us repeat the same experiment with electrons inside a cathode ray tube. Exact same setup, except that the conventional gun is replaced by an electron gun, and in place of the wall we have a fluorescent screen marking impact locations. We fire a bunch of electrons. The result will be something like this: This result cannot be explained by classical physics. The electrons do not behave like bullets from a gun. Rather, the pattern we get is more akin to an interference pattern characterizing waves. Waves that reach the barrier, pass through the two holes, and then proceeding from these two holes interfere with each other. This makes no sense from the perspective of classical physics. The math behind this is fairly straightforward but not intuitive. We do not have a brain that is wired to intuit the quantum world. We need to follow through step by step with the math. The actual math is not terribly hard, but it involves differential operators and complex numbers so I’ll skip the details. The essence: we systematically replace, in a rigorous algebraic process, the positions and momenta (quantities of motion) characterizing the system with “operators”. These operators, acting on the state of the system, yield numbers that we can make sense of as probability densities. The resulting equations no longer describe a specific path for an electron. Rather, they describe all possible paths, with the probability densities obeying a wave equation. It is this wave equation that is responsible for the interference pattern we see with the electrons. But in the end, the probability density tells us the likelihood of the electron impacting at specific locations on the screen. So when the electron arrives (i.e., when its position is measured) it is seen as a particle. But when the electron travels, its travel is governed by the wave-like behavior of that probability density. Like it or not, this is how the world works, as countless experiments demonstrate. It should remind us that Nature is under no obligation to appeal to our intuition. On the other hand, it’s a testament to human science that we could make sense of all this nonetheless, and today, the quantum world is “ours” to play with, building, among other things, the remarkable technology that allows you to read these very words, wherever you are in the world, seconds after I hit Next and complete this post. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: When electrons become entangled, are they entangled forever (isn't that romantic?); or will they entangle with other electrons willy nilly (isn't that promiscuous?).
Answer: When you think about entanglement, keep in mind how badly words can mislead us. Normally, everything is entangled with everything else. When we say that we entangled two particles, what we really mean is that, however briefly (within the constraints of the experiment), but we managed to keep those two particles isolated from the rest of the universe as much as possible. So at least temporarily, they were only entangled with one another, with minimum interference from the environment. Thus, the two-particle system can act as an isolated quantum system, not interacting with other things. So when electrons become entangled, they just continue what they’ve been doing all along, staying entangled. But (briefly) they’ll remain mostly unentangled with other things. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Was Heisenberg the first one to promote the use of tensors in physics?
Answer: No, it was not Heisenberg. Let me show you a snapshot from a page from an interesting paper: Sure, the notation is a bit archaic, but what you are looking at is the Cauchy stress tensor, which characterizes the stresses and pressures in a medium. This snapshot is from a later reprint of Cauchy’s 1827 paper, De la pression ou tension dans un corps solide [Ex. Math. 2 (1827) p. 42]. So as you can see, tensors were already in use in mathematical physics two centuries ago. Later, in the early 20th century, tensors became the essential tool for relativity theory, especially general relativity. The reason is that the tensor concept perfectly captures the difference between the geometric object (which exists independently of any choice of coordinates) vs. its representation in a specific coordinate system. The independence of physics from the coordinates used to represent it is a fundamental concept in relativity theory (and, well, modern physics in general). Heisenberg, incidentally, did not use tensors much to my knowledge. His matrix mechanics was something else: it was a means to represent the observables of quantum physics, for instance, positions and momenta that do not behave like the ordinary numbers of classical physics, specifically they do not commute under multiplication. Later it was shown that Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics was mathematically equivalent to representing the same quantities using function operators acting on Schrödinger’s wavefunction. But those matrices were not used to represent tensor quantities. However, tensors entered the world of quantum physics with a vengeance, starting with the 1930s, with the development of quantum field theory. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible to use Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to bend space-time and achieve faster-than-light travel without violating the principles of relativity?
Answer: No. The uncertainty principle has nothing to do with bending spacetime. In fact, arguably nothing has anything to do with "bending spacetime", as "bending spcaetime" is just an inuitive, convenient interpretation of the gravitational field, and Einstein himself cautioned us against reading too much, too literally, into this geometric interpretation... but I digress. The uncertainty principle itself is a consequence of a more deeper relationship, the fundamental canonical commutation rule of quantum physics: p q − q p = − i ℏ , where p and q are the generalized momenta and positions of the quantum system. This relationship alone tells us that positions and momenta cannot be simultaneously represented by numbers, otherwise we'd have p q − q p = 0. Instead, we can represent them using mathematical entities like matrices or operators acting on the state of the system; the state, which may be represented, e.g., by the famous wavefunction can, in turn, yield probabilities for various classical measurements, which yield numbers. The uncertainty principle arises as a consequence: How closely can these probabilities nail down competing positions and momenta? There is a limit (otherwise we’d violate the commutation relation) and that limit is what’s expressed in the uncertainty principle. Now about relativity theory. In quantum particle physics, even in relativistic versions, these probabilities do not go promptly to zero even for measurements that would involve fast-than-light signaling. The probabilities diminish rapidly, exponentially even, but they're there. However, in relativistic quantum field theory such influences are explicitly and completely canceled. The probability of sending a signal from one place to another faster-than-light? Precisely zero. This is in fact one of the major arguments in favor of quantum field theory: that unlike quantum particle physics, quantum field theory is fully causal. No faster-than-light engines, no time machines either I’m afraid, much as I’d love to see Dr. Who’s TARDIS pop up in my back yard one day… If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What are the major differences between special and general relativity and is general relativity just a final draft of special relativity?
Answer: It might help to contemplate for a moment the history of the subject. In 1905, Einstein published what then became known as the theory of relativity. Its main claim was the existence of an invariant speed (which we know as the vacuum speed of light) and the resulting change in how reference frames that are in motion relative to one another are related to each other. The old, Galilean transformations between reference frames that involved absolute time were replaced by the Lorentz group of transformations according to which both space and time are measured differently in reference frames that move relative to one another. Contrary to some popular accounts, this version of relativity theory can deal with both inertial and accelerating motion. However, accelerating reference frames are “second class citizens” of the theory. They need to cope with fictitious forces such as the centrifugal force, which are absent in inertial frames. Therefore, the laws of physics are different for inertial vs. accelerating observers. Einstein’s ambition was to find a more general framework, which he referred to as the Generaltheorie, that would treat inertial and accelerating observers as equals. Early on, in what he described as his “happiest thought”, he came to the realization that such a theory necessary must involve gravity. The reason: gravity is universal. Freely falling objects near a freely falling observer will accelerate at the same rate, so from this observer’s perspective, they’d either be at rest or move at uniform velocity. Which is to say that for this observer, absent any distant points of reference, there is no difference between freefall in a gravitational field vs. floating in empty space. Thus a theory that can describe the world from the point of view of accelerating observers should automatically apply to observers in gravitational fields as well. Einstein’s effort was successful, and the general theory of relativity was born in 1915. In the absence of gravitation, the theory reduces to the “old” relativity, albeit with a more robust mathematical framework that no longer distinguishes inertial and accelerating observers. So the old, 1905 theory can be thought of as a special case, a limiting case in the absence of gravity, of the general theory. This is why the 1905 theory eventually became known as the special theory. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why is the concept of "gravity slowing down time" used instead of "time moving more slowly near massive bodies"?
Answer: I was prepared to write an answer questioning if there is even a difference between the two statements but, well, there is. It would have been wrong for me to dismiss this question as silly. It isn’t. Yes, clocks tick more slowly in a gravitational field than elsewhere. This is part of relativity theory: it relates reference frames that may be moving relative to each other (special relativity) or may be in different gravitational fields (general relativity). Yes, massive bodies are a source of gravitation. But the statement I just made about clocks does not care about sources. It does not matter what the origin of that gravitational field is, or how close we are to its source. The field itself has physical existence: it carries energy and momentum, it carries information, it is, in a very literal, physics sense, a thing in ways neither space nor time are things, for instance. And clocks tick more slowly when in a gravitational field. The clock does not know what the origin of that field is. Is there a massive body nearby? Is this a passing gravitational wave? Is it a gravitational anomaly of cosmological origin? Doesn’t matter. The stronger the field, the slower the clock. This is well-reflected by the first statement but not the second, which implies that a) a massive body must always be present nearby (not true) and that b) a massive body directly influences the clock (also not true, the influence is mediated by the gravitational field, it’s due not some “action-at-a-distance” by the massive body). Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not?
Answer: None of the above incompatibilities are true. First, Newton himself knew that his gravitational theory is incomplete. It involved “action at a distance” between celestial bodies, with no means, no medium to mediate that interaction. To quote the man himself (letter to Bentley, Feb 25, 1692/93): "That gravity should be innate inherent & {essential} to matter so that one body may act upon another at a distance through a vacuum without the mediation of any thing else by & through which their action or force {may} be conveyed from one to another is to me so great an absurdity that I beleive no man who has in philosophical matters any competent faculty of thinking can ever fall into it. Gravity must be caused by an agent {acting} consta{ntl}y according to certain laws, but whether this agent be material or immaterial is a question I have left to the consideration of my readers." Einstein completed this theory, though by no means was he the first to try. In the wake of the success of Maxwell’s theory, especially after special relativity made it clear that the electromagnetic field is a fundamental entity, not just waves of some medium (the luminiferous aether), many sought a similar field theory of gravitation. It took a while to understand why a scalar theory would not work, and why a tensor theory necessarily doubles as the observed geometry of spacetime. Einstein succeeded, and by doing so, ultimately answered the riddle posed by Newton more than two centuries earlier. And of course Einstein’s theory yields precisely Newton’s in the weak field, nonrelativistic limit. General relativity is a classical field theory. It is not fundamentally incompatible with quantum physics. We can do quantum field theory on the curved background of general relativity. (Indeed, popular topics such as Hawking radiation arise precisely as a result of such an approach). We can even have quantum matter act as the source of classical gravitation, in the form of semiclassical gravity. We find this unsatisfactory, however, in much the same way Newton was not satisfied with his own theory of gravitation: We sense that it is not the final word on the subject and further improvements are needed. But we would expect such an improved theory to yield Einstein’s in the semiclassical limit, and yield Newton’s in the semiclassical, nonrelativistic limit. No incompatibilities there, just gradual improvements in our understanding, one step at a time. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: The distortion in space and time created by the mass of the Earth is extremely small, less than one part in a billion. Isn't that too little to make things accelerate at 9.8m/s2 towards the ground?
Answer: It is true that the change in observed spacetime geometry, time dilation in particular, here on the surface of the Earth is tiny. It is characterized by the dimensionless quantity G M / c 2 r ≃ 7 × 10 − 10 so indeed, less than one part in a billion. However, gravitational acceleration is a tad larger: it is c 2 / r times this quantity, which indeed comes to about 9.8 meters per seconds squared. So no, that tiny quantity is not too little, nor is it too great. It is precisely what it takes to accelerate things here on the surface of the Earth at one standard gravity. But one standard gravity is a tiny, tiny, acceleration when you consider more extreme cosmic objects. On the surface of something like a neutron star, gravitational acceleration is tens of billions of times greater. That puts neutron stars deeply in the relativistic regime insofar as gravitation is concerned. In contrast, here on the Earth, the consequences of relativity theory amount to, you guessed it, typically one part in a billion or thereabouts.
