Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: In quantum mechanics, is there any context where an electron has a definite position and velocity simultaneously? If such a context exists, are there known real-world situations where this is observed, or is it purely theoretical?
Answer: No. A “definite” position or momentum (let’s be pedantic here and use momentum in lieu of velocity) means that both position and momentum are number-valued. That is to say, the particle is simultaneously in a “position eigenstate” and a “momentum eigenstate”. Let me explain what that means. In quantum mechanics, positions ^ q and momenta ^ p are not representable by numbers (hence the little “hat” over the symbols). They can be represented using a form of matrix algebra, or they can be represented using function operators. The fundamental statement of quantum physics is that these two things do not commute under multiplication: ^ p ^ q − ^ q ^ p = − i ℏ , where i is the imaginary unit and ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. Pretty much everything else in quantum physics follows from this commutation relation, including the famed uncertainty principle. Whether we express positions and momenta using matrices or operators, these things act upon the state of the system (which may be represented by the famous wavefunction). In the Copenhagen interpretation, we interpret this wavefunction as a probability amplitude, and use it to estimate the probability of a future experiment based on measurement results available to us at present. But measurement results are numbers, whereas ^ p and ^ q are not. Except when they are being measured! An act of measurement confines either ^ p or ^ q to an “eigenstate”, which is to say that when it acts of the wavefunction, it’s action is like multiplying the wavefunction by a number. This number is our measurement result. Now suppose that we somehow find a trick and simultaneously measure ^ p and ^ q so they are both numbers. But numbers commute under multiplication! The quantity p q − q p = 0 is always zero (notice that I dropped the hats, as p and q are supposed to be ordinary numbers now). This violates the fundamental canonical commutation relation. So either quantum mechanics is wrong, or this cannot happen: ^ p and ^ q cannot simultaneously be numbers. We know from countless experiments that quantum mechanics is not wrong, however weird it can be. Therefore, we are left with the conclusion that no, a particle cannot simultaneously be in a position and a momentum eigenstate. This was of course just a very superficial sketch of the math behind quantum physics, and, yes, it’s counterintuitive. As I stressed many times, do not expect to intuit the quantum world. It does not work that way. It’s one of those rare instances where intuition not only does not help you, it might become a formidable obstacle. Like it or not, to make sense of the quantum world, math is essential, as math is the only language that we have by which this world can be made sense of. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do different colors and wavelengths of light have different speeds when traveling through space-time?
Answer: No, they do not, and this is indeed a very important property of light. The speed of a light ray in the vacuum does not depend on its energy or frequency (i.e., its color). All light rays follow the same “null geodesics” of spacetime, as determined by the gravitational field. This would not be the case if the particles that mediate electromagnetism, photons, were massive. In that case, the photon’s speed would depend on its energy. In a gravitational field, light rays of different color would follow different trajectories. When light rays are deflected by a massive body, such as the Sun, different colors would be deflected by a different angle. We’d see white light split into the colors of the rainbow. We do not see this with gravitational lensing. Not with the Sun, not with distant astrophysical lenses. In fact, gravitational lensing observations are one of the means by which we can establish experimental limits on the maximum mass that photons could have without us noticing. (There are other methods, some even more sensitive.) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What would it look like to see a planet go through a wormhole as an observer?
Answer: Poor wormholes. So badly misunderstood. First of all, even though they exist as legitimate solutions of Einstein’s field equations, these solutions almost certainly do not represent real physics. A stable wormhole? Even if it is possible to “construct” one (by “construct”, I mean in the mathematical sense, with pencil and paper, using equations), their existence is subject to a great many conditions, many of which are likely unphysical, which preclude their existence in the actual, physical, universe. But putting that aside… A wormhole that is large enough to swallow a planet without ripping it to shreds first due to differential (tidal) gravity would need to have a mass in the many ten billion solar mass range. And even then, the planet would not go through unscathed; the tidal forces may not be large enough to rip it apart, but they’d certainly be large enough to disrupt it completely. To avoid that, the wormhole would need to be even bigger, maybe in the several trillion solar mass category? But now we’re talking about a wormhole with a Schwarzschild radius measured in light years. To watch a planet approach, and go through, such a wormhole at a feasible velocity… might take thousands of years or more! So no, don’t expect to see planets traversing wormholes, except in badly written science-fiction series where gigantic wormholes are needed to plug gigantic plot holes. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can you explain why the pressure inside of a black hole becomes infinite?
Answer: The interior solution describing a collapsing astrophysical object turns out to be the same set of equations that would describe a collapsing cosmos. A hapless observer who found himself falling into a black hole, after crossing the event horizon, would find himself in such a collapsing “mini-Universe”. Depending on the size of this mini-Universe (determined by the amount of matter that fell, and will ever fall, into it), it may take anywhere from a millisecond to many hours, but the mini-Universe collapses. The observer would not live to see this, as ever increasing tidal forces would rip his body apart before the end. But that end (at least for a spherically symmetric black hole) inevitably happens: the famed “singularity” is not some bad spot that you can bypass by clever maneuvering, but a future moment in time at which (insofar as this mini-Universe is concerned) time itself comes to an end. So it’s not so much that pressure, density, etc., become infinite at this moment but rather, this moment literally is not part of existence: Whatever is inside the mini-Universe ceases to exist at this point. For outside observers, however, none of this ever happens. Even the event horizon itself remains forever in their future. Only by falling through it can the event horizon be experienced. That is the “classical” picture anyway. If we account for quantum physics, the answer is, we don’t really know what happens. In the absence of a quantum gravity theory, we can only take educated guesses, invoking what is known as the “semiclassical approximation”. One possibility (if you asked me, I think it’s the most likely one) is that the collapse never even happens as the black hole evaporates before its event horizon forms. In which case, there is no “inside” at all. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Near Earth, in the Newtonian limit, gravity is 99.9999% due to warping of time (the “gravitational time dilation”) and only about 0.0001% due to the warping of space. How do you calculate these values?
Answer: The actual calculation gets a little bit involved, as it requires writing down the equations of motion (geodesic equations) of a particle in the Schwarzschild metric (characterizing the gravitational field of a spherically symmetric body outside of that body) and then using a suitable approximation, such as the post-Newtonian approximation, to find approximate solutions. However, the result, especially for a particle initially at rest, is fairly simple. Its initial radial acceleration in the gravitational field of a mass M is given by a = − G M r 2 ( 1 − 2 ( β + γ ) G M c 2 r ) . The first part of the expression on the right-hand side is just the Newtonian acceleration (inverse square law). It is, however, multiplied by the term in parenthesis, which contains contributions both due to the nonlinearity of gravity, characterized by β , and the spatial curvature, characterized by γ . For general relativity, β = γ = 1 , but these so-called Eddington-parameters can also accommodate alternative theories of gravitation. When you calculate the magnitude of the correction, it comes to about 2.8 parts in a billion, give or take, here on the surface of the Earth. Once the particle is in motion, the post-Newtonian equation of motion becomes more complicated, but this simple expression should give you an idea as to the magnitude and nature of the correction. (See also https://descanso.jpl.nasa.gov/monograph/series2/Descanso2_all.pdf where these so-called post-Newtonian equations of motion are discussed in detail and put to practical use.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Light is deflected by gravity. But look at this explanation: Why is there deflection of starlight in the Newtonian model? Shouldn't it simply be straight? https://qrcd.org/5VmM Reply
Answer: Newtonian gravity would predict a deflection if light if light consisted of particles. Newtonian gravity, however, does not predict a similar deflection if light is described as a wave theory, namely as electromagnetic radiation in Maxwell’s theory. General relativity, in contrast, predicts a deflection in both cases. Moreover, the deflection it predicts is twice the deflection that one would predict using Newtonian gravity. That is because, to get a bit more technical, in addition to the temporal part of the metric tensor (which is what’s behind Newtonian gravity) for anything moving at or near the vacuum speed of light, the spatial part offers an equal contribution, doubling the deflection. This is why the deflection of light was offered as a crucial test of general relativity, and why Eddington’s 1919 solar eclipse expedition, which confirmed Einstein’s prediction, was so important. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why is it challenging to comprehend quantum mechanics? Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty?
Answer: Why is it challenging for a language model like GPT-4 to reason about geometry? The answer is simple: It doesn’t have the hardware to visualize geometry. It is forced to reason it out, step-by-step, in a process that is prone to mistakes. Our problem with quantum physics is similar. Our brain has wonderful hardware to visualize and intuit things in a classical universe. A universe in which quantum effects are averaged out, so what remains is basically geometry. And unlike GPT-4, our brain is wired to visualize geometry. But Nature doesn’t care. Nature doesn’t care about Einstein’s perspective either. The quantum world works differently, and our brains are not wired to intuit it. So like GPT-4 when it tries to reason about geometry, we have to do it step-by-step, in an error-prone, difficult process. Mind you, some of our attempts to “make sense” of quantum mechanics only made it worse, and personally, I list the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics among these. According to the Copenhagen interpretation, the present does not fully determine the state of a quantum system. This state is represented by a wavefunction that can be interpreted as a probability amplitude, which can be used to compute probabilities, but not certainties, when it comes to the outcome of future observations. Then, the act of observation, or “measurement” somehow magically “collapses” the wavefunction in a process that is not included in the equations of quantum physics; this collapse is instantaneous and applies everywhere even retroactively, as we replace one wavefunction with a different one. As to what a “measurement” is, and whether or not it can be done by an instrument, a cat, or if it requires a human, the Copenhagen interpretation remains silent about. Einstein was right in my view to be unsatisfied about this line of reasoning and the fact that it described the universe as fundamentally probabilistic. Unfortunately, he did not live long enough to see Bell’s theorem, which demonstrated beyond doubt that quantum physics is fundamentally nonlocal: that measurements are correlated even when they are so separated that no signal can pass between them, and that this correlation cannot be explained by “hidden variables” that the quantum system carries. If we fully embrace this nonlocality, all that probability stuff becomes unnecessary: The act of a future observation, the fact that the quantum system in the future is confined to an interaction with a camera, a cat or a human, constrains its wavefunction in the presence. No “collapse” needed and best of all, this nonlocality does not even violate causality: Much as we’d like to do so, it is not possible to use it to send signals from the future to the past. The constraints on the wavefunction imposed by its future interactions do not lead to observable consequences in the present. I have a feeling that Einstein would have embraced this direction. Alas, he died some nine years before Bell published his result. In any case, Bell’s theorem notwithstanding, quantum physics remains impossible to make sense of using our classical intuition. We need to do it the hard way, work it out, step-by-step, using the power of reason (expressed using the language of mathematics) as we lack the brain hardware to “see” quantum physics. Any attempt to “make sense” of quantum physics using our classical intuition is not only doomed to fail, it becomes an obstacle to understanding since quantum physics is manifestly not classical. Question: If an object that is falling into a black hole never reaches the event horizon from the perspective of an outside observer, how do we observe black holes gaining mass?
Answer: When you watch something fall into a black hole, it vanishes from sight. As it approaches the black hole, any signal from it is subject to runaway gravitational time dilation: it will be redshifted and weakened into oblivion. So insofar as we outside observers are concerned, the object has become part of the black hole. The entire black hole is technically in a “frozen” state (in the older and some of the foreign literature, black holes are in fact called “frozen stars” for this reason) just before horizon formation; but the mass is all there, and it increases over time if more stuff falls into this object. So it is one thing that we know that technically, that horizon formation remains forever in the future and technically, all the stuff that ever fell into the black hole is still in the process of never-ending collapse, the end result of which we will never get to see. It’s another thing that in terms of what we observe, this makes precious little difference: All the infalling stuff vanishes in an immensely strong gravitational field from which no signal appears to escape. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why does a particle wave exist, and is there a way to comprehend it?
Answer: I presume this question is about quantum mechanics. In the classical world, we’re used to things working, well, normally. Take a flying cannonball. At any given moment in time, we can describe its position x and we can describe its velocity, or rather, its momentum p (same thing as velocity, for all practical intents and purposes.) The quantities x and p are numbers (maybe sets of numbers, i.e., coordinates or coordinate components, but expressed using numbers nonetheless.) Because they are numbers, we can multiply them in any order: the products p ⋅ x and x ⋅ p represent the same thing. This all makes perfectly good sense, but Nature has this nasty habit of not obeying our expectations when it comes to what we think makes good sense and what does not. As it turns out, things in Nature do not obey this simple arithmetic. Particles are not acting like miniature cannonballs. They do not have positions and momenta. They have states. And to the extent that they exhibit properties that can be interpreted, viewed, measured as positions or momenta under the right circumstances, these can be represented in mathematics by so-called operators like ^ x or ^ p , acting on a state ψ . And these operators do not obey the (commutative) rule of multiplication: ^ p ⋅ ^ x ≠ ^ x ⋅ ^ p . This is the essence of quantum physics. And this has two consequences. First, that state of the quantum system, ψ . It is governed by the famous Schrödinger equation. That equation is a “wave equation”, which is to say, under most circumstances it will give some kind of a periodic solution. So the state of this quantum system will have wave-like behavior, which includes, e.g., constructive and destructive interference, something cannonballs never do. Second, those operators I mentioned, for positions and momenta: Under the right circumstances they yield measurable numbers. So with the right experiment, that quantum system still exhibits behavior that makes it appear like a miniature cannonball. So when you fire, say, an electron, while the electron is en route it does not have a position of a momentum in the classical sense. Its existence is described by the state ψ , its wavefunction. But when it impacts, say, the fluorescent screen of a CRT, that interaction confines it to a well-defined position. Its position operator ^ x , acting on its state, produces a set of coordinates, the location where you see a flash on the screen. If this explanation appears a little abstract, a little hard to make sense of, that is no accident. Quantum physics cannot be intuited. To use a stupid analogy, almost all of us had a chance to play with language models like ChatGPT in the past year or so. Ignoring their more recent attempts to integrate language and visual capabilities, the original language model has no visual experiences. No ability to intuit or visualize anything related to space or geometry. It can still reason about these things, but often it struggles, as its words are not connected to any experience that it would have at its disposal. We humans are in the same situation with quantum physics. Just as language models have no visual cortex, our brains lack a “quantum physics cortex” that would allow us to intuit the quantum world. Therefore, like the language models, we have to resort to painful, slow, step-by-step reasoning, relying on the reasonably precise language of mathematics. However painful this feels, it is important to remember that any attempt to visualize quantum physics using our intuition that is rooted in classical physics is not only doomed to fail, it will likely become an obstacle to understanding. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What happens to matter when it falls into a black hole? Is it destroyed or stored as energy? Can you provide an explanation for this phenomenon?
Answer: The problem with questions like this can be summed up with that one word used in the question itself: “when”. You see, a black hole is not just some physical object that exists here and now. We are talking relativity theory here, after all, extreme relativity, with both space and time involved. How much time? Well, that’s the tricky part. The closer something gets to a black hole, the stronger the gravitational field in its vicinity. And a strong gravitational field means time dilation. Not just minute time dilation, mind you, like here on the surface of the Earth, where clocks one part in a billion, give or take, slower compared to clocks in deep space. Extreme time dilation. Long story short, concerning that “when”: The question as to when an object falls into a black hole is answered, for us outside observers, by a simple word: never. That is to say, near the black hole’s event horizon, time dilation becomes divergent. Infinite. The moment when an infalling object would reach the event horizon remains forever in the future for outside observers. What about infalling observers? Well, they’d find themselves in a collapsing mini-universe, consisting of all things that ever fell, ever will fall into the black hole. This universe has a (very) finite lifespan. The famed singularity? That’s not some place you can avoid. It’s the future moment in time when this mini-universe comes to an end. But for outside observers, that never happens. Stuff falling into a black hole never reaches that black hole. In fact, this is precisely why black holes, in some of the older or foreign literature, were often called “frozen stars”. So in a very real sense, all that matter is still there, in the process of falling. Invisible to us due to the same time dilation that causes extreme redshift, so any signal from infalling matter is shifted into oblivion. So the black hole, for all intents and purposes, appears “black” (that is, not visible) but we know, assuming that our math is correct, that it represents a state of continued collapse (the title of the famous 1939 Oppenheimer-Snyder paper, which first described such collapse, reflects this: On Continued Gravitational Contraction.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does energy have a gravitational field like matter? E.g., has a charged cell battery higher field compared with an empty one of similar mass?
Answer: Very much so. In fact, It is energy that is the source of gravitation. Remember the famous (and often colossally misunderstood) equation, E = m c 2 ? Its proper name is mass-energy equivalence relation. To clarify, allow me to quote the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduces this relationship: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” The answer given by the paper is in the affirmative, but the title itself should tell you what you need to know: What we know as a body’s inertia, i.e., its rest mass, is, in fact, its energy-content. The equation E = m c 2 is not about converting anything into anything. It is simply the statement that what we measure as the energy-content of a body, E , can also be measured as its resistance to motion, m , the two measurements being related by the conversion factor c 2 . That conversion factor exists only for cultural reasons, because we humans have chosen incompatible units to measure mass and energy, or ultimately, distance and time. We do so for convenience. But in so-called “natural” units, c = 1 and the mass-energy equivalence relationship is simply E = m . When it comes to gravitation, the source of gravitation is not “matter” (however we define it): It is the energy-content (more precisely, the so-called stress-energy-momentum tensor, but for ordinary matter, that tensor’s only dominant component is the body’s energy-content). This is the mathematics behind the concept of the weak equivalence principle: The gravitational interaction does not care what a body is made of, only its energy-content matters. What form that energy takes is irrelevant. So what happens when you charge a battery? You increase that body’s energy-content. So yes, its inertia changes and by extension, since the gravitational field of a body is sourced by the same inertial mass, its gravitational field changes as well. The change is minuscule. The amount of electrical mass-energy you pump into a battery when charging it is typically a small fraction of a trillionth of the mass of the battery itself, far too small to be measurable. But it’s there. And it should come as no surprise. After all, even for the discharged battery, the bulk of its rest mass is, well, energy! That is to say, almost all the mass of an ordinary object is due to the masses of its constituent baryons (protons and neutrons). Those baryons are made of quarks, but the quarks contribute roughly 1% of their mass. The remaining 99% is the strong force binding energy that holds those quarks together in those protons and neutrons. So next time you lift a heavy object such as a brick, consider: the resistance you feel when you lift it up is almost entirely due to the energy-content of the strong force that ties its subatomic constituents together on microscopic scales, reacting to the Earth’s gravity. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If the “one-way” speed of light hasn’t yet been measured and we can just affirm the average 2-way speed of light for all points & perspectives is what measures c, what does that mean for ancient nighttime stars we see, that light’s not from long ago?
Answer: Questions like this pop up regularly, and they are not silly. However, it is important to understand that ultimately, we do not measure speed, one-way, two-way or otherwise. We also do not measure distances. The only “pure” measurement that we can do without hidden assumptions is counting the ticks of a reliable clock. Of course even this measurement is based on an important assumption: Namely that in this universe, reliable clocks exist. Clocks that tick in sync; clocks that, when brought apart and later brought back together, will still continue to tick in sync (though they may have counted a different number of ticks in the meantime, while they were apart). All other measurements are derived from clock ticks. But… rulers! Oh, if idealized rulers existed… Well, then we wouldn’t have relativity theory, would we! An idealized ruler is perfectly rigid. Move one end and the other end moves instantaneously, no matter how far it is from the first! Spin the ruler at one end, and the other end will move around rapidly, perhaps many times faster than the vacuum speed of light! No such thing exists. Real rulers are physical objects, and when you move them around, different parts move at different speeds, depending on the material properties of the ruler, the speed of sound in that material and such things. In the end, the only way to properly calibrate a ruler is, you guessed it, by using a clever arrangement of reliable clocks and light signals. Yes, light signals. Because when two clocks are apart, we have no other means of relating their readings. So for instance, when we calibrate a ruler, we can attach a clock to one end, send a light signal to the other end and let it return, and then use the time elapsed on that clock to infer the length of the ruler. We can repeat this experiment using a clock on the other end, even a clock in the middle, but ultimately this is all we have: clocks and light signals. So we really have to turn things upside down. Forget about measuring the speed of light; assume that the vacuum speed of light is universal, then make a bunch of measurements, and check if the results are consistent with that assumption. They are. Of course you are free to propose alternatives. You are free to propose an alternative theory in which the speed of light is not constant, depends on direction, etc., and see if you can come up with results that are consistent with observation. However, unless your proposal is conceptually simpler than special relativity, do not be surprised if it is not received with enthusiasm. When two theories yield identical predictions, we generally prefer the one that’s simpler. And special relativity has a whole bunch of other factors supporting it, not the least the fact that Maxwell’s beautiful equations found a “native home” in four-dimensional spacetime, on account of the fact that the vacuum equations are conformally invariant in such a spacetime, and even in the presence of charges, the theory remains invariant under the Lorentz-Poincaré group. So for electromagnetism alone, special relativity is the native “playground”. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does the proton have a finite lifetime? What is the evidence for that? Please respond. This question is very important to me. I want your answer?
Answer: There is no observational evidence of proton decay. The only evidence that we have is that if protons do decay, their half-life is incredibly long, on the order of 10 34 years or more. In the Standard Model of particle physics, there’s no mechanism for proton decay. As a general rule a decay happens if there exists a combination of particles with less rest mass-energy than the original particle, while preserving all strictly conserved quantities such as angular momentum or electric charge. There is no known “end product” for protons that would satisfy this criteria. You might wonder if perhaps an electrically neutral, zero-spin hydrogen atom might decay into something, but the answer again is no: combining an electron and a proton yields a neutron, which has more rest mass-energy than the hydrogen atom itself. Having said that, there is a possible decay route even for protons, or rather, I should say bulk matter, but on time scales much, much longer than a mere 10 34 years: quantum tunneling through a microscopic black hole state that instantaneously evaporates in the form of Hawking thermal radiation. Does such tunneling happen? I’d be inclined to say yes, but we’ll likely never know, as it is not going to be observable by any conceivable experiment. I kind of like the idea because it is “neat” in the sense that it leads to the prediction that in the extreme far future (when the number of digits expressing number of years itself is a number so big that it requires an insane number of digits) everything, all matter evaporates into thermal radiation that, in turn, gets redshifted into nothingness by continuing cosmic expansion. But history taught us over and over again that Nature does not care what views appeal or appeal to us, so don’t take my musing too seriously. In any case, on human timescales, insofar as our experiments are concerned, the proton appears to be a stable particle, not subject to decay. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Has Einstein's general relativity been proven by any experiments? Is it still considered a theory until proven by an experiment?
Answer: First, let me clarify the meaning of the word, “theory”. Hint: It’s not about idle theorizing. Here’s the definition from the American Heritage Dictionary: theory (thê´e-rê, thîr´ê) noun plural theories 1. a. Systematically organized knowledge applicable in a relatively wide variety of circumstances, especially a system of assumptions, accepted principles, and rules of procedure devised to analyze, predict, or otherwise explain the nature or behavior of a specified set of phenomena. b. Such knowledge or such a system. I hope this clarifies the “still considered a theory” part. Yes, general relativity is (still) considered a theory, and it will remain a theory, but not because it lacks plenty of experimental and observational proof. In fact, when the theory was born, Einstein himself proposed “three classical tests” of general relativity: In addition to these three classical tests, Shapiro in the 1960s proposed a fourth: rays of light or, for that matter, radio waves, passing near a massive object like the Sun, would suffer a delay that is the combined effect of the light rays following a slightly curved path and also slowed down (as measured by us, distant observers in our reference frame) due to gravitational time dilation. This Shapiro delay has been confirmed numerous times using spacecraft, and has been used ever since the 1960s as a routine part of precision radio-navigation software codes navigating spacecraft in the solar system. Since then, we have had many more confirmations of the effects of general relativity. Folks often mention the GPS constellation, which of course would not work at the desired precision if we didn’t account for general relativistic correction. There have also been other experiments involving, e.g., clocks in orbiting spacecraft. Coming up to the present day, high-accuracy atomic clocks are sensitive enough to detect changes in the gravitational field due to a few ten centimeters or less of a change in altitude. Take two such clocks, one on the floor, one on a laboratory bench and right there, you can measure a key prediction of general relativity, gravitational time dilation. So the general theory of relativity represents well-established science, with robust experimental evidence supporting its predictions here in the solar system and in laboratory environments. Whether or not the theory will survive cosmological tests remains a bit of an open question: our persistent failure to detect dark matter and dark energy directly in numerous experiments probing different hypotheses for their existence, along with the existing issues that affect the standard cosmological model leave the door ever so slightly open to modified theories of gravitation that would predict deviations from Einstein’s theory on galactic and extragalactic scales. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Will we ever build a rocket to take us light years away to other galaxies?
Answer: First of all, “light years away” is not “other galaxies”. This universe in which we live is insanely, insanely big. “Light years away” merely takes you to the nearest star. This one galaxy in which our solar system lives is host to several hundred billion stars. As to the nearest major galaxy like ours, it is some two million light years from here, give or take. Can we build a vehicle that can reach another star? Perhaps. It is technically feasible. It would require more than mere chemical (or even most forms of nuclear) propulsion, but there are proposals ranging from solar sails to interstellar ramjets that might solve the problem without exotic physics. The journey may still take generations but, well, build a large enough ship with a self-sustaining ecosystem and the descendants of the original crew may reach another star system. But, to use a silly analogy, it’s like learning how to cross a creek. Getting to another galaxy? That’s like crossing a whole freaking ocean and then some. I doubt humans will ever travel to other galaxies. Not unless we discover exotic physics far beyond our wildest guesses. Even a relativistic spaceship would require millions of years by the reckoning of those left behind to travel from here to Andromeda. Sure, the travelers may age (a lot) less thanks to relativity theory, but what good is it to travel such a faraway place when millions of years pass back home by the time you return? Even if such a trip becomes possible, chances are it’ll be a one-way trip: settlers, not visitors. Then again, perhaps our machine descendants in the far future will establish a galactic civilization with extragalactic outposts. Time might mean something else if you are a machine, perhaps enjoying a form of physical immortality thanks to interchangeable parts. None of this will happen anytime soon, mind you. Our most distant spacecraft to date is still less than one light day from us. To get to the nearest star (not galaxy!) it’d have to travel more than a thousand times that distance. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: In the Sagnac experiment it is claimed that rotation of earth at about 500m/s is detected. Can Earth’s orbit around the sun at 30km/s be detected by rotating the Sagnac apparatus as in the Michelson Morley experiment?
Answer: That is not really how the Sagnac experiment works. The standard Sagnac scenario involves a rigid platform on which light can go around in two opposing directions (using, e.g., mirrors). If the platform rotates, the two light beams will have different travel times and will show interference. Since the Earth rotates around its axis, we can attach the experimental platform to the Earth and it, too, will rotate, which can be detected by a Sagnac interferometer. The orbital motion of the Earth is something else. To detect it using a Sagnac experiment, we’d need a platform that is attached to… the solar system? The Earth’s orbit? The thing is, there is no rigid body rotating here. It might be possible to carry out a Sagnac-type experiment, without a rigid platform, by placing spacecraft around the Sun on approximately the same orbit that the Earth follows. These spacecraft would definitely detect the ~30 km/s orbital speed of the Earth. The fact that the spacecraft will not form a rigid platform adds a bit of a complication and implies a generalization of the Sagnac effect, but nothing terribly outlandish, it can definitely be done. But… what would be the point? If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can a wave length of a wave be changed? I mean from gamma rays or x-rays to change (by changing the wave length) into ultraviolet waves, radio waves, etc.
Answer: The wavelength of light is not an intrinsic property. It depends on the observer. Want to change a wavelength? Run towards the source and it will appear shorter. Run away from the source and it will be longer. (Doppler blue- or redshift). Gravity works, too. But what you need to change is the relationship between the clocks characterizing the emitter vs. the clocks characterizing the detector. That is because wavelength (talking about electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, to be clear) is inversely proportional to frequency, i.e., the number of wave crests and troughs per second. Wave crests and troughs do not get created or destroyed en route, so the only way to change the observed wavelength (i.e., frequency) is by either changing the rate at which you receive them (moving towards, or away from, the source can do that) or by changing the rate at which your clock ticks compared to the clock at the emitter (movement contributes to this, too, due to special relativity; gravity as well, due to general relativity.) Of course you can always do something the old-fashioned way and put something in the way of that light: a transparent material with a refractive index will of course change wavelength, by altering the speed at which the wave travels. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it true or false that the general theory of relativity predicts light should go straight down into a black hole whereas advanced quantum mechanics predicts that there should be a swirling torrent of gamma rays around a blackhole called a firewall?
Answer: Not exactly. In general relativity, a black hole is eternal. In fact, to outside observers its formation process takes forever. (The first paper that seriously explored this topic, the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper from 1939, is titled “On Continued Gravitational Contraction”). Anything that gets trapped by the formation process, including rays of light, remains trapped forever. Then there is the semiclassical picture, that makes a connection between classical general relativity and quantum field theory. Granted, it does not include a quantized theory of gravitation as no such theory exists (yet?) but it is also not needed. In the vicinity of an astrophysical black hole quantum gravity effects, if any, remain negligible. What the semiclassical picture tells us is that in the vicinity of an object, in a state of “continued contraction”, gravitational vacuum polarization produces outgoing radiation. This outgoing radiation is extremely weak and low in frequency. (The characteristic wavelength is about 20 times the black hole’s Schwarzschild radius.) So it takes an insane number of years (a number with as many as 70 or more digits) for the entire mass-energy of the collapsing object to be converted into radiation. But it’s all there. An outside observer could, in principle, watch an infalling object, never quite reaching the horizon even after that 70-digit number of years, all the while encountering this very weak Hawking radiation. But due to extreme relativistic time dilation, to the infalling object the process may only take seconds! So it encounters the same amount of energy in the form of Hawking radiation, but not as very weak radiation over an insane number of years but as a blast of radiation compressed to mere seconds. [Just to be clear though, the black hole firewall proposal goes beyond this, and proposes a blast of radiation to resolve what is known as the information loss paradox. That is not a subject I wish to touch in this answer, though.] Anyhow, a ray of light still goes down into a black hole, quantum physics or no quantum physics. The main difference is that if Hawking radiation is taken seriously, the black hole is not eternal; its lifespan is finite. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does a black hole destroy matter but not light?
Answer: It doesn’t destroy either. Not right away anyhow. From the outside, a black hole is a massive, very compact thing. Its gravity is very strong when you are near it, but you have to get really, really close. From afar, its gravity is exactly the same as the gravity of any other object of the same mass. If we were to replace the Sun with a black hole of the same mass, we’d no longer have sunlight of course, but the Earth would continue in the exact same orbit as before. When you approach the Sun, even if you could withstand the heat, you cannot get any closer than about 700,000 km from its center, because at that distance, you’d run into the Sun’s surface. A black hole of the same mass has a radius of a mere 3 km. So you can get more than 200,000 times closer to its center and still be “outside”. Since the gravitational force is proportional to the inverse square of distance, this close to the black hole the gravitational force is more than 40,000,000,000 times stronger than the gravitational force at the surface of the Sun. But, I stress, this extreme gravitational force requires getting really close to the black hole, just over 3 km! At 700,000 km, the gravity of a black hole with the same mass as the Sun is exactly the same as the gravity of the Sun 700,000 km from its center (i.e., at the solar surface); at 150,000,000 km (the Sun-Earth distance) the black hole’s gravity is the same as the Sun’s at this distance, which is why it’d keep the Earth in the same orbit. When something gets too close to the black hole, the black hole’s strong gravity means that it can no longer escape. Whether it is a particle of matter or a ray of light makes no difference. No escape means no escape. As to what happens to things that do get too close: once inside the event horizon of the black hole, it’s game over. The “interior” is like a mini-universe: it contains all the things that ever fell, ever will fall, into the black hole. But unlike our “outside” universe, this mini-universe is in a state of collapse. The time it takes may range from milliseconds to hours, depending on the size of the black hole, but it’s finite, very finite indeed. And once it’s over, it’s over, for matter and light alike. Time itself ends inside the black hole. But this is not something we ever see from the outside. Gravitation means time dilation (clocks slowing down). Extreme gravitation means extreme time dilation. As viewed from the outside, time dilation becomes truly extreme indeed near a black hole’s horizon; no matter how long we watch, we can never see things reach the horizon or the horizon to form. Things would disappear from sight (due to gravitational redshift, any signal becomes weak and undetectable) but no horizon is ever seen. For this reason, in some of the older/foreign literature, black holes had another name: “frozen stars”. So there: far from destroying either matter or light, as seen from the outside black holes appear to be doing the exact opposite: “freezing” all infalling stuff forever! Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Hypothetically, if you were carrying a torch and you entered the black hole and switched it on, then what would you see?
Answer: Nothing special, actually. For the sake of this thought experiment, allow me to assume that the black hole is a) a supermassive black hole (so that tidal forces don’t kill you at its event horizon, and you can live longer than mere milliseconds after reaching the horizon), b) fully formed (an actual, physical black hole is always in the process of formation insofar as external observers are concerned; as an infalling observer, you’d be witnessing that formation, i.e., you’d be surrounded by all the matter and radiation ever consumed by that black hole), c) it’s in an otherwise empty universe (so we don’t have to worry about, e.g., you being killed by starlight blueshifted into hard X-rays as you fall deeper in the black hole’s gravity well even before hitting the horizon) and d) there is no Hawking radiation or other semiclassical effects… So really, just a purely geometric black hole, Schwarzschild’s vacuum solution in other words, with a mass parameter large enough to be survivable at least for a few seconds. What would you see? Absolutely nothing. Before or after the horizon, you are still in empty space. Your torch will reveal nothing. In fact, without detailed calculations, you would not even know when you crossed the horizon; to you, everything would continue to appear normal in your vicinity, just like before. If you are freely falling, just wearing a spacesuit, you’d feel like floating in empty space. No change when crossing the horizon. If you’re inside a spaceship, everything would appear perfectly ordinary. If you were eating your dinner while falling through the horizon, you’d be taking your next bite, oblivious to the fact that you just crossed the horizon. Your fate, of course, would be sealed. Once you cross the horizon, you are irreversibly cut off from the rest of the universe. Anything that ever fell, anything that ever will fall into the black hole is there with you, forming a collapsing “mini-universe”. Though you may be moving relative to the bulk of matter around you, an observation would reveal that you are, in fact, in a universe not unlike the “big” universe out there, described by similar equations (the Friedmann equations), but unlike the “big” universe, which is expanding, yours is collapsing, shrinking. Shrinking rapidly as a matter of fact. Even if it is one of the largest supermassive black holes out there, you only have a few hours left. Or less: Long before the final moment, local differences in gravitation, i.e., tidal forces, will rip you to shreds no matter what you do. But a torch? It won’t reveal anything special just because you’re in a black hole. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can you explain the difference between general relativity and Einstein's field equations?
Answer: It’s like asking about the difference between electromagnetism and Maxwell’s equations. The two really are the same thing: the classical theory of electromagnetism can be stated by writing down Maxwell’s equations. Similarly, the theory of general relativity can be stated by writing down Einstein’s field equations, which define the relationship between a tensorial gravitational field and the stress-energy-momentum of matter. That is the essence of the theory. Modern treatments tend to present both theories in the form of the corresponding Lagrangian densities, from which the theories’ field equations can be derived using the action principle. This Lagrangian description has some technical advantages, especially if the goal is to go beyond the basic theory. But the information content of presenting the theory in terms of its field equations vs. in terms of its Lagrangian functional is basically the same. So when a theoretical physicist announces, say, a modified theory of gravitation, the next thing his professional audience expects to see is either the theory’s field equations or, preferably, its Lagrangian. No words are needed. If I see your theory’s Lagrangian (or its field equations), I know what your theory is and I can immediately deduce some of its properties simply by inspecting that mathematical expression. Question: If an airliner (e.g. Boeing 747 800) was magically transported to the same altitude as the International Space Station, how quickly would it depressurise?
Answer: It would be surprisingly slow. Keep in mind that at normal cruising attitude, outside pressure is already pretty low, less than 20% of sea level pressure. So the pressure-induced stress on the aircraft fuselage at ~400 km altitude (where the ISS orbits) would not be much greater than during cruise. So nothing dramatic happens… other than, of course, all engines failing due to lack of air, along with any auxiliary power units (APUs), so the only things operating on that aircraft at this time would be minimum emergency equipment running off battery power. Having said that, assuming that the aircraft is properly pressurized and there are no undue leaks or valves left open, the leakage rate of a well-maintained aircraft seems to be surprisingly low. I found some data: According to a conversation at PPRuNe Forums, it took some 30 minutes to reach a cabin pressure altitude of 10,000 ft in one new aircraft. In the same conversation, someone else quotes 500 ft/min as the leakage rate of a brand new A320. So even a conservative guesstimate suggests at least 15 minutes before pressure drops within that fuselage to dangerously low levels. Which creates an interesting scenario. If that aircraft was magically lifted to 400 km altitude without being accelerated to orbital speed, it won’t stay up that high for very long. Rather, it’d start to fall, and fall rather rapidly since there is no noticeable air resistance. In fact, without air resistance it would reach the ground in something like 5 minutes. Of course in reality, it would run into denser and denser air that would ultimately slow its descent. The question is, would it be survivable? No, it’s not about heat shields. Heat shields are needed for spacecraft re-entry because they enter the atmosphere at orbital speed. This hypothetical aircraft of ours would start off slow, and never reach speeds at which heating due air resistance becomes a major concern. Even so, it probably (almost certainly?) would not survive, especially considering that at this point, the pilots have no control over the aircraft; there is no power, and of course no air for the control surfaces to operate on. Before the pilots can do anything useful, the airplane would have to descend to an altitude where there is enough oxygen to start up at least an APU. That would be, what, maybe 20 km or less? Far too late. Much earlier, the aircraft would be falling at supersonic speeds, at an uncontrolled attitude, encountering denser and denser layers of air. (Recall that the space shuttle Columbia broke up at an altitude of ~60 km; it was much faster of course, but it should tell you that even at 60 km, there’s already more than enough air to cause structural failure for a fast-falling aircraft.) However, if by some miracle, that aircraft makes it to 20–25 km altitude without losing important bits like a wing or two, and an APU could be restarted, I think it is conceivable that the pilots might be able to regain control and slow the aircraft down without substantially more structural damage, as it continues to descend. I have no idea (I don’t think anyone does) how a 747 would fly at Mach 3 at 20–25 km but who knows, perhaps it would manage to stay attached to most of its wings as the pilots bleed altitude and speed? (I am thinking of China Airlines Flight 006 as I am writing down these somewhat optimistic words.) The point is, should that miracle happen, during the 5–10 minute ordeal at no time would cabin pressure drop to a level that would seriously harm or kill the occupants, unless something else (structural failure, a stuck valve, etc.) causes the cabin to depressurize rapidly at an altitude that is still too high for the oxygen masks to be effective (above ~20 km outside pressure is low enough for our blood to boil at body temperature). The big if is whether or not the airplane would survive the fall through the upper atmosphere in one piece; and the answer is that it almost certainly would not. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Would the first light in the universe early on "at average" traverse distances at another rate than now, because of the more frequent bending by gravity in a denser universe?
Answer: No, there would be no significant “bending” except for light rays that happen to pass too close to massive, compact mass concentrations too often. In terms of the average, it’s helpful to keep in mind that what dominates gravity in the nonrelativistic limit is time dilation, not the change in spatial geometry. A light ray coming from the surface of a compact, massive object will appear redshifted to an observer in space, because clocks on that surface tick slower than identical clocks in deep space. Similarly, light coming from the distant past appears redshifted, in part, because the average gravitational field was greater back when matter was much denser. (Another reason is the Doppler redshift due to the rate of expansion itself, but at deep cosmological distances, time dilation dominates over Doppler.) As to the matter of distances, that concept becomes very tricky on its own right! When objects are nearby and their distance remains unchanged or changes slowly, we can measure that distance more or less directly by the exchange of light rays. But over cosmological distances, that is not necessarily possible even in principle; you may send a light ray to a high-redshift, distant galaxy, but you will never observe that light ray catch up with that galaxy, so there will be no response. In the absence of such a direct measurement even in the form of a thought experiment, we must resort to other definitions of “distance”: e.g., distance deduced from the luminosity of the object or distance deduced from the angular size of that object. These inferred quantities are at best poor substitutes for what you or I would consider “distance” in our intuition. In light of this perhaps it makes a tad more sense when someone tells you that, e.g., a high-redshift galaxy was “only” a few billion light years from here when its light was emitted; that light nonetheless traveled for more than ten billion years (so the “light travel distance” is in excess of ten billion light years); and that at the present day, the so-called “comoving distance” to that object is several ten billion light years. All these numbers are valid; none of these numbers describe an ordinary, “sensible” distance, as no such distance can be measured. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If space is expanding (or perhaps 'stretching' is a better verb) at a rate we call the Hubble Constant (or thereabouts), at what rate is time expanding (in seconds per kilometer per petasecond - s/km/Ps)?
Answer: You stumbled upon one of the silliest, most persistent misunderstandings concerning cosmology. No, space is not expanding. Nor is it contracting or dancing the tango. Or perhaps it does… if it did, we would not know. Space does not have little markers attached to it by which it could be measured. Space is not a physical entity that would carry energy or momentum. In short, space is not a thing. But, but… cosmic expansion! The Friedmann equations! The Hubble-parameter! Well… the famous Friedmann equations, which also define the Hubble parameter, represent a specific application of Einstein’s field equations, for the case of a cosmos that is filled with matter such that the distribution is homogeneous in space (i.e., uniform density) and isotropic (no preferred direction). But… Einstein’s field equations! It’s all about the bending of space and time! Er… Not really. There are two things in Einstein’s field equations: The gravitational field, represented by a so-called tensor quantity, and the energy-momentum of matter, also represented by a tensor quantity. It is true that Einstein’s field equations can be interpreted geometrically. So what? We can also interpret electromagnetism using geometry (just ask Weyl, or consider how the electromagnetic interaction is introduced through a covariant derivative in quantum electrodynamics.) What makes gravity special is that matter is introduced into the equations solely through its energy-momentum; what the stuff is made of makes no difference. This, namely the so-called weak equivalence principle, implies that the geometry we see is the only geometry that can be measured. In contrast, in the case of electromagnetism the geometry that we see depends on the charge-to-mass ratio of the object used to measure it, so there is no one-and-only, unique geometry. (I shall refrain from quoting Einstein himself again, as I’ve already done so many times in the past here on Quora, arguing against taking the geometric interpretation, which he called a mental aid, too literally, too dogmatically.) Anyhow, back to cosmology. What those Friedmann equations tell us is how the gravitational field changes on the one hand, and how the density of matter changes at the same time. If we think of matter as particles, that implies that the characteristic distance between particles changes over time. This characteristic distance can also be thought of as part of geometry, thus characterize the gravitational field itself. But, I stress, the geometry part is interpretation. The actual, physical things in the equation are matter and the gravitational field. In the standard form in which the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric (i.e., the gravitational field) is written, we have d s 2 = c 2 d t 2 − a ( t ) 2 d R 2 , where a ( t ) is the time-dependent “scale factor”. When it is applied to a universe dominated by matter with little or no pressure (that is, ordinary nonrelativistic matter, or also “cold dark matter”) that a ( t ) indeed serves well as the measure by which the typical distance between particle changes over time. Note that time itself does not have a factor like that. And a ( t ) ceases to be a valid measure of this change of density if the matter in question is not predominantly “pressureless dust”. Which, incidentally, is already the case today, as (at least according to the prevailing ΛCDM cosmological model) about 70% of matter in the present universe is “dark energy”, stuff with large negative pressure, the density of which remains constant over time. But putting all that aside: In terms of actual, observable effects, what we see of course is that light from distant objects is shifted in frequency. For objects relatively close to our Milky Way galaxy, this shift in frequency is mainly a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift, as those objects are receding from us (or we, from them). But for objects that are very far from here, high-redshift objects, the dominant contribution to the redshift is gravitational, which can be thought of as a result of changing gravitational time dilation as the average gravitational field in the distant past (when matter was more dense) was greater than it is today. As to the Hubble parameter, it kind of captures both effects (it is defined as H = ˙ a / a where the dot represents differentiation with respect to time) but keep in mind that it is not really a constant at all; as its definition itself implies, since a ( t ) is a function of time, so is H ( t ) . I know, I know, this is not the kind of simple, concise answer that you might have hoped for. But I am trying to follow Einstein’s advice: Make things as simple as possible but no simpler. Relativistic cosmology may not be the most complicated subject in modern physics, but that does not mean it is easy to grasp or always intuitive. Question: How can I prove this in tensor way ∇ × (𝛼𝑎⃗) = (∇𝛼) × 𝑎⃗ + 𝛼 (∇ × 𝑎⃗)?
Answer: Just recall that the cross-product is expressed using the Levi-Civita symbol: a × b = ϵ i j k a i b j . (Einstein summation convention implied.) This form remains valid even when the product is formed using the derivative operator and a tensor. So then, starting with the left-hand side, let’s rewrite this using indexed objects and then use the product rule: ∇ × ( α a ) = ϵ i j k ∂ i ( α a j ) = ϵ i j k ( ∂ i α ) a j + ϵ i j k α ( ∂ i a j ) = ( ∇ α ) × a + α ( ∇ × a ) . So yes, the product rule of differentiation remains valid even when the product in question is the vector cross product. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does a black hole maintain its structure despite its density and mass?
Answer: I think this question implies a misunderstanding of what a black hole really is. Allow me to distinguish between two “black holes”: When an astrophysical object collapses, the collapse never actually ends insofar as outside observers are concerned. The infalling material approaches, but never quite reaches, the famous event horizon; in fact, the event horizon’s very formation remains forever in any outside observer’s future. This is a result of ever increasing gravitational time dilation, as a result of which to outside observers, the collapse occurs in ever increasing slow motion. In fact, this is implied already by the title of the famous 1939 paper by Oppenheimer and Snyder that first described this process: “On Continued Gravitational Contraction”. So there really is no structure to maintain; on the contrary the collapse happens precisely because an object (e.g., a heavy star at the end of its life, having run out of fuel) cannot maintain its structure. The end state, e.g., a Schwarzschild black hole, is mathematics, not physics, at least insofar as outside observers are concerned. It represents the state that the collapsing object approaches, but never quite reaches (due to time dilation). An infalling observer, however, would reach and cross the horizon in finite time as measured by his own clock. This observer would find himself in a collapsing mini-universe, and his future would be sealed: Depending on the size of the black hole, it could be milliseconds or hours or days, but ultimately, his existence will come to an end. (At least in the spherically symmetric Schwarzschild case.) So again, there is no structure that would be maintained; the collapse continues until its bitter end. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Einstein believed quantum mechanics wasn’t fundamental and there must be a deeper theory. Was he correct?
Answer: Well… yes and no, but context is all-important here. Einstein passed away in 1955. At the time, modern quantum field theory was still in its infancy. Yang-Mills theory that proved fundamental to the development of the Standard Model was just a few months old. In any case, I doubt Einstein had more than a very superficial familiarity with then-recent developments. The quantum mechanics that he was familiar with was basically quantum particle theory, characterized by the Schrödinger equation or maybe the relativistic Dirac equation, which were predominantly interpreted in accordance with the Copenhagen school as equations that yield a probability amplitude. Quite clearly, Einstein was not comfortable with physics that yielded only probabilities. Moreover, the Copenhagen interpretation assigns a role to the “observer”, which is fundamentally at odds with a world view in which Nature does what it does, regardless of whether it is observed or not by a human, a cat, or some instrument. So what do we know that Einstein didn’t? For starters, modern quantum field theory and the Standard Model of particle physics. Then there’s also Bell’s theorem that demonstrates that quantum physics is essentially nonlocal, which is to say, the behavior of the system is governed, in part, by constraints that cannot be nailed down to any specific location in space or moment in time. What it means, in practice, is that the state of a quantum system is constrained not just by the past and the present but also by the future, yet the physics remains causal in the sense that rearranging something in the future has no observable consequences on the past (sorry, no quantum time machines). In light of this, the probabilistic interpretation gains a new meaning: ignore the future constraint and the system becomes underdetermined. Instead of telling us what the future will be, the (underdetermined) wavefunction now indeed just yields probabilities. When the future becomes the present, and the outcome of an experiment becomes known, the probability becomes a certainty and we can replace the old wavefunction with a new one (“wavefunction collapse”) in our description of the system. Would this have made Einstein more comfortable? I don’t know. But I do believe that this is markedly different from the quantum physics Einstein knew. Which implies that yes, he was right to criticize quantum mechanics and, in particular, its Copenhagen interpretation. As a local theory, quantum mechanics is necessarily incomplete (again, I am alluding to Bell’s theorem here) and leads to the unsatisfying probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. But what we got in exchange is, in some ways, even weirder. Yes, quantum field theory has spectacular successes. It can do what quantum mechanics could not ever do, model how particles are created and destroyed. It is also robustly causal and relativistic. But it is just as nonlocal as quantum physics has ever been, and with Bell’s theorem, we know that this nonlocality is not going to go away. Then there’s the problem of renormalizability: We have no renormalizable quantum field theory of gravitation. To many, it seems to imply that the Standard Model (and by extension, quantum field theory as a whole) is just a useful “effective” theory, which will fail at the Planck energy scale, to be replaced by something more fundamental that would unify particle physics with gravity in a more satisfactory way than, say, semiclassical gravity. But much of what I described here happened after Einstein’s death. The quantum theory that he was critical of was really not modern quantum field theory, but quantum particle physics, along with the probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. I think his criticism of that school of thought was spot on. What was not spot on is his relentless attempt to construct a more fundamental classical theory, which consumed much of his time in the final decades of his life, but ultimately proved futile, little more than a half-forgotten footnote in the history of modern physics. (To anyone seriously interested in the subject, beyond the superb scientific biography of Einstein by Abraham Pais, I’d recommend the hard-to-find 1966 monograph, Einstein’s Unified Field Theory, by Marie-Antoinette Tonnelat.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Were the space shuttles capable of aborting a descent from orbit and re-establishing that orbit? That might have saved the Columbia shuttle if it were possible.
Answer: No, unfortunately that’s not the way it works. Let’s do a teeny bit of math. What do you think requires more energy? To lift a spacecraft to an altitude of around 400 kilometers, where the ISS orbits, or to accelerate the spacecraft to orbital speed? Well, the gravitational potential energy can be estimated crudely using E = m g h . Let’s just use g = 10  m / s 2 , and we get about 4  M J for every kilogram of spacecraft. Kinetic energy, in turn, is E = 1 2 m v 2 , and orbital speed is roughly 8  k m / s . So that would be roughly 32  M J . In other words, almost 90% of the energy spent to launch that shuttle was used to accelerate it, not to lift it. Now about that re-entry. It begins with a small burn that alters the shuttle’s orbit so that it basically intersects the upper atmosphere. The atmosphere does the rest, slowing the spacecraft down. All that kinetic energy (almost as much energy as that of a small nuclear bomb!) is converted into heat, which is why there is a need for some really serious thermal shielding. Returning from a partial descent to orbit would have required another large fuel tank like the one the shuttle used for its initial ascent. In other words, no, that is not possible. And what would have been accomplished by that anyway? The shuttle had limited consumables on board. It had to return. No, what might have saved Columbia was immediate action upon observing the foam impact during ascent. Taking the concerns seriously instead of dismissing their significance. Letting the astronauts know what they face. Authorizing impromptu repairs, even though the probability of success was low. Accelerating the preparations to launch Atlantis, while saving consumables on board Columbia as much as possible, to prolong the mission. All these options were risky of course, but they could have turned a disaster into a success, just as decades prior, the Apollo 13 disaster was turned into a spectacular, historic success by luck, clever engineering and perseverance. Then again, this is all hindsight. What if nothing had happened and Columbia survived re-entry with only minor damage? Nobody would even remember STS-107. It would be a minor footnote somewhere, something to the effect of, “STS-1xx was delayed due to extensive repairs required by Columbia after its left wing was damaged during launch of the STS-107 mission and suffered further damage upon re-entry. Launch procedures were adjusted to reduce the chances of a similar debris impact in future missions.” Sadly, that’s not what happened and seven brave souls were lost, along with a magnificent flying machine. It was eerie to watch images on CNN like the one below. As far as I can recall, these images were broadcast live (courtesy of WFAA I believe), so we CNN viewers already knew that something awful happened, even while NASA engineers were still desperately trying to reach Columbia through backup radio channels. “Columbia, Houston. UHF comm check…”

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What would it look like if gravitational waves came at us and were strong enough to be visible? Like if two ton618 sized black holes collided nearby. Just so that the wave could make a visible distortion in space. What would it look like?
Answer: Visible is the wrong word to use here as there’s nothing to see. However, you might hear it! Let us assume a “clean” collision, two black holes with no other material, so no visible light, no gamma rays, nothing that would kill you or vaporize you, just gravitational waves. And you get close enough. Well, when the merger is between two stellar black holes, the peak gravitational wave emission happens at frequencies that fall well within the audible range. Which means that if you are close enough (but not too close!), you might actually hear (literally, hear) the result, as the passing time-varying tidal effect moves wiggles parts of your body, including all those little bits inside your ear. The technical nature of the waves (transversal waves traveling at the vacuum speed of light) is different from sound waves (longitudinal pressure waves in a medium, traveling much slower than the vacuum speed of light) but the effect is similar: mechanical excitation of bits that are particularly sensitive to the frequencies in question. Mind you, don’t get too close: Just as a powerful blast of sound waves can kill you, so can a too powerful gravitational wave. Now that’s two stellar black holes. You mentioned TON 618. They are much too big for anything audible to happen. The frequencies in question would be measured in a microhertz or less, which is to say, a period measured in days. You would neither hear nor see anything until you are close enough to experience powerful tides on a time scale of days. So if such an event were to occur in our relative stellar neighborhood, the effect could be an unexplained tide, which, depending on how close we are to the event, could be minor or devastating. Question: What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave?
Answer: Intelligence has nothing to do with it. “Classical” has a lot to do with it. Let me explain. A “classical” entity: a human, a cat, a brick, a video camera, has well-defined states. A brick is either on the table or on the floor, never both. A human is either moving or standing still, never both. A cat is either alive or dead, never both. (Putting aside pointless philosophical musings about cats being, after all, “quantum” since they consist of a very large but finite number of uncorrelated quantum degrees of freedom… true, but for all practical intents and purposes, bricks, cats, etc., are classical. Any quantum behavior is averaged out to the extent that it vanishes.) A “quantum” entity is different. A quantum entity does not have a classically defined position or momentum. Rather, it has a state. That state, which may be described (depending on your mathematical preference) by a vector in an abstract space, or by a fancy wavefunction, can be used to calculate the probability of finding that quantum entity with a certain value for its position or momentum when it interacts with something classical. Let me explain how. What the equations actually tell us is that the state of the quantum entity evolves such that it is constrained by its past, present, and future interactions, including interactions with classical things such as bricks, cats or humans. Quantum physics is manifestly nonlocal (this is the essence of Bell’s famous theorem) so it is subject to constraints that can be arbitrarily far in space or time, yet curiously, somewhat counterintuitively, it remains causal (it is not possible to arrange the future to induce an observable influence on the past). A quantum entity is neither a particle nor a wave, it just displays behaviors of both under the right circumstances. The state of that quantum entity obeys a wave equation including the ability to exhibit interference patterns. But when a quantum entity interacts with a classical thing, the interaction may be localized, creating the appearance of something resembling a miniature cannonball, i.e., a particle. Concerning the double-slit experiment, the quantum entity may be a photon or an electron (so let me just call it an electron from now on), which is confined by three things: a) the location and time of emission; b) the slits; and c) the location and time of detection. These are the constraints that determine the wavefunction that characterizes this electron’s state. One possible interpretation, obviously inspired by the uncomfortable consequence of quantum nonlocality, namely that the location and time of detection is one of the constraints characterizing the system, is to take that constraint out of the picture initially. We then describe the state of an electron that is characterized by the location and time of emission, and the presence of the slits. The resulting wavefunction can be used as a probability amplitude, characterizing the probabilities of possible locations and times for the electron’s detection. When we actually do detect the electron, the picture changes: We now have a new wavefunction that is also constrained by the location and time of detection. This rather abrupt replacement of one wavefunction with another we call “wavefunction collapse”. Now it is true that this interpretation requires an intelligent creature, such as a human who prefers this probabilistic interpretation (the Copenhagen interpretation). But apart from some (not generally accepted) extensions of the quantum theory that treat wavefunction collapse as a physical process, the collapse is only a clumsy mental aid. It is a philosophical musing, not physical reality. In reality, that electron was always governed by a wavefunction subject to nonlocal constraints (again I stress, this is the fundamental essence of Bell’s theorem.) So to sum up, a quantum entity (photon, electron, etc.) is neither a particle nor a wave; its state is governed by a wave equation so it sometimes exhibits the consequences of wave-like behavior; its interactions may be highly localized, giving the impression of a particle; and intelligent observers have nothing to do with this unless we buy into the controversial concept of objective collapse (of the wavefunction), and perhaps not even then. Question: There are reports of stars disappearing, one solution is that they collapse into a black hole without a supernova. How does this happen?
Answer: So-called core collapse supernovae are massive stars with massive cores, which are no longer supported by sustained nuclear fusion against the pull of gravity. When the core collapses, a tremendous amount of energy is released, mostly in the form of neutrinos, but with a neutrino flux so great, it is sufficient to heat up and eject the outer layers of the stars, material amounting to many times the mass of our Sun. The collapsed core, depending on its mass, may form a neutron star or a black hole. It is also possible for it to initially form a neutron star, only to collapse further some time (seconds, hours, days) later, as more stellar material falls back onto the core. However, depending on details such as the size of the core and its chemical composition, the core may collapse directly into a black hole with very little energy released. In this case, there is no significant brightening, resulting sometimes in what is known as a failed supernova, or perhaps not even that, as the outer layers of the star also collapse onto the black hole. Apparently, at least some of these events may be associated with gamma ray bursts (GRBs). This kind of collapse may happen in particular when the star in question is extremely large to begin with, so when its core collapses, it’s too massive and no neutron star forms, and the collapse is rapid enough for there to be no significant neutrino production, no significant shock wave to produce a large explosion. So when we observe the even from afar, especially considering that we don’t watch all the stars continuously all the time, all we see is that one day, a star is there; and the next time we image the same corner of the sky, perhaps days, weeks, months later, that is no longer there.
