Question: Is there a semantic difference between the redshift caused by gravity wells and the redshift caused by the expansion of space?
Answer: First of all, allow me to take exception at the (granted, commonly used) expression, “expansion of space”. Space is not a thing. More specifically, it does not have any little markers attached to it by which its expansion, if any, could even be measured! No, it is things (galaxies, gas, dust, etc.) that are flying apart. It is the density of matter that decreases over time. And it is the gravitational field that changes as a result: a physical field that, however, can also be interpreted as the metric of spacetime. It is when folks take this interpretation a little too literally and a little too dogmatically that we end up with “expansion of space”. So then, putting these qualms aside… redshift happens as a result of the relationship between the world lines of the transmitter and the receiver. If the distance (the actual distance, which may be measurable by means of exchanging light signals, for instance) between the transmitter and the receiver changes over time, there is a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift. If clocks at the different locations (or times!) tick at different rates, there is a gravity-induced redshift (gravity manifests itself primarily in the form of time dilation in general relativity, i.e., the rates at which clocks tick relative to one another.) It is time dilation that yields an observed redshift for light coming from a gravitational well, and it is predominantly time dilation when it comes to the redshift of “high-z” objects, that is, objects very far from here with substantial redshifts. There are some qualitative differences: when it comes to a gravitational well, we’re basically looking at a static configuration, and simply the fact that clocks deep inside that gravitational well tick slower, right now, than clocks elsewhere. When it comes to cosmological redshift, what we see is that in the distant past, matter was much denser, consequently the average gravitational potential was greater and clocks were ticking more slowly back then than they tick today. So truly, it’s gravitational redshift in both cases, just two distinct scenarios: One is the gravitational redshift due to a compact object’s gravitational field here and now, the other is gravitational redshift due to the average gravitational field characterizing the cosmos in the distant past. But fundamentally, it’s gravity in both cases. A consequence of Einstein’s field equations that connect, no, not the “geometry of spacetime” but rather, the tensor field of gravitation with the stress-energy-momentum of matter. It’s due to the weak equivalence principle that we can interpret the tensor field of gravitation as geometry, but as I stressed in many of my answers in the past, Einstein himself cautioned against taking this interpretation too literally. Otherwise it becomes an obstacle, preventing us from thinking about alternate theories of gravity that may not obey the weak equivalence principle, or quantizing gravity as a force. Einstein himself never stopped referring to gravity as a force, the utility of the geometric interpretation notwithstanding. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: A photon has no rest mass, but something called relativistic mass. What is relativistic mass?
Answer: The concept of relativistic mass thankfully fell into disuse in recent decades. It is based on what really is a gross misapplication of the famous formula, E = m c 2 , mass-energy equivalence. Energy is mass, right? So if a photon has energy, it must contribute to its mass, right? Er, not so fast. Einstein’s original 1905 paper on the subject used a very clear expression in its title: Energieinhalt, or energy-content. The energy associated with motion, kinetic energy, is not “energy-content”. It depends on the observer. A moving train has a lot of kinetic energy in the station’s reference frame, but in the train’s own reference frame? There, it is stationary and its kinetic energy is zero. In fact, from the train’s perspective it’s the station that’s moving backwards. Why on Earth would the train’s mass be affected by the fact that some distant stations are moving relative to it? And of course the answer is that it isn’t. As a matter of fact, when we look at that formula again, we might realize that it is just a special case of what is known as the dispersion relation: E 2 = ( m c 2 ) 2 + ( p c ) 2 , where p is the object’s momentum (quantity of motion). So E = m c 2 is valid only when p = 0 , i.e., in the object’s own reference frame in which the object is at rest. Photons have no such reference frame because they are never at rest. For photons, m = 0 , and the dispersion relation becomes instead E = p c . The photon’s energy is proportional to its momentum; its speed is always the vacuum speed of light c in all observer reference frames. Having said that, it is possible for photons to contribute to rest mass, albeit indirectly. For this, imagine a box lined on the inside with perfect mirrors. Let in some light. That light will continue to bounce back-and-forth forever. Now try to push the box. The near wall of the box will also accelerate some photons (that is to say, add to their kinetic energy) when they bounce off it while you’re pushing. Meanwhile, the far well, accelerating away from the photons, will receive a little less help from the photons while you push. The net result is that it is a bit harder to push the box with the photons inside. The box’s inertia, its rest mass, increased a little. By how much? You guessed it: exactly by the amount of kinetic energy that those photons carry, as measured in the box’s own center-of-mass reference frame. But this is not really the rest mass of any individual photon. Rather, it is the energy-content of the “photon gas” that fills the interior of the mirror-lined box. Question: What effect does gravity have on a photon moving directly away from a massive object?
Answer: You stumbled upon one of the three “classical tests” of general relativity theory proposed by Einstein when the theory was new. The other two are the anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of rays of light by a gravitating body. This one, however, is about redshift. Namely that rays of light, photons, arriving from a “deep gravitational well”, will appear to have lost energy. Key to understanding this is gravitational time dilation: remembering that a “perfect clock” appears to tick more slowly when in a gravitational field, compared to an identical clock that is far from any gravitational source. So then, imagine a ray of light, say, a very blue/violet ray of light with a wavelength of 400 nm leaving the surface of a compact, heavy object. Suppose that the object is so heavy, clocks there appear to tick at a rate that is 2/3rd the rate of a clock in deep space, far from sources of gravitation. That 400 nm light ray corresponds to an electromagnetic field that oscillates 750 trillion times a second (750 THz). That is, 750 trillion oscillations while a clock near the light source counts 1 second. Now imagine someone in deep space detecting this light ray. That person uses his own clock to measure time. and his own clock appears to tick faster. While the clock on the surface of the object counted 1 second, this clock in deep space will have counted 3/2 times 1 second, which is to say, one and a half seconds. So it takes one and a half seconds to receive those 750 trillion oscillations. Which means that in one second, this detector will have seen only 500 trillion oscillations. That is to say, it will have observed that light ray at 500 THz, not 750 THz. The corresponding wavelength, then, is not 400 nm but 600 nm. What started off as very blue light arrives at the detector as light that appears very much more like orange. And this, then, is the effect of gravity on a photon. As it climbs out of the “gravity well”, the photon loses energy, which is to say, its characteristic frequency shifts down, the corresponding wavelength increasing. Question: If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow?
Answer: No, it does not, and that is a very important point. The refractive index of transparent materials tends to depend on wavelength. That is to say, light rays of different color will travel at different speeds in that material, and therefore follow different paths. This is why a lens, a prism can split a white ray of light into its constituent colors, creating a rainbow pattern. Gravitational lensing is different, and this has to do fundamentally with the weak equivalence principle. Gravitation is an “equal opportunity” interaction: It does not care about the material properties of the thing that is affected by it. Two rays of light following identical trajectories will be deflected by an identical amount, regardless of their color. This would not be the case, mind you, if the speed of light itself depended on wavelength. And that would be the case if light was a result of an interaction mediated by a particle with mass. But electromagnetism, the interaction behind light, is not mediated by a massive particle. It is mediated by photons, which are massless, so always travel at the vacuum speed of light regardless of their kinetic energy (which in turn determines their frequency, i.e., their color.) So red light and blue light, for instance, despite being substantially different in terms of the energy of the individual photons, will follow the same path in a gravitational field. Having said all that, it is still possible for a gravitational field to produce a rainbow-like effect, but for a different reason. Here is an example of a simulated projection by a gravitational lens with that is not perfectly spherical (i.e., it has a quadrupole mass moment), of light from a point source onto a projection surface: The reason why the colors of the rainbow appear in this image is not because the gravitational lens affected light of different color differently. Rather, it has to do with the constructive/destructive interference of the light wavefront as it arrives at the projection surface; the peaks and valleys of this interference pattern are wavelength-dependent, so we see, e.g., red peaks vs. blue peaks at different locations. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: According to general relativity theory, is there a reason for matter bend space? Are there any new discoveries at that?
Answer: No, there isn’t, and it doesn’t. Before I continue, let me quote a gentleman who knew a thing or two about general relativity: “Sie haben vollständig recht. Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.” — “You are perfectly right. It is wrong to think that the "geometrization" has significant meaning. It is only a kind of a clue helping us find numerical laws. Whether you connect a 'geometric' view to a theory is entirely a private matter.” The gent in question was a certain A. Einstein, in a letter written to a fellow named Reichenbach on April 8, 1926, as quoted by Lehmkuhl (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326.) In short: Do not take the geometric interpretation of general relativity literally or dogmatically. That does not mean it’s a bad or useless interpretation. On the contrary! And there is a darn good reason why this interpretation makes sense: the weak equivalence principle. According to the weak equivalence principle, all material objects are accelerated by gravity the same way, regardless of their composition. But this also means that if you are freely falling, surrounded by other objects, those other objects will either fall at the same rate (so they are motionless relative to you) or they move in a straight line, at uniform velocity, in your freely falling reference frame. In other words, if your happen to be inside a windowless chamber, you can never tell if you are freely falling in a gravitational field or just floating in empty space. But this also implies that a geometric transformation exists between the two cases. Or that conversely, the effects of gravitation can be effectively neutralized by a clever geometric transformation. Which implies, on the other hand, that a geometric theory that can deal with accelerating reference frames can also serve as a theory of gravitation. This was the essence of Einstein’s insight, his happiest moment, and it is more or less how the general theory of relativity was born. Yet he himself cautioned against taking this geometric interpretation too far, too literally. He never stopped referring to gravitation as a force and with good reason. You see, if we want to take the next theoretical step and perhaps… maybe unify gravity with the other forces (Einstein spent the last few decades of his life trying to construct a theory unifying classical electromagnetism and gravity). Maybe developing a quantum field theory of gravitation. Maybe exploring gravity beyond general relativity, constructing a modified gravity theory to account for some oddities in galaxy dynamics or cosmology… a dogmatic, geometric interpretation becomes an insurmountable obstacle. So no, matter does not “bend space”. We wouldn’t even know if it did; space does not have little markers or other means by which its bending could be measured. (Or time. The effects of Newtonian gravity are primarily temporal, not spatial, in the metric.) But the gravitational field of matter does alter how we measure the geometric relationships between events in space-time because everything, including all our measurements, is subject to gravity, in accordance with the weak equivalence principle. Question: Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time?
Answer: Oh, in quantum mechanics, a particle like an electron is always a particle, an actual, immutable particle. The waves (which is to say, the wavefunction) determine the physical properties, including the position and momentum of this particle. In the Copenhagen interpretation, this wavefunction is interpreted as a probability amplitude, and it is used in conjunction with the concept of an idealized, classical measurement apparatus, to compute the probability of finding the electron somewhere, or moving with some momentum. In quantum field theory, there are no particles, only fields. The fields are quantum fields, which is to say, just like the position of that poor electron in quantum mechanics, the field does not have definite values at specific places and times; rather, a wavefunction determines (at least in the Copenhagen interpretation) the probability of finding the field with specific values at specific places and times. However, another property of these quantum fields is that when they interact, their values go up or down one unit at a time. It is these unit excitations that we observe, in localized interactions, with particle-like behavior. So to sum up/reiterate, in quantum field theory, an electron is an excitation of the corresponding fermionic field (the electron field). The wavefunction (not to be confused with the field proper) may be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probabilities of finding the field in a definite state using a classical instrument. Interactions between fields create and destroy excitations (“particles”). In contrast, in quantum mechanics particles are eternal, there are no fields, and the wavefunction can be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probability of finding the particle in some state somewhere using a classical instrument. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is the range of gravitational force infinite, diminishing toward but never reaching zero?
Answer: None of the fundamental (or even not-so-fundamental) forces disappear, but the manner in which they diminish differs. Gravitation and electromagnetism are said to have “infinite” range, because the potential decreases “only” as the inverse of distance, and consequently, the force, which is to say, the gradient (rate of steepest change) diminishes as the inverse square of distance. So it still becomes rather tiny at a great distance from the source, but it’s still there. In contrast, forces mediated by massive particles in the quantum picture are said to have a “finite” range. Near the source, these forces behave just like gravity or electromagnetism. But when you reach a characteristic distance (which is proportional to the inverse of the mass of the force carrier particle) the potential, hence the force, begins to drop very rapidly, exponentially as a matter of fact. Examples fot this include the “weak” force (not really that weak, but it has a very finite range as the force carrier particles, the W and Z-bosons, are very massive), and also the “residual strong force”, aka. the “nuclear force” that is responsible for holding protons and neutrons together inside atoms. As to what the nuclear force is a residual of, whoa, things get really interesting there! The strong force, which holds quarks together, actually increases with distance! When the quarks are very close together, there’s barely any force. The quarks behave like free particles, or almost (this is called asymptotic freedom). But start pulling them apart and the force stiffens. You might think that this implies infinite range, but it really doesn’t; rather, when you pump enough energy into the system pulling two quarks apart, that energy is converted into a new quark-antiquark pair, and the bond “snaps”. Kind of like pulling a string: as you pull, eventually the string breaks, and you end up with two strings, with new endpoints. Ultimately of course all these pretty pictorial representations are just approximations; what we are really describing is a multitude of interacting quantum fields and their excited states. The “virtual particles” that may be used to describe them have no physical reality whatsoever; rather, they are convenient mathematical bookkeeping devices as we keep track of terms in a mathematical expression (a perturbative expansion). Question: Apparently as a mass approaches C, further acceleration requires exponentially greater energy. But, if any non-accelerating object can consider itself to be at rest, then why shouldn't any subsequent change to its velocity be as easy as at V=0?
Answer: Oh, but it is just as easy. However, you must not forget how velocities are added in special relativity. So you have an object, happily traveling at… well, 0 m/s in its own reference frame. It’s a spacecraft. It turns on its rocket engine briefly and accelerates to 1 m/s relative to its earlier inertial reference frame. But this spacecraft was already traveling, say, at 299,792,450 m/s in your reference frame. Just 8 m/s short of the vacuum speed of light. And it turns on its rocket engine. So now you calculate its velocity in your own reference frame. Using, say, v 0 and Δ v for the initial velocity and the change in velocity, you use the relativistic velocity addition formula compute v = ( v 0 + Δ v ) / ( 1 + v 0 Δ v / c 2 ) and get… 299,792,450.00000005337 m/s. In other words, in your reference frame, the object’s velocity increased by just over 53 nanometers per second. For a more elaborate exposition of this problem, I recommend looking at one of the oldest Physics FAQ’s on the Interwebs, this description of The Relativistic Rocket. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished?
Answer: Here's a quote from a recent video by Sabine Hossenfelder: [...] I wasn’t offered a job because I’m a woman. I'm not guessing that that’s what happened, I know, because they told me. You see, the guy who was head of the institute told me that, since I'm female I should apply for a scholarship that was exclusively for women in the natural sciences. Because then the institute wouldn't have to pay for me. I met Sabine (at the Perimeter Institute). My impression was that she radiated self-confident knowledge and competence. To the extent I am qualified to judge, she came across as a very sensible, good physicist with a well-earned reputation, who has put a lot on the table in her career as a professional physicist, and who would never pull the “gender card” to complain. The situation she describes sounds awfully familiar, probably repeated far too often at universities and research institutes around the world, even today. Women face a multitude of obstacles, starting with the cultural: the “hard” sciences are often presented as male pursuits, whereas women should supposedly be more interested in, I don’t know, arts, crafts, or raising babies. I suspect that this already discourages far too many talented young women. Then there is human biology: the birth of a child can burden any parent, but the burden is obviously disproportionately the mother’s, starting with pregnancy and childbirth itself. Family expectations may pile on top of cultural stereotypes: The young mother may be expected to stay at home with the children, while the father assumes the traditional role of breadwinner. Obstacles like that which Sabine encountered may not even be based on downright gender prejudice. Institutions may simply be worried that hiring a woman is like playing the lottery: The woman may get pregnant, perhaps multiple times, absent from her position for extended periods of time. But yes, old-fashioned, ugly gender prejudice is likely still present at times, not to mention unacceptable behavior like harassment or worse. I recall a discussion I once had with someone, about Sabine: the person I was conversing with questioned her competence, unfavorably comparing her to a much younger (male, of course) physicist who has not yet published anything notable at the time. It was clear to me that I was witnessing an outburst of classic, old-fashioned sexism. And it doesn’t take much to change the statistic. When you look at Nobel laureates, they represent an extreme, one of the trailing ends of the Gaussian curve characterizing the scientific community. All it takes is a small shift of the curve to the left, barely noticeable in its central part, for there to be an order-of-magnitude difference near the trailing ends. In short, even if I boldly assume that we no longer need to worry about gender bias in the Nobel selection process that may have deprived the likes of Lise Meitner, Emmy Noether, Cecilia Payne, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Vera Rubin or Chien-Shiung Wu, just to name a few examples (if the names are unfamiliar, look them up, it’s worth your time), of well-deserved recognition, the cards are still far too often stacked against women by both biology and society. Writing this reminded me of one of my heroes, a person who surely would have deserved a Nobel prize, if only computer scientists qualified for one. I am of course talking about the amazing Grace Hopper, mathematician, computer scientist, and rear admiral of the United States Navy, at the time of her retirement the oldest serving commissioned officer in the armed forces of the United States. One of the things she is known for may not be universally liked but it is still widely in use today, nearly 65 years after its invention: The COBOL programming language.

Question: Could you surround an object with gravity sensors so small and accurate that you could have an exact 4D map of the object down to the atomic level, with 3 spatial dimensions and 1 time dimension. For example, could you copy a human brain like this?
Answer: There is no conceivable sensor that would come even close. We are talking about a difference measured in dozens of magnitudes when it comes to what sensors can measure vs. the gravitational field at the atomic level. Having said that, in principle, it would certainly be possible to map an object like that. In fact we’ve done this, sort of. Satellite experiments like GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) have used nothing more than the varying distance between a pair of satellites orbiting the Earth to map the gravitational field of the Earth with exquisite precision, coming up with maps in which the main geographic features of the Earth are recognizable! Unfortunately almost all — scratch that, make it all images that I can find already have the contours of the continents helpfully predrawn, making it hard to discern how much of it we could infer from the observed gravitational anomalies alone. Anyhow, here’s one example: So there, a rather simple “gravity sensor” (again, two satellites connected by a microwave or laser link) mapping the Earth in three, even four (GRACE was able to track changes in the gravitational field over time, e.g., as a result of seasonal ice cover) dimensions. The catch? The ratio of the mass of the Earth vs. the mass of a single proton is a 52-digit number. So no, I don’t think anyone’s brain will be mapped anytime soon at the atomic level using gravity sensors. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the equation that states that an object's observed mass increases with its velocity?
Answer: There is no equation that states that an object’s observed mass changes with its velocity. Rest mass is an intrinsic property of any object and it is invariant unless the object interacts (exchanges mass-energy) with some other object. Unfortunately, especially in older texts about special relativity, there used to be this very misleading, incorrect application of the famous E = m c 2 equation, suggesting that, when an object is in motion, its kinetic energy should be added to its energy-content, increasing its mass by the famous factor 1 / √ 1 − v 2 / c 2 . This is patent nonsense. Unlike rest mass, which is an intrinsic property, kinetic energy depends on the observer. What is the kinetic energy of your luggage next to you when you are on a moving train? Why, it’s zero in your reference frame. It’s nonzero in the station’s reference frame, and even larger (a lot larger) in a heliocentric reference frame. So which value is its “mass”? The answer: none of the above. Because you see, E = m c 2 is only valid in an object’s rest frame of reference. In reference frames in which the object is moving, the correct expression is E 2 = ( m c 2 ) 2 + ( p c ) 2 where p is the object’s momentum. Conversely, m = √ ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 is the object’s rest mass. And this value of m is the same for all observers, regardless of their motion relative to the object. As I said, it’s an invariant. But it’s only in the object’s rest frame, where p = 0 , that we get back E = m c 2 . If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: How do we obtain covariant matrix from contravariant matrix? Is the product of contravariant metric tensor and covariant metric tensor equal to kronecker delta?
Answer: Indeed, the inner product of the covariant and the contravariant forms of the metric yield the Kronecker-delta: g μ ν g ν κ = δ κ μ . Matrices are (or rather, can be) representations of tensors in a specific coordinate system. There is no such thing as a “covariant matrix” or a “contravariant matrix”. If we wanted to be absolutely pedantic about it, a covariant rank-2 tensor should be represented by a row of rows (i.e., a matrix of only one row, with its elements themselves row vectors) and a contravariant rank-2 tensor would be a column of columns; only a mixed-index tensor could be represented properly by a matrix of numbers. But we “cheat” and use matrices anyway for both covariant/contravariant and mixed-index tensors, dropping a bit of pedantic rigor for the sake of convenience. In any case, the general rule is that we use the metric to raise and lower indices, i.e., turn something covariant into something contravariant and vice versa. So to turn a contravariant rank-2 tensor into a covariant one, we’d need to multiply by the covariant metric tensor twice: A μ ν = g μ κ g ν λ A κ λ . So then, if we choose to forego pedantry and represent g μ ν and A κ λ as matrices g and A , it would amount to multiplying A by g on the left and the transpose of g on the right: A ′ = g ⋅ A ⋅ g T , where I used A ′ for the matrix representing A μ ν . Of course the metric is (usually) symmetric, so g = g T . If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: Isn't a supernova an instantaneous event? Why is it said that the last supernova was visible in the sky for 23 days? Shouldn't the explosion only be seen for some seconds?
Answer: Have you seen motion pictures of large explosions? Nuclear tests? The actual explosion is as instantaneous as they come: it’s over in milliseconds or less. Yet in the first millisecond, you don’t even see much. It takes several seconds, minutes even, for the gigantic fireball to flare up, grow, reach its maximum brightness and eventually fade. And that’s a man-made explosion. Large by the standards of us lowly humans, but absolutely nothing compared to a supernova. An explosion that involves several times the mass of the Sun (i.e., several million times the mass of the Earth). An explosion that heats up this material to astonishing temperatures, causing it to fly apart in a gigantic fireball. So don’t be surprised if the light curve reaches its maximum only hours, or more likely, days after the actual event (depending on the type and size of the supernova); and especially don’t be surprised that it then takes weeks or months for the remnant to fade, as the fireball grows in size and becomes fainter. And of course it never quite goes away: e.g., here are the remnants of a fireball that was observed by Chinese astronomers 970 years ago, in 1054: It’s the famous Crab Nebula. Not visible to the naked eye, sure, but still there if you know where to look with a backyard telescope. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: Who has the most tragic backstory from the Fallout universe?
Answer: Just stumbled upon this question and I feel compelled to offer my take: I’d nominate Randall Clark, aka. the survivalist, a person we know only from his scattered journal entries from the Honest Hearts DLC of Fallout New Vegas. From a great distance, he saw the city where his family lived, destroyed in the nuclear holocaust. He was torn by survivor’s guilt. He helped others survive. Finally, he found someone again, only to lose her a few years later, along with their unborn child. It’s been years since I last visited Zion National Park in Fallout NV, but this journal entry still gives me the creeps: Baby was breech. Would've been a son. Michael. Did my best to turn him. Failed. Must've done Caesarean too late. Had to put Sylvie out and she never woke up. Buried them south of the narrows. Well. This time I was by their side. So much better. I think I can finally do it. Blow my fucking brains out all over this goddamn cave. And that’s all we know about him. These journal entries, his skeletal remains (he died alone, killed by lung cancer), some verbal history remembering him as a demigod, and some leftover loot. As a close runner-up, I’d also nominate Christine (from the Dead Money DLC). I understand that there were technical reasons why an NPC from a DLC could not return to the main game, but it was still heartbreaking, having to leave her behind in the Sierra Madre.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If really the black hole and the Bermuda Triangle were brought together, what kind of power or force would happen?
Answer: I don’t think you appreciate just what a black hole really is. The smallest astrophysical black hole has a mass that is roughly three times the mass of our entire solar system. Bring one to the solar system, no closer than, say, Neptune’s orbit, and it will wreak havoc already: orbits will be altered, the Earth’s orbit in particular might be messed up badly enough to render the planet uninhabitable. As to what it will do to the orbits of smaller bodies, asteroids, comets, heaven knows but chances are that for millions of years afterwards, the Earth will be subjected to far more major asteroid impacts than it is today, which would certainly not be good news. The Bermuda triangle is a loosely defined geographic area, which was made famous decades ago by the “discovery” that an unusual number of disappearances (aircraft, ships) happened in this region. Except that there really is nothing unusual. When you look at the number of vehicles that traverse the region, and consider that it is an area frequented by tropical cyclones, the number of incidents turns out to be perfectly normal, nothing out of the ordinary. In any case, should a black hole come any closer than, say, Jupiter’s orbit, the Bermuda triangle would be the least of your concern. Far more important would be the fact that the Earth’s orbit would be drastically altered, perhaps even causing the planet to escape the solar system altogether. If the black hole gets even closer, tidal effects would become significant, causing major floods, earthquakes, large-scale, global geological disasters. And long before the black hole could get anywhere near the Bermuda triangle, the whole planet is ripped apart by tidal forces, forming a hot, rapidly rotating accretion disk around the black hole, to be slowly swallowed by its gravity. You see, as I mentioned above, even the smallest black hole is very, very big. Its “Schwarzschild radius” may be deceptively tiny (around 10 km) but its mass? It weighs about a million times as much as the Earth. Bermuda triangle? Forget it. Our whole planet amounts to nothing more than a speck of dust. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole?
Answer: It might. The jury is still out, given that Hawking radiation represents an approximate solution to a rather tough family of problems. But first things first. Black holes, first and foremost, are mathematical abstractions. That is to say, they are neat mathematical solutions to Einstein’s field equations, but as we know thanks to Oppenheimer and Snyder’s landmark 1939 paper and many other studies on the subject since, we know that the black hole is the “asymptotic end state” of gravitational collapse. In other words, a black hole is what an outside observer would see after waiting an infinite amount of time. At any finite time, no matter how far into the future, the observer would see “continued contraction” (an expression used in the title of the Oppenheimer-Snyder paper), subject to ever greater time dilation, never ending, never reaching the end state characterized by an event horizon. An infalling observer, however, would supposedly reach the event horizon after a finite amount of measured (proper) time. The horizon, for this observer, is a moment in time: once it is reached, there is no going back, as a return to the horizon would necessitate time travel to the past. That’s the classical picture. Now enter quantum field theory, in a so-called semiclassical approximation. First of all, forget that neat but fundamentally incorrect depiction of particles and antiparticles created near the horizon, one with positive, one with negative energy, with the latter swallowed by the black hole. Yes, this depiction comes straight from Hawking’s book, even though it contradicts his own 1974 landmark paper that reveals the true nature of Hawking radiation. It has to do with collapse. Namely that a black hole is, as Oppenheimer-Snyder told us, in a state of continued contraction. This means that the past and the future are not symmetric. Express this statement in the language of quantum field theory, in the presence of the strong gravitational field of the collapsing object and presto: you get outgoing radiation. The characteristic wavelength of that radiation is roughly 20 times the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole that is yet to be formed. The consequence of Hawking radiation is that the energy-content of the collapsing object evaporates in finite time. A very, very long time to be sure, but finite. This statement seems to suggest that in this case, no event horizon ever forms in the first place. It is indeed my inclination to jump to that conclusion but I need to be careful. The semiclassical picture if fraught with traps for the unwary. We treat gravity in this scenario as entirely classical, ignoring any possible contributions from quantum gravity. And of course part of the problem is that all this is the kind of physics that may remain forever untestable. To create an experiment, we’d need to create black holes which requires several times more mass than the mass of our entire solar system. Then we’d have to wait an unimaginably long number of years, typically characterized by a 70-digit number, give or take, before the evaporation completes. Throughout most of this time, Hawking radiation is so incredibly weak, no conceivable instrument, present or future, can detect it. (Don’t be mislead by breathless pronouncements of laboratory “black holes”: these are analogous experiments that, at best, replicate some superficial aspects of black holes.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Where is the "end" of space/time within the boundaries of our observable Universe if a black hole has an event horizon?
Answer: Before I answer the question, let me stress a word in the question itself: space/time. Naive visualizations of “spacetime” as something static, an image frozen in a given moment of time, will not do. Spacetime includes all of time, it’s not a snapshot of space at some specific moment of time. So where is the end of spacetime? Well… it’s more like “when”. One “end” of spacetime in the standard cosmological model is that past moment we sometimes call the “Big Bang”: the initial singularity that marks the beginning of time. The standard model cosmology describes space as infinite, without boundary, but it has a finite age. The initial singularity is not part of spacetime. To make sense of it, imagine the mathematical concept of all positive numbers. This set “ends” at zero, but zero itself is not part of it: it is not a positive number. And the set has no other end; no matter how large a number you pick, larger numbers always exist. The same thing with the other “end” of spacetime: it doesn’t have any. The standard model cosmology has an open-ended, eternal future. Black hole event horizons are different animals, but there are also some similarities. For starters, no black hole event horizon exists “now”. That is to say, any black holes forming as a result of gravitational collapse have not completed that process formation, and will not complete it in any amount of finite time as measured by observers outside. No matter how long you wait, the matter forming the black hole might change its mind (or perhaps a previously unknown physical process might kick in) and fly apart, which it can do in principle, because there is no event horizon yet. That event horizon is a forever-future moment in time, not a specific location in space. This is true even if you were unfortunate enough to fall into a black hole; the only difference is that in that case, you would reach the moment in time called the event horizon in a finite amount of time by your own reckoning, and after that, the event horizon will be a past moment in time for you, something to which you cannot return without a time machine. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Everywhere we are surrounded by a lot of visible electromagnetic waves. Why don’t we see a lots of black patterns of destructive interactions of light waves?
Answer: Actually, you see them all the time. Take a light source, preferably something that has a narrow beam of light. Aim it at a wall. You see a spot of light. Everywhere else on the wall, you see no light. (None from that source anyway.) Now take the wave equations that govern that light as it is emitted by the source and travels through space to arrive at the wall. That wave equation does not vanish outside the light beam. It’s there, everywhere. However, there is no significant constructive interference outside the projected spot of light. Destructive interference prevails. The wall remains dark. How do I know? Say, I wish to solve the wave equations in this case to arrive at a robust, wave-theoretical solution of the projection. Again, the waves are there, everywhere, characterized by a messy integral expression in the mathematical model. That integral usually does not have a neat, clean solution. Rather, I am forced to utilize sensible approximations, for instance the so-called method of stationary phase. The method of stationary phase explicitly picks the light path that corresponds to the strong constructive interference between waves, and discards those paths that are characterized by destructive interference. The result is the calculated spot on the wall. I.e., the method yields the light path that I would calculate using geometric optics, as it tells me precisely where the spot of light will appear. Going beyond either geometric optics or the method of stationary phase, more sophisticated numerical methods might reveal something more than a single spot; the spot may be surrounded by concentric rings of light or similar artifacts, rapidly diminishing in brightness. Here, I have an actual example from work I’ve done in the past. Although this one depicts a case of gravitational lensing, the principles are the same: The image on the left shows an “Einstein cross” (four spots of light) due to a particular (slightly off-axis) gravitational lens, calculated using the method of stationary phase, i.e., geometric optics basically. The image on the right shows the exact same thing, but a more sophisticated numerical integration reveals that there is also light between the spots. In any case, the key message should be clear. The very fact that, despite the fundamental wave nature of light, we see the result of geometric optics everywhere — rays of light, spots of light, shadows, etc., indeed the very fact that our eyes work and can form sharp images — is a result of the combined effects of constructive and destructive interference. In these two images, too, light is everywhere; it’s just that in places where the image appears black, destructive interference won the game. Question: Does the space bend like this: The closer to the center of the mass you are, the smaller it is, things tending to go where it is smaller, explaining gravity?
Answer: No. What we experience as Newtonian gravity is primarily related to the rate of clocks. The stronger the gravitational field, the slower clocks tick in it compared to other clocks in deep space. This results in altered trajectories, objects falling onto, or orbiting, other objects. Spatial effects of relativity theory only begin to play a substantial role when either the gravitational field is very strong (neutron stars and beyond) or the particles probing the field move near the vacuum speed of light. In fact, this leads to Einstein’s famous prediction that particles of light, i.e., photons, will have trajectories near a mass that would be deflected by twice the amount one would calculate using Newtonian gravity alone. This prediction was first confirmed by Eddington’s famous expedition in 1919, observing a solar eclipse and the slight displacement, visible during the eclipse, of stars that appear in the sky near the Sun. Question: How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation?
Answer: Distinguish between local measurements vs. measurements made from a distance. Suppose a photon zings by and you measure its speed: It’s 299,792,458 m/s. Other observers, at the same place where you are and at the same time, measuring the same photon, will measure the same speed even if those other observers are moving relative to you. However, when you look at distant photons, the situation changes. What you observe is subject to relativistic effects such as length contraction and time dilation. The speed you deduce can be anything. If you are on the surface of a neutron star and measure events far from that neutron star, you’ll see things unfold rapidly, as if you viewed them in fast forward mode. Conversely, if you are floating in deep space and check what happens on the surface of that neutron star, things will appear painfully slow, including photons. But even in these cases, as you look at those distant locations, if there are observers there with clocks and meter sticks, you will be able to verify that according to those clocks and meter sticks, co-located with the photon, light still travels at 299,792,458 m/s, always, so long as it’s a vacuum outside. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Did Einstein say that general relativity is not a mechanism for gravity? If so, can you cite those sources?
Answer: Not to my knowledge. If anything, the opposite appears to be the case. His “happiest thought” was the realization that as gravity is universal (weak equivalence principle) it must necessarily be included in a general theory of relativity, which has the ability to relate freely falling reference frames to inertial frames far from any source of gravitation. One thing Einstein did say, however (and perhaps it’s this that may have inspired the question) is not to take the geometric interpretation of the gravitational theory too literally. Evidence for this is that he never stopped referring to gravity as a force in later work, but perhaps the clearest indication is from a letter he wrote in 1926: “Sie haben vollständig recht. Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.” [Einstein to Reichenbach, 8 April 1926. In English: “You are perfectly right. It is wrong to think that the ‘geometrization’ has significant meaning. It is only a kind of a clue helping us find numerical laws. Whether you connect a 'geometric' view to a theory is entirely a private matter.” Quoted by Lehmkuhl, Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326, DOI: 10.1016/j.shpsb.2013.08.002] If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: A neutron star has an intense gravitational field.Would the neutron stars gravitational field intensity increase significantly, if (somehow) it was accelerated to near c?
Answer: Remember that speed is relative. From the neutron star’s perspective, it is you, the observer, who is moving near the vacuum speed of light in this example. Why would the neutron star care that you are moving that fast? Why would it even know? And the answer is, it would not. It would be the same happy neutron star, always at rest in its own reference frame. The fact that you can transform the neutron star and its gravitational field into another reference frame that moves relative to the neutron star’s own frame of reference has no physical consequences. In this new reference frame, you’ll see, instead of a static, spherically symmetric gravitational field, an axially symmetric, time-varying gravitational field. But it’s still the same gravitational field, no physical change whatsoever, just a different perspective. In old textbooks, sometimes you may have encountered the concept of “relativistic mass”. Thankfully, this concept fell into disuse because it is nonsensical. Misinterpreting the mass-energy equivalence relationship, this concept summed the intrinsic rest mass of an object and its observer-dependent kinetic energy. This should never have been done. Why? Because E = m c 2 is not about “relativistic mass”. The actual meaning of the mass-energy equivalence relationship, made abundantly clear by Einstein even in the title of his seminal paper from 1905, is that an object’s inertia(l mass) is determined by its energy-content. Energy-content means all the energy “in” the neutron star, not the kinetic energy of the neutron star as measured by a distant observer. Short answer: No, an object’s gravitational field is not affected by the relative velocity between object and observer, even if it is expressed differently in the reference frame of the moving observer. Question: If a neutron star was made entirely of neutrons, would it eventually collapse into a black hole?
Answer: No, a neutron star does not collapse into a black hole unless it is heavy enough to do so. In a neutron star, neutrons are pushed apart by what is known as neutron degeneracy pressure. It is a direct consequence of neutrons being fermions, subject to the Pauli exclusion principle: Two neutrons cannot be in the same quantum state. However, this degeneracy pressure is not infinite. When the mass of the neutron star reaches what is known as the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit, strange things start to happen. The reason why I am being vague is because at this point, the story becomes less certain. Neutrons, after all, are not elementary particles, but composites: They consist of triplets of quarks. When the TOV limit is reached, neutrons break down and… form what? If anything? As far as I know, no one ever calculated with certainty what happens at this point, but the general consensus is that once neutron degeneracy pressure is reached, the neutron star collapses into a black hole. But again, it requires mass, something between 2 and 3 solar masses (the exact number is not known, only range estimates). So it’s not about what a neutron star is made of, it’s about how much of it is there. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: If excitations in the "electron field” look to us like electrons and positrons, and excitations in the "photon field” look to us like photons, what do we perceive excitations in the "electric field" or "magnetic field" or "gravitational field" as?
Answer: Electric and magnetic fields are both manifestations of the electromagnetic field (i.e., the “photon field”). How the electromagnetic field appears to split into these components is observer-dependent. For instance, an observer standing next to an electron will see an electrostatic field and no magnetic field; another, moving observer, looking at the same charge, would see a time-varying electric field in his moving reference frame, along with a magnetic field. Whether or not the gravitational field is a quantum field remains an open question. If it is a quantum field, we expect that its excitations would, under the right circumstances, appear as “gravitons”. However, given how weak the gravitational interaction is, we may never be able to “perceive” gravitons directly with any conceivable present or future experiment. There are occasionally proposals though that might (or not) help us confirm the quantum nature of the gravitational field. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is light both a particle and a wave at the same time, or is it sometimes a particle, and sometimes a wave, or does it appear to be one or the other depending on how you look at it?
Answer: None of the above. What we call light is an excitation of the electromagnetic field far (at least a few wavelengths away) from any sources. These excitations are governed by a wave equation, so that are called electromagnetic waves. But… But the electromagnetic field itself is a quantum field, which means that its behavior is not like that of a classical medium. Classical things have well-defined positions and momenta (quantity of motion). These positions and momenta are represented by numbers. Quantum things only have states; these states are interpreted as probability amplitudes that tell us how likely we are to measure certain values of positions or momenta if we were to measure the thing. These states are governed by a wave equation (nothing to do with the wave equation I mentioned above): the Schrödinger equation. Moreover, when the quantum field is a thing, its excitations come in well-defined units. When the field interacts with something else, the number of excitations is bumped up or down. These interactions are often perceived as highly localized, i.e., they will register in measurements as “particles”. So there… Light is not a wave and light is not a particle. Light is a propagating change in the quantum electromagnetic field, a change governed by a wave equation, of a field the state of which is governed by another wave equation, solutions of which are quantized excitations that may appear as particles. And that is the simplest way that I can express this without omitting anything essential. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: When a star or other heavy structure curves spacetime, trajectories of approaching objects get curved and longer. If the object falls towards a blackhole, won’t its trajectory assymptotically approach the event horizon forever, never reaching it?
Answer: Depends on who is looking. This, after all, is what relativity theory is all about. Suppose you are watching that object from the outside. As it approaches the event horizon, you will see events unfold ever more slowly, due to extreme gravitational time dilation. (That is the “curved” trajectory: It’s not a change in direction in space, but a change in the rate of time relative to the distant observer.) The moment when the object would reach the event horizon remains forever in your future. Or, to put it another way, if the object is a very powerful rocket, it doesn’t matter how long you wait, you can never be certain that it won’t be turned on, allowing the object to escape. But if you were to travel with the object, things would be very different. You would reach the event horizon alright. You’ll find yourself in a closed “mini-universe”, containing anything and everything that ever falls into the black hole. This would be a collapsing mini-universe, with very little time left. How little? Well, if it’s a stellar sized black hole, we’re talking milliseconds or less. Mind you, if it’s a stellar sized black hole, by the time you got near the event horizon, you’d have been ripped apart by extreme tidal forces (spaghettification) anyway. At least that is the classical picture. When we allow quantum physics to enter the scene, e.g., by way of Hawking radiation, things change, but that’s a whole other matter, with no clear answers yet. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the most promising propulsion technology for theoretical manned Interstellar travel? What percentage of the speed of light could be theoretically reached?
Answer: If I had to bet, I’d bet on the Bussard ramjet. Yes, I know it that there were studies questioning its feasibility. I read some of them. Still. The reason? It is the only approach I know of that a) does not rely on exotic physics, and b) does not require a spacecraft to carry absolutely insane quantities of propellant. A Bussard ramjet works by collecting interstellar hydrogen using a large, very powerful magnetic field, and then burning that hydrogen in a fusion engine. As such, a Bussard ramjet does not have a theoretical limit as to how close it can get to the vacuum speed of light, as it can accelerate forever. Much as I enjoy Star Trek, I am not keen on the concept of warp drives in the real universe. I mean, they look great on paper as theoretical solutions of Einstein’s field equations, but hey, I can also have theoretical solutions that involve closed timelike curves, and I have yet to meet Dr. Who with his lovely TARDIS. There is a world of a difference between building a mathematical construct of a universe that may be consistent with Einstein’s field equations, vs. taking this, one-and-only, universe in which we live, with ordinary matter in it, and bring that matter together in a configuration that creates a “warp field”. Call me small-minded but I do not think that is possible; not because of limits of technology, simply because warp drives, just like time machines, don’t exist in this universe. Same goes (even more so) for wormholes and other exotic solutions. What about super-efficient rockets? There we have a problem. Even if we have a maximum efficiency photon rocket powered by matter-antimatter annihilation, we still need absolutely insane quantities of fuel to accelerate a given spaceship to relativistic speeds. The rocket equation stands in our way: soon, when we calculate a round trip to a distant star, which we would like to execute within the lifetime of a human astronaut, we find that to accelerate our, say, 100-ton spaceship to the requisite speeds requires megatons of fuel. Do we really want to sit on top of megatons of antimatter, even if we knew how to manufacture antimatter in quantity, which we don’t? Is that ever going to be practical? And even if it is, once that spaceship runs out of fuel, it’s dead in space… whereas our Bussard ramjet only needs a small amount of residual fuel to be started, and then it starts collecting its own fuel again, with increasing efficiency as it accelerates. Of course things can change. New technologies may be invented. There may be new breakthroughs in theoretical physics that completely change its landscape. But in the here and now, I consider the ramjet the most promising approach, despite the spectacular technical challenges that might stand in its way. Question: Is this new story proof in physics that MOND is finished? Https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/is-dark-matter-s-main-rival-theory-dead-the-cassini-spacecraft-and-other-recent-tests-may-invalidate-mond/ar-BB1maqMN?ocid=hpmsn&cvid=31541f6e52e74450
Answer: A story on a news Web site is only proof that the news Web site still works and that its journalists are working. As to the study that the Web site references, it certainly presents a challenge to MOND. Unfortunately, over the years MOND has become a straw man for the modified gravity paradigm. It should not have. MOND is not a proper field theory of gravitation. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton’s second law. A modification that does not even obey basic conservation laws. It is designed to fit spiral galaxy rotation curves, which it does, though not always; but as it is not a theory, just a formula, it cannot say much about the numerous other challenges facing modified gravity, from precision solar system tests to cosmology. Meanwhile, by virtue of its unspecified interpolation function, and the even more mysterious deus ex machina, the External Field Effect, MOND can be made to fit anything and everything; I swear I’d not be surprised if one day someone showed how, with the right choices, MOND could be used to make stars do the hula-hoop. (Yes, I am exaggerating, but not by much. Maybe I should write an April 1 paper on this?) My advice would be, sure, feel free to use the MOND formula if it proves to be a valid approximation of a respectable gravitational theory in a certain regime. But do not mistake that formula for the real thing, a proper field theory of gravitation. Whether or not such a field theory will ever succeed as an alternative to the dark matter/dark energy paradigm, time will tell. There are arguments both ways; the standard cosmological model remains the leading contender, but issues such as the Hubble tension, mature early galaxies, not to mention the failure of all such experiments so far to detect dark matter directly, all suggest that perhaps, just perhaps, modifying the field theory of gravitation is the way to go. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is dark energy a scalar field like the Higgs, for example?
Answer: We don’t know what dark energy is. Its properties are not consistent with the kinetic term of a scalar field, like the Higgs. Its properties may be consistent with a strong self-interaction potential in a hypothetical scalar field. That is to say, for a massless scalar field, its equation of state would be something like w = [ ˙ ϕ − 2 V ( ϕ ) ] / [ ˙ ϕ + 2 V ( ϕ ) ] . For dark energy, w = − 1 , which we get if V ( ϕ ) dominates in the preceding expression. That is to say, if the self-interaction term dominates, it behaves as a perfect fluid with negative pressure, which is the behavior of dark energy. The Higgs does not work this way. (The scalar doublet does not have this kind of behavior, and as for the Higgs boson after symmetry breaking, it’s a massive, unstable, particle to begin with, so the wrong candidate.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it possible for LIGO to detect gravitational waves from space elevators or other large structures moving at relativistic speeds?
Answer: No. For starters, space elevators have nothing to do with relativistic speeds. The concept is to let a structure, either anchored or orbiting, life things from the surface of a planet to high orbit, without the need to spend copious quantities of rocket fuel. The speeds involved, at most, would correspond to typical orbital velocities, which in the case of the Earth, is several km/s (depending on orbital radius), which is a tiny fraction of what would be called relativistic speeds. In any case, motion, relativistic or otherwise, does not produce gravitational waves, just like a moving charge does not produce electromagnetic waves. For that, you need acceleration. Not just any acceleration, mind you. It is a peculiar nature of gravitation that there are no dipole gravitational waves; linear acceleration does not produce gravitational waves, nor does the acceleration associated with the rotation of an axially symmetric body (e.g., a spinning planet or star). What we need is a nonzero quadrupole moment, deviation from axial symmetry. Then there is the fact that gravitational waves are very, very, weak. LIGO is designed to detect gravitational waves produced by events that, very briefly, outshine the entire visible universe (not an exaggeration!) when we compare the peak gravitational wave output to the electromagnetic output of all visible galaxies combined. Compared to that, an artificial structure is nothing! And then there is the fact that LIGO is “tuned” to specific frequencies by its design: Its peak sensitivity is around 200 Hz, roughly the A sound below middle C. Stray too far from ~200 Hz, and LIGO’s sensitivity drops dramatically. So unless the system produces gravitational waves in his frequency range, LIGO will be oblivious to it, even if the signal would otherwise be powerful enough for LIGO to detect. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Where can I find an explanation of the Standard Model Lagrangian that explains the meaning of each term?
Answer: In a book. Specifically, let me recommend the book that, to me, is the “go to” reference on the Standard Model: The Standard Model, by Burgess and Moore (2007). Very elegantly, cleanly written, it systematically constructs the Standard Model Lagrangian from first principles, exploring the significance and properties of each term. In fact, it is thanks to this book that I resist the temptation to try and offer an explanation here, in the form of a short Quora answer. That is because I realize that the book, in a mere 500-odd pages, offers the most concise, yet sensible presentation of the model. Sure, I could copy-paste the LaTeX of that monster Lagrangian here just to show what a clever boy I am, but without the background, the details that are in the book, the symbols mean little. So rather than trying to impress folks with a nasty multiline equation occupying the better part of a full printed page, let me just recap its essence: It is a Lagrangian that incorporates an S U ( 3 ) c × S U ( 2 ) × U ( 1 ) gauge theory of quarks and leptons, combined with the Higgs mechanism. Here, S U stands for the symmetry group of unitary matrices with positive determinant; these matrices can be used to represent families of particles with certain behavior. U ( 1 ) , similarly, is a rotation in the complex plane, again suitable to represent certain particles mathematically. The “gauge” nature of the interaction is represented by the fact that the force carried by the interaction is described mathematically using covariant derivatives. The S U ( 3 ) c part of the Lagrangian represents an interaction (the strong force) carried by a family of eight massless spin-1 particles (gluons). Particles that interact by way of exchanging these gluons are said to carry “color” charge. The S U ( 2 ) × U ( 1 ) part corresponds to a family of four spin-1 particles. Here, the S U ( 2 ) part of the symmetry is “broken”, because of an additional interaction with a scalar field, the Higgs field. As a result, the three spin-1 particles mediating the S U ( 2 ) part (i.e., the weak interaction) are massive. The remaining, massless vector boson is the well known photon of electromagnetism. The particles that interact with these fields are fermions. They include fermions that participate in the strong force (quarks) and fermions that only participate in the electroweak interaction. Of these, the charged leptons such as electrons have electric charge; neutrinos do not. There is also the handedness of neutrinos that is encoded in the Lagrangian. This fermionic content is repeated three times to represent the three generations of quarks and leptons. Finally, the model is completed by a term that represents the Higgs field, with its peculiar potential and interactions with the other fields, which allow for the mechanism of symmetry breaking through which charged leptons and quarks also acquire masses. The strength of this model is that it yields a renormalizable (no crazy infinities) representation of all the known particle content of the universe, successfully predicting the outcome of many difficult experiments, indeed leading to the theoretical prediction, later confirmed experimentally, of the existence of particles like the Z-boson, the top quark, and last but not least, the Higgs boson. The specific form of the Lagrangian and the particle-content that it represents are all based on experimental evidence. Missing from the Standard Model is any mechanism to endow neutrinos with masses; any explanation as to why there are three generations of fermions; the nature of neutrinos vs. antineutrinos; and, of course, a proper unification with gravity. These omissions and the ways in which they might be addressed are also covered in the Burgess and Moore book. Well, that’s the gist of it. Beyond this, I think you really need a textbook or two. Burgess and Moore is great, but it assumes that you understand the basics of quantum field theory, so you might have to start somewhere else. The book, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory by Peskin and Schroeder, might be a good choice, it’s one of the best (if not the best) reasonably up-to-date textbooks out there. Question: If you take energy out of an electric field, will it disappear? Also, since electric charges have an electrical field, do they have infinite energy since their electric fields don't seem to disappear?
Answer: Maintaining a static electric field does not require a continuous input of energy. The energy-content of the field is finite and unchanging when the charge is at rest (or moves at uniform velocity) so there is no exchange of energy between the charge and the field. The electric field, by the way, is just one manifestation of the electromagnetic field. In fact, how we “split” the electromagnetic field into an electric and a magnetic part depends on the observer; e.g., an observer standing still next to an electric charge sees a static electric field, whereas another observer, moving by at some speed, sees a combination of an electric field that varies over time, and a corresponding magnetic field. Any change in the electromagnetic field involves the exchange of energy between the field and the charges with which it interacts. The (one-and-only) electromagnetic field is always present; its value varies from point to point in space and from moment to moment in time, as a result of its interaction with charges, and also as a result of its “free” behavior, such as the transmission of electromagnetic waves, far from any sources. Question: If gravity is a warping of space-time, why is it that we see no distortions in our visual field?
Answer: Well, the main reason is that Newtonian gravity is primarily about distortions of time, that is to say, the rate at which clocks tick. The stronger the gravitational field, the slower clocks tick in it compared to other clocks situated elsewhere. Compared to this temporal distortion, spatial distortion is exceedingly tiny. As a matter of fact, the temporal distortion is tiny, too. Here on the surface of the Earth, terrestrial gravity alters the rate of clocks by roughly one part in a billion compared to clocks in deep space. It would take several decades before the difference between two such clocks reaches one second. Yet the distortions are visible, just not with the naked eye. In 1919, an expedition lead by Arthur Eddington was measuring just that: the visual distortion due to the Sun’s gravity during a total solar eclipse. As expected, some stars that appeared near the solar disk (its light blocked by the Moon) were displaced by a tiny amount. How tiny? About 1.75 arc seconds. For comparison, that would be like looking at an object that is a mile away, and noticing that it is displaced by about half an inch. Curiously though , in the case of light both spatial and temporal distortions play an equal role. That is to say, half of that 1.75 arc seconds was due to temporal distortion but the other half was due to spatial distortion. As a result, this value is double the value one would predict using Newtonian gravity. This was therefore seen as a much celebrated confirmation that Einstein’s theory of gravitation is the correct one. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How likely is it that antigravity is possible? What are some possible ways that anti-gravity could exist, if any?
Answer: Well, in a sense it does exist, but not necessarily in a form anyone might consider useful. You may have heard of dark energy, driving the accelerating expansion of the universe. Why accelerating? Normally, gravity would slow down the expansion, perhaps even reverse it, since it is pulling things together. However, there’s a subtle but important point when we switch over from Newtonian gravity to general relativity. In Newtonian gravity, the source of gravitation is mass density. This is formally written in the form of Poisson’s equation as ∇ 2 U = 4 π G ρ where U is the gravitational potential and ρ is the mass density. In general relativity, however, that ρ is replaced with ρ + 3 p / c 2 , where p is the pressure. (As for the rest of the symbols, G is the gravitational constant, c is the vacuum speed of light, and ∇ in this case is the gradient operator.) Normal matter has pressure, but after divided by the square of the speed of light, that pressure turns out to be negligible compared to mass density. But dark energy! Dark energy not only has pressure, but it is a) negative, b) huge. How huge? For dark energy, p = − c 2 ρ . Put that into Poisson’s equation and there you have it: For dark energy, ∇ 2 U = − 8 π G ρ . Repulsive gravity. Stuff in regions of space dominated by dark energy are pushing away from each other, accelerating cosmic expansion. As I said, not very useful unless you are into universe-building. But there you have it, antigravity, an essential feature of our cosmos if our standard cosmological model can be believed. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is MOND a statistical artifact and how do new gravity models answer the question of dark matter any more accurately?
Answer: MOND is an “artifact” alright, in the sense that it is something created by humans, but it is not statistical in nature. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton’s second law, purportedly to model the anomalous rotation curves of spiral galaxies. That’s all. Take F = m a , and replace it with something. A particular something that, in MOND’s case, does not even obey basic conservation laws. Unfortunately, MOND has become synonymous with a much broader, reasonably respectable area of research, modified gravity. In fact, it has become a straw man unfortunately: It’s easy to see how many different ways MOND can go wrong, and all too often, it is seen as a failure of modified gravity theories in general. A modified gravity theory has to do a bunch of things. For starters, its effects must be absent in the laboratory, and here in the solar system. Which is to say, the theory’s predictions for observations like precision orbit calculations, GPS data, lunar laser ranging, planetary radar ranging, the Shapiro delay, Cassini radio science, Viking radio science, must all produce the right results. For spiral galaxies, the theory must match the empirical predictions of the so-called Tully-Fisher law. For smaller systems, such as globular clusters, it still needs to produce velocity dispersions that obey Newtonian physics. On the other hand, for galaxy cluster dynamics, it must produce something that resembles the observed distribution of stellar mass, gas (X-ray emissions) and weak lensing. Last but not least, on the cosmological scale, the theory must accurately reproduce things like the matter power spectrum (the large-scale distribution of galaxies) or the angular (acoustic) power spectrum of the microwave background. MOND does almost none of the above. Which should come as no surprise: It is not a modified theory of gravitation. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton’s second law. It is, of course, possible to build a more respectable modified gravity theory, and people have been trying to do that utilizing a variety of approaches for many years, starting with Jordan-Brans-Dicke theory from more than 60 years ago (but anticipated a century ago by Eddington, who first introduced expressions that can be used to parameterize families of modified gravity theories.) Some of these theories have been falsified by data, including, among other things, the “multimessenger” (gravitational and electromagnetic) observations of neutron star mergers. Other theories, like, say, Mannheim’s conformal gravity or Moffat’s MOG theory*, remain in contention. More recently, these theories have gained a little bit of traction, in particular because of the persistent failure of attempted experiments aimed at detecting dark matter directly. But the bar is set very high for modified gravity. It is insanely hard to produce a theory that successfully deals with all of the challenges that I listed above. Which is why the standard, “Lambda-CDM” model remains the leading contender, despite challenges such as the failure to detect dark matter, or contradictory results like the famed “Hubble tension” or the unexpected number of early mature galaxies seen by the JWST. But none of this has anything to do with MOND. MOND is just a silly phenomenological formula, that works for (some) spiral galaxies and does nothing else. It should not be treated as a straw man for modified gravity. *Disclaimer: I worked with Moffat on the MOG theory extensively over the past 20 years.
