Question: Planck length is the smallest measurable length, and the scale at which we require new laws of quantum gravity. If we defined laws of quantum gravity, allowing us to predict interaction at these lengths, could we measure these lengths? Cite papers!

Question: As as a European that either travelled to the United States or never visited the country, do you view the Americans as very rude people? Do you think Europeans are kinder than Americans?
Answer: I was born in Europe. I arrived in Canada as a landed immigrant in the mid-1980s, in my early 20s. I’ve been to the US many times in the past 30-odd years. Question: The universe is 13.8 billion years old. But the fraction we are permitted to observe has an approximate radius of 47 billion light years. So, is space-time structure continuously expanding? Or, does it happen an inflationary era after the Big Bang?
Answer: The problem here is that “distance” may not mean what you think it means in an expanding universe. Indeed, the most distant parts of the universe that we are able to observe would be “presently” at roughly 47 billion light years from here. But we are not observing them at the “present”. We are observing them as they were 13.8 billion years ago, when they were much closer to us. In fact, much closer than 13.8 billion light years but that, too, is misleading; the average gravity of the universe back then was much stronger, which means substantial gravitational time dilation (the main reason for cosmological redshift for very distant objects) so from our perspective, light from these things was moving much slower, too. In cosmology textbooks, you will find a variety of distance measures. The 47 billion light years figure is simply the coordinate distance in so-called “comoving coordinates” of these things from us. It has no direct physical meaning. There are other distance measures, like “luminosity distance” (how faint something is compared to its brightness at a known distance) or “angular diameter distance” (how small something appears in the sky compared to its apparent size at a known distance). And yes, “light travel distance”, which, unsurprisingly, is exactly 13.8 billion light years for an object from which it took 13.8 billion years for light to reach us. Finally, yes, the universe continues to expand, but no, it’s not “space-time structure”. It is things. Clusters of galaxies flying away from each other, the distance between them increasing, their density decreasing over time. Do not confuse this with the hypothetical concept of inflation: that represent a brief but significant period in the history of the very early universe, when things were pushed away from each other by repulsive gravity (present due to some hypothetical field that, much like a cosmological constant or a “dark energy” component, produces gravitational repulsion due to its negative pressure), accelerating the rate of expansion. This era supposedly ended when the universe was still very young, but that does not mean expansion stopped; it simply means that expansion, from this point onward, began to slow because attractive gravity is trying to pull things back together. More recently in the standard cosmological model, repulsion again took over because of the presence, and now dominance, of dark energy so for the past 5 billion years or so, the rate of expansion has been increasing; at least this is what we appear to deduce from observations of distant supernovae, supported by the “standard”, so-called Lambda-CDM, cosmological model. Question: Why a free isolated electon cant fully absorb a photon?
Answer: It has to do with conservation laws. A photon’s energy and momentum are proportional to one another: E = p c . Now look at an interaction involving an electron absorbing a photon. Specifically, look at it from the coordinate reference frame in which the electron’s direction of motion changes but its speed remains the same. This means that there is a change in momentum (a vector quantity, which changes if its direction changes even if its magnitude remains the same) but no corresponding change in energy (the electron’s energy in this reference frame is the same before and after the absorption event.) This is a contradiction: it means that the electron absorbed zero energy but nonzero momentum, which is incompatible with the nature of a photon. (Similar reasoning also applies to electron-positron annihilation, explaining why, as a minimum, two photons must be produced in such interactions.) Now if the photon is not confined to the “mass shell”, things are different. Such photons do not exist as actual particles: they are “virtual particles”, essentially mathematical mnemonic devices that help us describe particle interactions. But these “virtual photons” do not obey the relationship, E = p c , therefore it is perfectly valid to speak of their emission or absorption by electrons, so long as we never forget that “virtual” literally means not real, i.e., we are talking about a computational bookkeeping device, not a physical particle. Question: Can you explain the concept of dark energy in the Big Bang theory? Is it considered a part of inflation?
Answer: Not precisely part of inflation, but related. The standard cosmological model assumes a universe that is the same everywhere (homogeneous) and has no preferred direction (isotropic). All forms of “matter” (and by “matter”, we mean anything and everything that’s not empty space) would be in the form of “isotropic perfect fluids”: that is to say, mediums that are characterized by its mass density ρ and pressure p . The ratio of energy density and pressure is a pure number: w = p / c 2 ρ . This “equation of state” characterizes the medium. The number w can be anything between -1 and +1 (yes, this includes negative pressure). It is substantially different from zero only for “relativistic” forms of matter: ordinary matter is well described by w = 0 , which is to say, its pressure is much, much less than its energy density. (Values below -1 would yield an unstable universe; values over +1 would yield a speed of sound that exceeds the vacuum speed of light, violating causality.) So then, the question becomes: What mixture of such perfect fluids yield the observed properties of the universe? When we take the totality of observations into account, we find that observable results — including the cosmic microwave background, its minute fluctuations, the large-scale distribution of matter, the luminosity-redshift relationship of Type Ia supernovae, and a host of other observations — can be best modeled if the universe is assumed to be “spatially flat”, with 30% of all matter in the form of w = 0 “dust”, and 70% in the form of w = − 1 “dark energy”. Ordinary matter amounts to only about 4%, so the remaining 26% of “dust” is assumed to be something invisible, dubbed “dark matter”. Though there are plenty of theories, we have no idea what either of these “dark” things really are; the names are basically placeholders representing our ignorance. There is a curious point concerning matter with significant, relativistic pressure. For ordinary matter, its gravitation is determined by the mass density ρ . However, when relativistic pressure is present, it must be included as a source of gravitation: we end up with ρ + 3 p / c 2 as the source. For dark energy, w = − 1 , this implies that gravitation will be proportional to − 2 ρ , that is to say, it is repulsive! This is why the presence of dark energy actually pushes stuff in distant parts of the universe away from each other, accelerating the rate at which the universe continues to expand. Note that this is not inflation. However, inflation is related. It was supposed to happen in the very early universe, when something akin to dark energy dominated the universe, accelerating its expansion for a very brief but significant period of time. Whatever was the source of that large negative pressure, however, is supposed to have undergone some kind of phase transition, its negative pressure vanishing. Afterwards, the rate of expansion began to decrease and continued to decrease for roughly 9 billion years, before (ordinary and dark) matter became sufficiently dilute so that dark energy became dominant, and the rate of expansion began to increase again. Bottom line: though the mechanisms are closely related, do not confuse inflation (rapid expansion in the extreme early universe) with acceleration (the universe slowly shifting from a decelerating to an accelerating rate of expansion in the past 4–5 billion years). Question: Can the Schrödinger equation model interactions in a field, or does it only work in a free field?
Answer: It certainly can. Fundamentally, the Schrödinger equation is just the quantum version of Hamilton’s equation. It incorporates both kinetic and potential terms. The kinetic terms represent free particles or fields; the potential terms represent interactions. That is to say, when you look at textbook forms of the Schrödinger equation, e.g., i ℏ ∂ t ψ = ( − ℏ 2 2 m ∇ 2 + V ( q ) ) ψ , the first term on the RHS is the free particle or field; the position-dependent potential term V ( q ) combines all interactions. The classical equivalent is Hamilton’s equation in the form E = p 2 2 m + V ( q ) , which basically tells you that the total energy of the system is the sum of the kinetic energies of the free system plus the potential energies of all interactions. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is the Theory of relativity considered to be completely accurate, or are there still aspects that are being researched or questioned?
Answer: I think the fairest answer that I can offer is… almost. That is to say, general relativity withstood every precision test here in the solar system. This includes laboratory tests, GPS, lunar laser ranging, planetary radar ranging, radio science with solar system probes, you name it. General relativity also accurately describes the orbits of close binary pulsars, including the loss of energy in the form of gravitational radiation, and more recently, the received gravitational wave signals from cataclysmic events like black hole mergers. So by and large, it’s a success story, with one possible caveat: On the largest of scales, galaxies and beyond, general relativity does not correctly predict what we see unless we assume the presence of unseen, “dark” matter and also dark energy. These forms of matter (yes, confusingly dark “energy” is also a form of matter, never mind the terminology) have been postulated to make sense of galaxy rotation curves and cosmological data, but their existence have not been confirmed; indeed, every experiment or observation to date that was designed to detect them produced a null result. That does not mean that dark matter and dark energy do not exist, but it raises the possibility that on such astronomical scales, general relativity may need to be modified. There are other, lesser but related puzzles (e.g., the apparent conflict between different ways of measuring the Hubble parameter) that might also indicate that the theory needs to be refined or revised. But that is far from a certainty. In fact, if you were to bet money on it, I’d still advise you to bet on general relativity prevailing (and I say this as someone who actually worked on modified gravity theories, so it’s not like I am dead set against the idea, quite the contrary.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can gravity be repulsive according to general relativity? How could this concept be tested through experiments?
Answer: Yes, gravity can be repulsive. In fact, repulsive gravity is the reason why, in the standard cosmological model, the expansion of the cosmos has been accelerating for the past five billion years, give or take. You may be familiar with the classical field equation for gravitation, Poisson’s equation: ∇ 2 U = 4 π G ρ , where U is the Newtonian gravitational potential, G is Newton’s constant and ρ is the mass density. (The inverse square law of gravitation follows from this expression, when \rho characterizes a compact source.) However, this equation must be modified when the medium has relativistic pressure, which is to say, when p / c 2 (with p being the pressure, c being the vacuum speed of light) is comparable in magnitude to ρ . In this case, we need to write ∇ 2 U = 4 π G ( ρ + 3 p / c 2 ) . The weirdest part is that pressure can be negative. In fact, any value between − c 2 ρ ≤ p ≤ c 2 ρ yields self-consistent physics. (When p < − c 2 ρ , the universe becomes unstable; when p > c 2 ρ , the speed of sound becomes greater than the speed of light, violating causality.) For the famous “dark energy” of standard cosmology, p = − c 2 ρ . This means that for dark energy, Poisson’s equation actually becomes ∇ 2 U = − 8 π G ρ D E . Note the change of sign. Question: Debroglie says wavelength is inversely proportional to velocity. But velocity is relative, and it is 0 in that particle’s resting frame of reference. So what does it mean for a particle to have infinite wavelength?
Answer: Well, if you think of the de Broglie wavelength as a means to characterize how a particle moves, in the reference frame in which the particle is at rest, infinite wavelength (zero frequency) simply means that the particle is not moving. I know, it sounds kind of tautological, but that’s what it boils down to: no movement, no wave, zero frequency, hence infinite wavelength. Of course keep in mind that we’re not talking about a physical wave here. The wavelength here is simply a mathematical characterization of the amplitude of the particle’s wavefunction, which determines the probability density of finding the particle in a given state. Zero momentum means that the particle is not moving, but it can be with equal probability anywhere. This also follows from the uncertainty principle, since precise determination of a particle’s momentum means its position is completely indeterminate. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Has it ever been considered that the cosmic microwave background at 2.73K is a kind of balance between matter and energy in the universe? I don't find anything googling, so maybe it's a no question?
Answer: It is indeed not a good question, though, I suspect, at the root of the question lies a misunderstanding of what “matter” and “energy” are in fundamental physics. To wit, “matter” is everything that’s not empty space. All the stuff that there is. In the cosmologist’s view, you are matter, Earth is matter, the Sun is matter, sunlight is matter, electromagnetic fields are matter, the presumed quark-gluon plasma that filled the early universe is matter, etc. As I said, everything that’s not empty space. As to “energy”, there are fundamentally two forms of it. The energy of motion (kinetic energy) is one; the “ability to do work”, i.e., create motion (potential energy) is the other. Motion is a property of matter; potential energy describes the relationship between bits and pieces of matter. The cosmic microwave background is basically a “photon gas” that fills the universe. I.e., a form of matter. This photon gas once interacted with other forms of matter, mostly ionized hydrogen gas and free electrons that filled the early universe. As the universe expanded and cooled, that ionized gas and the free electrons recombined into neutral atoms, forming a gas that is transparent to electromagnetic radiation. Which is to say, the “photon gas” and the (mostly) hydrogen gas that filled the universe were no longer interacting with each other. We can describe this process using our mathematics, and predict the result, in very specific ways as a matter of fact. And then we can compare these results against observation. Here’s a plot from earlier work by yours truly, showing one of the predictions (the so-called angular power spectrum of the CMB) against data from the Planck satellite. The calculation behind this plot involves modeling the various forms of matter (namely, the expanding mostly hydrogen gas, as well as the photon gas) along with their motion and interactions, i.e., energy. But no, not some “balance”; such a thing does not exist. Energy is not balancing matter, it is a property of matter, characterizing its motion and its interactions. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Without the Higgs field, can virtual photons still have mass?
Answer: One of the most prevailing misunderstandings about the Higgs, no doubt inspired in part by that despicable title, “The God Particle”, of Leon Lederman’s book, is that the Higgs is why things have mass. No. It is due to the Higgs mechanism that certain particles have nonzero rest mass. These particles include charged fermions, and also the massive vector bosons. But rest mass exists, Higgs or no Higgs. The neutrino rest mass has (as far as we know) nothing to do with the Higgs mechanism. The rest mass of the Higgs boson itself has nothing to do with the Higgs mechanism per se. And more importantly, mass-energy exists, Higgs or no Higgs. Roughly 99% of the masses of protons and neutrons, of the mass of ordinary matter, is not due to the Higgs mechanism. And yes, virtual particles — which, I stress, are called virtual because they do not exist, because they are mathematical conveniences when it comes to enumerating terms in the series expansion of an integral over all possible values of 4-momentum — would still cover the range of all possible values of mass-energy between negative and positive infinity. Question: Could gravitational redshift account for all cosmological redshift? If it includes all the matter inside the sphere between source and observer (radius)?
Answer: No, quite the contrary: most of the observed redshift of distant galaxies is due to the velocity-related Doppler effect related to expansion (i.e., the distance between those galaxies and the Milky Way increases over time, which is to say that they are receding from the Milky Way, or the Milky Way, from them.) It’s only in the case of very distant objects, billions of light years from here, that gravitational redshift begins to dominate over recession velocity. But no, it has nothing to do with matter inside the sphere. Rather, it’s due to the fact that light from these very distant objects was emitted when the universe was substantially more dense on average than today, and that means a stronger average gravitational field, which means gravitational time dilation compared to clocks today. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why can’t there be massless electron neutrinos?
Answer: Actually, unless there have been recent developments that I am not aware of, a massless neutrino species cannot be excluded. But it won’t be the electron, the muon, or the tau neutrino. Neutrinos come in three flavors, yes. But their “mass eigenstates” and “flavor eigenstates” do not coincide. Observed neutrino masses are determined by a matrix quantity, the PMNS (Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata) matrix, which effectively mixes up neutrino masses and flavors. In actuality, it means that if an experiment fixes the neutrino’s flavor, its mass remains indeterminate; conversely, if an experiment fixes the neutrino’s mass, its flavor becomes uncertain. This is the actual mechanism behind the observed solar neutrino oscillations that, in turn, led to the realization that the massless neutrinos of the Standard Model of particle physics just don’t cut it; that the model must be extended to allow neutrinos to have mass. However, neither the theory nor existing observational constraints exclude the possibility that one of the three neutrino mass eigenstates is, in fact, massless! Now as I said, it won’t be the electron neutrino (that would be a flavor eigenstate, not a mass eigenstate) but it would, by definition, still be the lightest of three mass eigenstates (since the other two would be massive). So yes, it is conceivable that a massless neutrino species exists. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why is weak equivalence principal not enough to describe gravity in relativity? What was the motivation behind extending WEP to EEP? And then How does EEP force us to reject gravity as a force on flat background of (special relativistic) space-time?
Answer: Well, actually, some would argue that the Einstein equivalence principle effectively follows from the weak equivalence principle. Or to turn it around, maybe I am wrong but I don't think anyone ever successfully proposed a theory that obeys the weak equivalence principle but not the Einstein equivalence principle. Not that it matters that much anyway. These principles serve merely as guides, as inspiration when it comes to constructing the theory. The actual theory is stated in the form of an action integral or maybe a set of field equations. We don't test inspirations; we test quantifiable predictions. And no, neither of these equivalence principles compels you to accept the geometric interpretation of gravitation, but there is a big caveat here. Consistently with the conceptual meaning of both equivalence principles, the tensor field of gravitation couples to matter "minimally and universally": That is to say, the stress-energy-momentum tensor of matter is obtained as the variation of the matter action with respect to the gravitational field tensor. In practice, it means that the gravitational field tensor defines observable infinitesimal spacetime intervals and four-dimensional volume elements. In effect, it distorts the observable quantities of Minkowski spacetime. Hence the interpretation of gravitation as geometry. Even so, Einstein himself advised against reading too much into the geometric interpretation, which he (in his own writing) described as a mental aid, not necessarily physical (geometric) reality. And indeed, when we venture into the fields of modified gravity, extensions of general relativity, or various directions towards a quantum theory of gravitation, a dogmatic geometric interpretation is not helpful. By way of example, Feynman, in his delightful Lectures on Gravitation, demonstrates how imaginary scientists from Venus, familiar with (quantum and classical) field theory but not with gravitation, would deduce the proper theory, without resorting to any geometric interpretation. Question: If Poisson's equation is nothing other than Einstein's field equation in the classical limit, why don't Newtonian fields interact with each other even linearly?
Answer: Poisson’s equation is the Newtonian limit of general relativity. What that means is that the equation includes terms to first order in ( v / c ) 2 , but discards smaller, higher-order terms. What’s so special about ( v / c ) 2 for a theory of gravitation? Well, remember the velocity formula for circular orbits, v = √ G M / r ? Let’s square it: v 2 = G M / r ; let’s divide it by c 2 , and we have ( v / c ) 2 = G M / c 2 r . Now G M / c 2 r is just a dimensionless (as in, no units of measurement attached) characterization of the Newtonian gravitational potential. The Newtonian gravitational field interacting with itself is the first non-linear, second-order contribution to gravitation. The magnitude of this interaction, the field interacting with itself, would be governed by ( G M / c 2 r ) 2 = [ ( v / c ) 2 ] 2 . These terms are too small to be included in the Newtonian approximation. How small? Well, calculate G M / c 2 r for the Earth’s surface. It’s roughly 7 × 10 − 10 . Its square is absolutely tiny, less than 5 × 10 − 19 . That’s why such small corrections are not important at the Newtonian level. Going beyond the Newtonian approximation, however, the small terms show up. The nonlinearity of gravitation, this exact term that we were just looking at, is what is responsible for the anomalous precession of Mercury’s orbit, to the tune of about 43 seconds of arc per century. And a similarly small term due to spatial curvature becomes significant for things moving at or near the speed of light, which is why the Einsteinian prediction of the deflection of light near a gravitating body is twice the Newtonian prediction. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What, if anything, is special about a 3 + 1 dimensional space time that makes it ideal for describing something like physics?
Answer: Well, we use 3+1 dimensional spacetime to describe physics, because physics is the science of stuff in our universe, and our universe appears to be 3+1 dimensional (excluding theories like Kaluza-Klein, string theory, or other offshoots in which additional dimensions exist.) But what makes 3+1 dimensions really special? Curiously, I think there is a reason. Let’s start with space. One-dimensional space is rather boring; it’s just the number line. No structures there. Two dimensional space: that’s the plane. It is possible to create reasonably complicated things in two dimensions, but there are severe limits. All it takes is to have three houses and three utilities: you just cannot hook up all three houses to the three utilities without intersecting connections. Ouch! Oh, and forget animals with an internal pass-through digestion system. You create an animal with a passage from its mouth to… you know, the other end, and in a two-dimensional world, the poor creature falls apart into two disconnected parts. So we pretty much need three dimensions as our playground. In three dimensions, we can connect complex graphs, have complex creatures with multiple networks of piping inside their bodies, we can even tie knots that can hold things securely. So why not four spatial dimensions, then? Surely that’s better? Well… maybe not. Remember knots? They don’t exist in four dimensions. You can always lift the string out in the fourth direction and eliminate the knot without untying it. Pipes won’t hold their content either. So maybe, just maybe, four spatial dimensions is too much of a good thing. We are stuck with three. OK, how about time? Well, obviously we need at least one time dimension in order for there to be change. But what if we had two time dimensions? Not exactly a good thing. Why? Because a world with two (or more) time dimensions will be acausal. Effects may precede causes and all that. So that really settles it: we are stuck with 3+1 dimensions if we want a causal universe that has enough spatial dimensions for complexity, but not too many spatial dimensions that would destroy complexity. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there an equation that allows us to know the weak force that a particle experiences?
Answer: Certainly. The full set of equations is rather complex, as the weak force does not exist in isolation and it is described, together with electromagnetism by a non-Abelian quantum field theory (i.e., the electroweak theory), but a simplified, “classical” version can inform us about the basic characteristics of the force. The weak force is characterized by the potential V ( r ) = − g 2 e − μ r / r where r is the distance from the source, g is the weak force coupling constant and μ characterizes its range. The corresponding radial force, then, is given by F ( r ) ∝ g 2 1 + μ r r 2 e − μ r . The range of the weak force is characterized (very roughly) by μ − 1 = 2.5 × 10 − 18  m , whereas the coupling constant is of O ( 10 − 6 ) . The reason why these values are only approximate is that the weak force comes in different flavors (mediated by both charged and neutral particles), not to mention that the coupling constant (really, coupling parameter) runs with energy (i.e., it’s not really constant) but this equation nonetheless conveys the basic idea. This equation is an example of a so-called Yukawa force, named after Hideki Yukawa, the Japanese physicist who first postulated such a force back in 1935 as a means to explain what holds protons and neutrons together in an atom. (He was not wrong in that that force also behaves effectively as a Yukawa force, but it is not to be confused with the weak force.) Its defining characteristics are that at short distances, it’s like the Coulomb force; but at large distances, it vanishes. For consider, if the distances are really short, μ r ≪ 1 , and the force is now simply proportional to g 2 / r 2 , i.e., it’s an inverse-square force like the electrostatic or gravitational force. But if μ r ≫ 1 , the exponential term becomes extremely small very rapidly, and the force disappears. This is why we say that the weak force has finite range. A Yukawa potential and the corresponding force can be obtained, in classical physics, from a modified version of Maxwell’s theory, in which the electromagnetic field has a mass parameter. This theory is called Maxwell-Proca (or sometimes just Proca) theory, named after the Romanian physicist Alexandru Proca who first proposed it, also back in the mid-1930s. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Viktor T. Toth said that life on Earth is made possible by the low enthropy energy we receive from the Sun. What is meant by “low enthropy energy” and in what sense is it necessary for creating and maintaining life on Earth?
Answer: As per the second law of thermodynamics, entropy cannot decrease in a closed system. Entropy is a measure of disorder: A disordered system will not spontaneously become ordered. The more disordered a system is, the higher its entropy. Life, ultimately, is about disordered raw materials combining to form complex, highly ordered structures. This represents a significant decrease in entropy. That decrease in entropy must be balanced, in turn, by an increase in entropy somewhere else, and the two systems must be connected. That somewhere else is the Sun. The Earth receives, from the Sun, energy mostly in the form of visible light, photons at (roughly) 6000 K (degrees kelvin). In turn, the Earth radiates into deep space energy mostly in the form of thermal infrared, photons at (roughly) 300 K. That means that for each incoming photon from the Sun, the Earth radiates about 20 photons into deep space. (The two must be in balance otherwise the Earth would boil or freeze, due to excess thermal energy or a deficit in thermal energy.) It goes without saying that 20 photons can represent a lot more disorder, a lot more randomness than 1 photon. In other words, the energy that the Earth receives from the Sun has a lot less entropy than the thermal “waste heat” that the Earth radiates into deep space. Some of the incoming solar energy is captured by living things, either directly (plants) or indirectly (e.g., humans eating a potato). This represents a low entropy source, allowing those living systems to become organized, create complexity, and radiate away excess energy in the form of higher entropy waste heat. But it need not be even about living things. Just imagine a simple machine that uses the heat from the Sun to boil water, which then drives a piston, which does useful work through a mechanism (e.g., a crane, lifting bricks to build a house, turning disorder into order). The used up steam, released from the piston, is allowed to recondense, its waste heat radiated into the sky (deep space), the water ready to be reused in the next cycle. If there was no “high entropy sink” (the sky), we could not recondense the water and the machine would eventually stop when its water reservoir is emptied. The biological cycle may be a tad more sophisticated than a simple solar steam engine driving a crane, but the thermodynamic principles are exactly the same. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can you explain the calculation for determining the time it takes for an object to fall into a black hole while traveling at the speed of light?
Answer: First of all, you have to disabuse yourself of the notion that an object is traveling at a speed of… whatever. Speed is not an inherent property. The theory of relativity is called relativity for a reason: Speed is always relative. It is a relationship between two reference frames. So let us look at an hapless traveler falling into a black hole. What is that traveler’s speed? Well, as I just said, it is meaningless to speak of that traveler’s speed as an inherent property. The traveler’s speed depends on who is looking. OK, so we are looking. From some safe position outside the black hole’s event horizon. What do we see? Why, we see the traveler approach the place where the horizon will presumably form. Except that, the closer he gets to that place, the slower he appears to us, due to extreme gravitational time dilation. In fact, we literally (and I mean literally, not some figure-of-speech) never get to see the traveler actually reach the horizon. That moment — indeed, the moment when the horizon forms in the first place — remains for us forever in the future, due to extreme, runaway gravitational time dilation. And this is where we have a paradoxical situation. We know that the traveler reaches the vacuum speed of light at the horizon; that’s how black holes work. But from our perspective, the traveler’s speed actually drops to zero because of extreme gravitational time dilation! Well, guess what: in our reference frame, the speed of anything, including light itself, drops to zero at the horizon. Except that “the horizon” is not a place here and now, but a moment in time in our infinite future: Which is to say, we will see things slow down, slow down exponentially, but the moment when the horizon forms, the moment when all those speeds reach zero in our reference frame, will forever remain in our future. In fact, in our reference frame there is no meaningful way to describe the horizon or what’s “inside”. That’s why the darn thing is actually called a “horizon”! OK, what about the traveler’s perspective, then? Well, apart from increasing tides, he’d experience nothing special if he’s not looking out through the portholes of his spaceship. If the black hole is very, very large, tidal forces won’t be excessive even as he approaches, and crosses, the horizon. But he is doomed: he is now in a mini-universe that is collapsing around him, with no means of escape unless he has a time machine, because for him, the horizon has now become a moment of time in the past, and the only way to escape, to cross the horizon backwards, is by traveling into the past. In due course his mini-universe collapses and the world ends. The calculations are not elementary but not particularly hard either. The key equation is the so-called geodesic equation that describes freefalling trajectories. To model things from the traveler’s perspective, we need a coordinate system that covers both the interior and the exterior of the event horizon; one such coordinate system is called Kruskal—Szekeres coordinates. Whatever coordinate system we pick, we can calculate the “proper time”, i.e., the amount of time the traveler would measure, to reach the event horizon of the black hole and to reach the singularity (i.e., the “end of the world” for the mini-universe enclosed by the horizon.) Lastly, I hasten to add that this is classical relativity. Once we introduce quantum physics, things change, since black holes evaporate in finite time, so the traveler may never experience the horizon in the first place. But that’s a different story. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: I always read Victor Toth that the singularity is a moment in the future, not a point in place. What will happen to an observer falling into a black hole as he sees it for himself? Will he be crushed?
Answer: To observers outside the event horizon of a black hole, never mind the singularity, the event horizon itself remains forever in the future, hidden from view by infinite time dilation. The way to think about it… imagine particles collapsing toward each other, accelerated by their mutual gravity. If no force pushes them back, eventually they would form a black hole. But when? Now imagine that these are not ordinary particles, but each and every one of them is a miniature spaceship equipped with a very powerful rocket. And suppose that each of these particles has a mind of its own. As they fall toward each other, perhaps one of the particles changes its mind at the last minute, last second, last picosecond, turns on its rocket and escapes. The point is, to you, the outside observer that last minute, last second, last picosecond might be the next day, the next year, the next five hundred trillion years. No matter how far into the future you go, you can never exclude the possibility that one of the infalling particles re-emerges, because in your reference frame, the event horizon has not yet formed! But you are asking what would happen to an infalling observer. Take one of those particles that is falling into the black hole. Let’s call this particle the observer. What would it see? Well, for starters, it’s surrounded by other particles, and above it, perhaps it still sees a clear view of space, with the distant stars. But the closer it gets to where the event horizon will form, the less sky it sees, because light from neighboring particles, even when it sets off in an almost vertical direction, would curve back down. The view “up” would become an ever narrower “tunnel”, until the tunnel disappears altogether, and the observer is just surrounded by other particles in all directions above and below. This happens at the moment the observer crosses the event horizon. When we look at the spacetime that this observer now finds itself in, it is actually much like the spacetime of cosmology: filled with matter (infalling particles) everywhere. From the observer’s viewpoint it will not be homogeneous (same everywhere) or isotropic (same in all directions) but that’s because the observer itself moves relative to the bulk of other particles. If the observer were to changes its trajectory, it might find itself in a homogeneous, isotropic, and collapsing mini-universe. Even without the trajectory change, it’s still a collapsing mini-universe, just not homogeneous and isotropic from the observer’s perspective. And the observer is doomed. This mini-universe only has a finite lifetime. It collapses, its density and temperature increasing beyond limit. The asymptotic final state is the singularity: a future, terminal moment in time that is not actually even part of this mini-universe. The existence of this mini-universe ends at that moment (it is “geodesically incomplete”). At least this is the case if the mini-universe has no net rotation. If it rotates, things get weirder and perhaps the observer might even avoid a terminal moment. We don’t really know: There have been several attempts to describe the interior of a rotating black hole solution, but no good solutions have been found, as far as I know. Anyhow, the important thing to remember is that relativity is about what different observers see. The singularity may be an unavoidable destiny for an infalling observer who has only a very short amount of time left, but to an observer outside the event horizon, it remains forever in the future. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Which one is more dangerous, antimatter or black holes?
Answer: Dangerous in what sense? I mean, look. Water is dangerous. You fall off a bridge into an icy river, you die. You fall off a ship in the middle of the ocean, you die. Oxygen is dangerous. It corrodes just about anything and everything, in some cases rather explosively. One careless act inside a wood frame house and you die a horrible, fiery death. Cats are dangerous. These cuddly little guys can give you scratches, can bite you, cause a wound to be infected, and if you’re not careful, you might even die. They can also carry rabies. Antimatter? Take a banana. It is slightly radioactive because it contains the naturally occurring radioactive isotope, potassium-40. These atoms decay, and rarely, maybe once in 100,000 decaying atoms, the decay produces a positron: the antimatter partner of the electron. Now, do you feel that you are in any danger in the presence of a banana because it emits a steady stream of antimatter particles? And then, black holes. Well… the nearest known black hole is a tad over 1500 light years away. That’s close to 300,000 times the distance from the Earth to the Sun. That particular black hole not particularly large insofar as black holes are concerned, only about 10 times the mass of the Sun. Dangerous? Well, let’s say you approach the Sun to within a distance of 1 million kilometers. Guess what… you’ll be fried to a crisp. At that distance, you’ll be exposed to 30 megawatts of thermal energy per square meter. For comparison, your kitchen oven uses a few kilowatts, no more. So it’s like being surrounded by several thousand kitchen ovens, all turned up to the maximum, dumping all that heat on you. I daresay that qualifies as dangerous, perhaps extremely so. In contrast… say, you approach a quiescent black hole of 10 solar masses within a distance of 1 million kilometers. What will you see? Nothing, really. Assuming your spaceship or spacesuit are functioning well, you’ll be happily floating in empty space, and as for the black hole, even if you knew where to look and had a decent telescope, it’d only appear as a very mild distortion of the starfield behind it. We can, of course, look at things from a statistical perspective. According to some US statistics (though I suspect other countries’ statistics would appear quite similar) poisoning is by far the greatest danger, causing some 45% of accidental deaths in 2022. Falls are next (20%) followed by motor vehicle accidents (also 20%), suffocation (3%), other injuries (2%), drowning (2% — see? I told you water is dangerous!), fire (1% — darn that oxygen) and then other, more minor causes. What I don’t see on this list is antimatter or black holes, neither of which, to the best of my knowledge, ever caused any harm to a human, one (antimatter) on account of its rarity, the other (black holes), on account of its distance and, well, benign nature compared to a hot, burning star for instance. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can you explain the difference between "dark matter" and "dark energy"? What is the proportion of each in our universe?
Answer: Certainly. It has to do with pressure. Cosmologists are simple-minded folks. They realized that on the largest of scales, the universe is rather uniform: it is more or less, on average, the same everywhere and it has no preferred direction. Which means, among other things, that its content can be modeled as an “isotropic perfect fluid”: a medium that has no shear, no viscosity, only density and pressure, and its pressure is independent of direction. But how much pressure? Well, for something this simple, there’s a rather simplistic mathematical representation: the “equation of state”, w = p / ρ . Here, p is the pressure and ρ is the energy density. (Remember, energy is just mass times speed-of-light squared, so energy density vs. mass density really are the same thing.) The beauty of this expression is that p and ρ are measured using the same units. How come, you may wonder? Well… pressure is force divided by area. Energy is force times distance; and volume is area times length (i.e., distance). So energy density would be (force times distance) divided by (area times distance), which is force divided by area… same as pressure. Therefore, the ratio w of these two is just a pure number, a “dimensionless” quantity. But what is it? Well… what if there is no pressure? That would be w = 0. Cosmologists call this “dust”. (Did I mention they’re simple-minded?) As it turns out, most ordinary matter is well approximated as “dust”. Only immensely hot matter, in which particles zip about at relativistic speeds, will have a value that substantially differs from zero. How substantially? In the extreme limit of an “ultrarelativistic gas”, w = 1 / 3. But the equations actually allow more extreme values, values outside the range between 0 and 1/3. In fact, we can have w = 1. Beyond that, w > 1 will not work as it implies a medium in which sound travels faster than the vacuum speed of light! But anything below 1 is okay. In fact, w can be negative! Yes, negative pressure. (Think about it: when particles of a gas repel each other, we have positive pressure. So if they were to attract each other, “clump”, that would be negative pressure.) As a matter of fact, any value w ≥ − 1 will do. (Stuff with w < − 1 would yield an unstable universe.) OK, one more piece to the puzzle: as the universe expands, the energy density of this stuff changes. But the energy density also involves the energy of interactions between particles of this stuff. For this reason, only the energy density of “dust” will change as the inverse of volume. In fact, at one extreme of the scale, at w = − 1 , the energy density of this stuff remains constant even as the universe expands! This is important, as you shall see in a moment. So then… our postulate is that the universe consists of such an isotropic perfect fluid, or perhaps a mix of isotropic perfect fluids. But what kind? How much? Well… we look at observation. The age of the universe. The statistical distribution of matter. Minute fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background. Distant supernovas. Long story short, we find that the universe “works” if it consists of roughly 30% “dust” and 70% of stuff with w = − 1 , together making up 100% of the so-called “critical density”, which is needed for a universe in which the geometry of space is Euclidean on average. The problem is that the actual stuff that we see: Stars, gas, dust (actual dust, not “dust”), etc., amounts to only about 4%. The remaining 96% has to be something else. We call the missing 26% of “dust” “dark matter”; and the missing 70% of stuff with w = − 1 “dark energy”. There is a lot of speculation as to what this “dark matter” and this “dark energy” are. But we don’t know. So far, experiments designed to detect these mediums directly all came up empty. We infer their existence from gravity and cosmological observations; we have not seen either. However, what we do know if our hypotheses are correct is that as the universe ages and expands, “dust” gets diluted; stuff with w = − 1 does not. So over time, “dark energy” dominates. In fact, it already does, which means that (due to its negative pressure) it is already accelerating the rate at which the universe expands. So there. That’s what dark matter and dark energy are, and this is pretty much all that we actually know about them. There’s plenty of speculation, to be sure, but speculation, even informed speculation, is not knowledge. Oh, how nice. Quora again offered some Stable Diffusion illustrations to accompany my answer. I actually like this one, so there. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: How do you manually compute sin, cos, or tan of any number? Something like sin 10, tan 13, cos 45.092?
Answer: First of all, I would restrict myself to positive angles less than 45 degrees. For other angles, I’d use trigonometric identities. Next, I’d convert angles to radians. This is important. To a reasonable approximation, it amounts to dividing angles (expressed in degrees) by 57.3. This means that the largest angle in radians that I’ll be dealing with will be π / 4 or about 0.785, so well below 1. Now I can use the Taylor series for the sine: sin x ≃ x − x 3 / 6... OK, let’s give it a try. Suppose you are asking me to compute the sine of 70 degrees. But 70 is greater than 45, so I’ll be computing the sine of 20 degrees instead, which is the cosine of 70 degrees. Converting to radians by dividing with 57.3, I get 0.349. To three decimals, 0.349 − 0.349 3 / 6 will be 0.342. Since this is the cosine of 70 degrees, I can calculate the sine by taking the square root of 1 − 0.342 2 = 0.883. There are ways of calculating the square root similar to long division, so it can be done on paper… or just use trial and error. The result is 0.940. So let’s double-check with a calculator: I get 0.93969262. Bingo! Mind you, this is not a very efficient thing to do, especially if you need a lot of trigonometry. You might be better off using a slide rule or a table of trig functions. Which were the common methods used by engineers before the advent of electronic calculators back in the 1970s*. Indeed, if you were to find yourself in a post-apocalyptic wasteland with all electronics dead and rotting away, and you are tasked with rebuilding civilization one calculation at a time, you might do yourself a favor pre-calculating sines and cosines (and exponentials and logarithms and square roots and the like) and create a set of nice tables for later use. *Or later. I sometimes calculated trig functions using this approach on the four-function calculator that was a gift from my grandmother 50 years ago. OK, it had square root and a built-in value of π , so that made things a tad more efficient. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How come vectors can have more than 3 elements? Shouldn't it only have 3 elements in Continuum Mechanics since it is a rank 1 tensor meaning it has 3 elements?
Answer: I suspect that there is a deeper misunderstanding behind this question than the words reveal, and I sympathize. Back in my student days, I harbored similar misunderstandings that proved to be tough obstacles to overcome as I was trying to make sense of vectors, tensors and matrices. For what is a vector? As a good, mathematically gifted student I learned it early enough; It is either a pair or a triplet of numbers, a set of coordinates, really, usually written down in column form. So far, so good. What I knew worked just fine: I was able to do things like adding and subtracting vectors, calculating inner products and cross products, doing the usual things a high school student might be doing with vectors. I also knew about matrices. But apart from matrices specifically constructed to represent transformations, they had little to do with vectors. But then, I learned about tensors. Or rather, I was trying to. It's been pressed upon me that a tensor is different from a matrix. A matrix can be used to represent tensors, but the tensor's existence is not predicated on this representation. In fact, the same tensor can be represented differently using different coordinate systems. Now it took a while for this to sink in. Longer than I care to admit. Because eventually I had to discover something important: that the same thing is true for vectors and their representations as doublets or triplets of numbers! Unfortunately, we use the same word for both, so the distinction was not clear; whereas in the case of tensors, the words (tensor vs. matrix) differ, which was helpful. So if a vector is not a doublet or triplet of numbers, then what it? Why, it is an arrow, maybe: an arrow with a direction and a length. We can draw arrows without ever representing them as doublets or triplets of numbers. We can use geometry to find the arrow that is a sum of two arrows. Okay, so finally it was becoming (somewhat) clear: vectors and tensors are geometry, columns of numbers (really, 2x1 or 3x1 matrices) or matrices are their representations. But... I realized that I was still confused, because... Well, what about higher dimensions? Why, that's kind of easy: I can "imagine" arrows in four, five, or seventy-seven dimensions, and it makes sense that the corresponding representation would be a column of four, five or seventy-seven numbers. But it was still not good enough. For starters, I kept reading nonsense that, say, matrices form a "vector space". Say what? And then there's all this stuff in physics textbook about the "phase space" characterizing a system. And sometimes it has a lot of dimensions! What the... Back to the drawing board, I guess. And back I went, reading a bit more about abstract algebra. And that is when things finally became clear. What are the most general properties of vectors, really? Well, we add two vectors, we get a vector. So that's one. Another one is that we can make a vector smaller or larger by multiplying it by a number, and the result is still a vector. Hmmm. These are fundamental properties. In fact, a set with elements that can 1) be added together to form another element of the set, and 2) be multiplied by a real number to form another element of the set is a vector space. Anything that has these properties is a vector space. Numbers form a vector space. Columns of two numbers, columns of three (or four, or five, or seventy-seven) numbers form a vector space. Matrices? Well, I add to matrices together, I get a matrix. I multiply a matrix by a number, I get a matrix. Sure sounds like a vector space! And of course arrows form a vector space. Now I was getting somewhere! This abstract definition of a vector space seems to encompass everything we need to know about vector spaces! So confusingly, we call tensors of rank-1 "vectors", but tensors of any rank actually form a vector space. Sometimes, language can be misleading! Back to classical mechanics. Let's start with the simplest: a point particle in space. Indeed, its position is well represented by a three-dimensional vector, which can be represented, in turn, by a column of three numbers, the three coordinates. But wait: simply knowing where a particle is does not tell us where the particle will go next. For that, we also need the particle's velocity! Velocities in three-dimensional space can also be represented by three-dimensional vectors. So to fully describe the dynamics of our particle, we actually need two such vectors, i.e., six numbers! But this six-dimensional thing nonetheless behaves like a vector: we can add two of them together, and we can scale them by a factor. So there: the state of the particle "lives" as a vector in an abstract six-dimensional space! Now take something rigid that's not a particle but larger. That something has a position but also an orientation. And when we describe its motion, we need to know not only its velocity but also its rate of rotation. We are now up to 12 numbers, forming a vector space of 12 dimensions! Again, it is a vector space since position vectors, velocity vectors, rotation vectors, angular velocity vectors are all individually vector spaces, so when we lump them together, we get an entity that behaves like a vector. Perhaps you can see where this is taking us. Consider a system that's more complicated: say, it has several lose bits. Now we have even more "degrees of freedom". An in classical mechanics problems, each positional degree of freedom is accompanied by a corresponding velocity of some kind. Soon we have a lot of dimensions! Now, I stress, these multidimensional vectors are not arrows in space. they are not even columns of many numbers, though they can certainly be represented as such. They are abstract mathematical entities that satisfy the two criteria I outlined above: They can be added together and they can be scaled, and the result is a multidimensional vector of the same kind. As you mention, a vector really is a rank-1 tensor. But what, really, are tensors? Remember those inner products? We were taught in school that you form them by multiplying Cartesian vector components with each other and then summing the result. But this is not really the full picture. It's an oversimplification that is valid only in special cases. More generally, inner products are formed with the help of a rank-2 covariant tensor. If you want to think of it as a matrix product, think of that tensor as a matrix, and write the two vectors down, one as a row vector before the matrix, the other as a column vector after. Now multiply. If the matrix sandwiched between the two vectors is the identity matrix, the rules are the same as the inner product rules you learned in high school. But the matrix can be something else. (That matrix, or rather, the tensor it represents, will be the "metric".) So what do tensors do? Why, a rank-2 covariant tensor lets us form the inner products of two vectors. So a rank-3 tensor will help form an inner product of three vectors. And so on. Finally, tensors are making sense as well: they make a connection between vectors (which scale with a change of coordinates) and scalars (which don't care about coordinates) by basically compensating for any change of coordinates when the inner product is formed. So there, in a nutshell. Vectors as bunches of numbers as representations of vectors as arrows with lengths and directions, which really are a special case of things that can be added and scaled, which is the true definition of an abstract vector space; and the idea in classical mechanics that lumping together all positions and associated velocities for all the degrees of freedom of a system forms a vector, possibly with a large-ish number of dimensions. So what about continuous dynamics? That would be a system with an infinite number of degrees of freedom since, in principle, every bit of that system has its own position and velocity. True. But in this case, we can look at the equations that govern the system and realize soon enough that the properties of the system obey the same equations at all points. So no we have vector fields: the values change from position to position (or from abstract "position" to "position" in the phase space of classical mechanics) but the rules, the differential equations that govern them are the same. I know I didn't answer all questions. A short Quora answer is no substitute for a proper textbook. But I hope that at the very least, I offered enough to help make better sense of those textbooks. Question: Does a spinning (Kerr) black hole precess about its axis of rotation; if so, relative to what?
Answer: No, a Kerr black hole does not precess. It is, by definition, an axisymmetric solution of Einstein’s vacuum field equations and as such, no precession is involved. A Kerr black hole in the process of formation may exhibit precession, e.g., as a part of the famous “ringdown” phase of a black hole merger that has been observed by gravitational wave detectors over the course of the past decade. Precession is not relative to anything: acceleration, including acceleration related to rotation or more complex motion like precession, is absolute. Or you could say that acceleration (including rotation and precession) can be measured as deviations relative to a local inertial (non-accelerating) reference frame, but that is a bit tautological. Question: Can time exist without the Higgs field?
Answer: Rather than trying to answer the question directly (what does it even mean for time to “exist”?) allow me to respond instead by enumerating what exists in the Standard Model of particle physics courtesy of the Higgs field. Courtesy of the Higgs field, we have massive vector bosons. As a result, only one vector boson (the photon) “survives” as a mediator of a long-range interaction (electromagnetism); interactions due to the rest, collectively labeled the “weak force”, become extremely short range, playing only a relatively marginal role in nuclear physics. Courtesy of the Higgs field, we also have charged fermions with masses. In the Standard Model, charged leptons (like the electron) and quarks start their existence as massless particles. But because of their interactions with the Higgs field’s so-called vacuum expectation value, they behave as though they were particles with nonzero rest mass, which allows, among other things, for them to form structures, including protons, neutrons, and ultimately, atoms. So without the Higgs field, we’d have no periodic table, no atoms, no matter as we know it. But “time”? All this takes place on the stage of spacetime. Particle physics exists in spacetime, with or without a Higgs field. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there observational evidence confirming the slowdown phase of the universe billions of years ago, or are these only theoretical conclusions?
Answer: It is somewhat unclear* what this question is about, as I can think of at least two cases of “slowdown” in modern cosmology. First, the end of inflation. In the inflationary model, the very early cosmos underwent a period of exponential expansion. This speculative idea is supposed to solve several issues with cosmology, including the “flatness problem”, i.e., why the universe is so uniform even today: Characterized by no or negligible spatial curvature and a uniform average mass density. If the “visible universe” really represents just a tiny, tiny part of the pre-inflationary universe, the problem would be solved. Or not… none other than one of the “founding fathers” of inflationary cosmology, Paul Steinhardt, expressed serious concerns that while inflation solves some problems, the price we pay is that it introduces problems more severe than the ones it addresses. In any case, we have no direct evidence of inflation or how it may have come to an end. It is, at present, an entirely theoretical and speculative idea. Second, perhaps the question referred to the “dark ages”, the period of time between the moment when the universe beame transparent (the so-called surface of last scattering, when the cosmic microwave background radiation was born) and the moment when the first stars began to appear (reionization). The problem is that some of the structures that emerged in the early universe are much too large and emerged much too quickly to make sense. So what if, in fact, during these “dark ages” the expansion of the universe experienced a slowdown, so the universe is actually older than we think it is, with more time available for early large structures to form? Makes a lot of sense, but this, too, is a highly speculative concept with no observational support. It is hard to study the early history of the cosmos. We do not see “behind” the cosmic microwave background and we also have no direct observational evidence of the “dark ages”, as there were no sources of light during this time. *I’ve since been enlightened that the question was originally intended to be about the first 9 billion years, give or take, of the history of the universe during which the rate of expansion was slowing down, as opposed to the last roughly 5 billion years when it began accelerating due to dark energy. This is pretty much based on direct evidence, in particular the Type Ia supernova data that led to discovery of accelerating expansion and earned its discoverers a Nobel-prize in 2011. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What is the Higgs field explained simply?
Answer: The Higgs field is one of the fields of the Standard Model of particle physics. What do particles have to do with fields? Well, in a quantum field theory, “particles” are quantized excitations (units of energy) in a field. Take the electromagnetic field, for instance. Light is electromagnetic radiation. It is a wave: countless experiments demonstrate its wave-like properties. Yet when we let light interact with a sensor, we find that the energy-content of the electromagnetic field is transferred to the sensor one unit of energy, one “photon” at a time. (Confusingly, this is *not* what people are talking about when they discuss wave-particle duality.) So in this sense, the Higgs field is just like the electromagnetic field; the field of electrons; the fields associated with other charge leptons, quarks, neutrinos, vector bosons, gluons. Fields interact. E.g., the field of electrons can interact with the electromagnetic field: we experience this, e.g., when an excitation of the electron field, i.e., a charged electron, accelerates and this creates electromagnetic radiation. The Higgs field interacts with other fields, too.. But the Higgs field has one additional curious property. Usually, a field is at its lowest energy state when it has no excitations. The Higgs is different: Its lowest energy state is an excited state. It has a nonzero “vacuum expectation value”. What this implies, however, is that the vacuum (containing the Higgs field with no excitations) can decay into a new vacuum state, in which the Higgs field has some excitations, but the overall energy-content is lower. This has very serious implications, because in this new configuration, we now have other particles interacting with what appears to be the vacuum, which contains these Higgs excitations! The effect of this is that these other particles, which originally had no rest masses, now have potential energy by way of these interactions. And as we know, energy is mass. This is how several particles of the Standard Model become massive. And the reason why this is important is that by starting with originally massless particles, the Standard Model can be mathematically consistent (it can be “renormalized”) yet in the end, thanks to the Higgs field, it yields massive particles after all. As an important side note, I should mention that the Higgs has nothing to do with gravity (not directly; gravity is sourced by energy-content, but the Higgs coupling is not in any way special in this regard) and roughly 99% of the mass of ordinary matter has nothing to do with the Higgs mechanism (it is the energy-content due to the strong interaction binding energy.) Question: If a black hole never fully forms, does this mean matter is frozen, waiting to move towards the center? Does this make it possible that lower density solid matter fills its volume faster than the eh expands, given its a large black hole?
Answer: That’s not exactly the way it works. A black hole never appears to fully form, as viewed by outside observers. This is due to exponentially increasing time dilation: The amount of time required for infalling particles to reach the event horizon, for the event horizon itself to form, is infinite in the reference frame of any outside observer. So as viewed by the outside observer, infalling matter indeed appears frozen. Or rather, it doesn’t appear as anything, as the same time dilation also causes extreme redshift, rendering any signal from infalling matter essentially invisible after a while. Do not try to intuit it using concepts like “lower density solid matter” or stuff like that. This is relativity theory: what we describe here is not what happens to matter, but how that matter appears to different observers. If you were to fall into a black hole (a very large black hole, large enough so that tidal effects don’t kill you) from your perspective you would a) reach the event horizon in a finite amount of time, and b) nothing particularly special happens when you do; in fact, your immediate surroundings (e.g., the interior of your spaceship) will appear perfectly normal throughout. OK, well, something special does happen but for a different reason. Suppose you descend towards the black hole. Even though the black hole has no surface and its event horizon is yet to form, you’d still see the black hole beneath your feet as a circular shadow, with optically distorted light around it, coming from distant sources. As you approach the black hole, this shadow would curl up, eventually appearing like a wall surrounding you. When it fully closes at the top, that’s the moment you cross the event horizon. At this point, from your vantage point, you’ll appear to be in a collapsing universe. In a very short amount of time, this collapsing universe will crush you, along with everything else therein, as its existence ultimately ends at the final singularity (ignoring quantum physics here which may or may not alter this outcome, and also ignoring black holes that spin or have an electric charge.) Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Do gravitational waves experience redshift with expansion of the gravitational field, like photons in the EM field?
Answer: Indeed they do. But don't think of it as gravitational waves "experiencing" anything. Neither gravitationl waves, nor light "experience" anything as they travel in an expanding spacetime from a source to a detector. They do not exchange energy, momentum, or angular momentum with their environment. Nothing happens to them, as a matter of fact. However, as a distant observer, chances are that you are moving at high speed relative to the source of these waves. This will certainly produce a Doppler effect: Each subsequent crest of the wave will have to travel slightly longer to reach you, so the interval between them will increase. Moreover, the waves may originate in the distant past, when the universe was denser and the average gravitational potential was greater. That means significant gravitational time dilation: Clocks of the past were ticking slower than clocks of the present, so a wave emitted at a given frequency back then will appear to have a lower frequency today. It is this combination of expansion-related Doppler and gravitational time dilation that are together responsible for the observed cosmological redshift in an expanding universe. Question: If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism?
Answer: If dark matter exists, it is indeed presumed to be present everywhere, though its density is very low compared to terrestrial densities. However, I’d hesitate to call it a “part of”, e.g., organisms. By way of an example that is known to exist with certainty, right now there are countless neutrinos going through your body. Are they part of your body? Not really. Why? Because neutrinos are effectively non-interacting. To them, your body might as well not be there. And vice versa, for your body the presence of the neutrinos makes no difference. Neutrinos still interact with ordinary matter though, just very, very, very weakly. An awful lot of neutrinos would be needed to make a noticeable difference. Sure, if you happened to be situated near an exploding supernova, the neutrino flux might be enough to evaporate you in an instant, but for that, the explosion of an entire giant star would be required, fairly close to you. In contrast, the millions, billions, trillions of neutrinos that pass through your body right this moment make no difference whatsoever. They are not part of you. The presumed dark matter of cosmology interacts even less with ordinary matter. So even if it is present right here, right now, it is not part of you, of animals, plants, or the Earth. It happens to be in the same place in space at the same time, but it might as well be in another galaxy far, far away: There is no interaction, no connection between that dark matter medium and your body. So no, whether or not dark matter exists remains to be seen, but it is definitely not part of the human body. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: If the constant G has an uncertainty of about 10^-15 m3 kg-1 s-2 why is the terrestrial GM product known to an accuracy of 10 digits m3 s-2?
Answer: Be careful not to put the cart before the horse. The “standard gravitational parameter”, G M , of a celestial body can be directly measured. If you observe the orbit of a satellite around the Earth, or the orbit of a planet around the Sun, you get an extremely precise value of G M . For instance, for the Sun, the value of G M is known to better than 11 significant digits! However, just because we know G M does not mean we know either G or M . And this is the root of the problem. We cannot just take the Earth and put it on a scale, measuring its mass. Nor can we do the same with the Sun. We can measure smaller masses directly, but smaller masses have very weak gravity, and in that cause, the gravitational force itself is so weak, any measurement of G M will necessarily be imprecise. So we either measure G M precisely but only guess M ; or we can measure M accurately, but G M very crudely. Either way, we can only infer G = G M / M , because there is no way to measure G directly. Which is why, insofar as G is concerned, four decimals is pretty much the best that we can do at present. And yes, this means that we only know the masses of celestial bodies like the Sun, the Earth, the planets do this accuracy, even though we know their standard gravitational parameters, the respective values of the product G M , very precisely. Question: If all of the mass energy of colliding black holes is contained within their event horizons, how does the collision release any energy? Stuff can escape from the event horizon if it collides with another?
Answer: But all the mass-energy of colliding black holes is not contained within their event horizons. You forgot about gravitational potential energy between the two black holes. Gravitational potential energy is zero when the black holes are very far apart, not interacting. As they get closer, that gravitational potential energy, which is negative (!), increases in magnitude. Since energy is conserved, this increase in negative potential energy must be accompanied by a corresponding increase in something positive. In this case, that something positive is the kinetic energy of the black holes accelerating towards each other. Now if the black holes were to collide head-on, this would be the end of the story: after the collision, the merged black hole would absorb all that kinetic energy. The total mass-energy of the system would be the same as before the collision: the sum of the masses of the progenitor black holes. But if the black holes approach each other off-center, they don’t collide right away. Rather, they will enter inspiraling orbits. This will produce gravitational radiation. The energy of that gravitational radiation will come at the expense of the kinetic energies of the inspiraling black holes. Now you’d think that would slow them down but orbital mechanics is tricky: as they lose energy, they enter into an ever tighter orbit, actually speeding up! This runaway process results in a gradual increase of the rate at which gravitational radiation is produced, reaching a final crescendo as the black holes get close enough to merge. Once the merger begins, the process rapidly comes to an end: a short “ringdown” phase occurs and the merger is complete. But in the meantime, a substantial amount of that gravitational potential energy, turned kinetic energy, is released as gravitational radiation and never becomes part of the mass-energy of the merged black hole. And in case you are wondering about actual, physical black holes that never quite reach the stage (as seen by us, outside observers) of forming actual event horizons, that makes no difference: though the respective event horizons remain forever in our future, the “asymptotic” behavior of the black holes is observationally indistinguishable from that hypothetical end state. Long story short: gravitational potential energy turns into kinetic energy that — in case of an off-center approach — turns into gravitational radiation before the merger is complete. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter?
Answer: Very simple: Direct detection. The existence of dark matter is widely assumed, as we observe gravitational behavior that cannot be explained otherwise within the context of general relativity: the same general relativity that, on other scales (e.g., within the solar system) works with spectacular precision. Now of course just because something works on a size scale measured by light-hours at most does not mean that it will necessarily work equally well on a size scale measured in the thousands or tens of thousands of light-years or more. Which means that there may not be dark matter at all: perhaps the laws of gravitation must be modified! But that proves to be an immensely tricky thing to do, because most modifications run into other observational constraints. Gravitational radiation, arrival times of gravitational and non-gravitational signals from the same event, cosmological observations… the bar is set very high for such modified theories of gravity. But until we have direct confirmation of dark matter, we won’t know for sure. And so far, all we have are null results: None of the attempts to search for dark matter by nongravitational means proved successful. So the jury is still out.
